statusMeaning.cross-checked: Copied automatically from the outcome's official page, and the Ministry's CSV file has the same words in the same order (ignoring punctuation and spacing; the CSV shortens some long statements, and then its words must match the start). Not yet checked by a person.

csvMeaning.match: The CSV has the same words.
csvMeaning.prefix: The CSV has the same words up to where it stops; it shortens long statements.
csvMeaning.mismatch: The CSV words the statement differently (see the outcome's notes).
csvMeaning.missing: The curriculum has a CSV file, but this code is not in it or has no wording there.
csvMeaning.no-file: The Ministry has no English CSV file for this curriculum.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the need for accounting in business.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 1: Introduction to Accounting (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Recognize and use the language of accounting (e.g., assets, liabilities, debits, credits).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify accounting related career opportunities (e.g., bookkeeping, general office work, clerk, payroll, receivables, payables).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Define financial accounting, cost accounting and management accounting.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Recognize forms of business ownership including sole proprietorship, corporation, franchise, partnership, and a cooperative model.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss how different forms of business ownership have led to the need for different accounting practices.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: List and classify types of business enterprises (e.g., resources, manufacturing, merchandising and service) within local community, Saskatchewan, Canada and globally.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss how different types of business enterprises (e.g., resources, manufacturing, merchandising and service) require different accounting practices.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify the role/purpose of accounting from the perspective of a manufacturer, producer, wholesaler, retailer, consumer and citizen in the business world.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Discuss how accountants’ training and practices will vary according to the type of employer (e.g., manufacturer, producer, retailer) and job description.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Examine the inquiry question: Why is accounting important?

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Label the steps of the accounting cycle (i.e., analyze originating transaction data, journalize, post, prepare worksheets, prepare financial statements, journalize and post adjusting and closing entries, prepare post-closing trial balance).

outcomes.statement: Explain the role of accounting standards.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 2: Identifying Accounting Standards (Core) · Suggested Time: 1-2 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Recognize that accounting handbooks exist to ensure accounting practices reflect current standards.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: List examples of accounting principles (e.g., Canadian Generally Accepted Accounting Principles [GAAPs]; business identity, going concern, accounting period cycle, objective evidence, unit of measurement, realization of revenue, matching expenses with revenue, historical cost, adequate disclosure, consistent reporting).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Relate accounting standards to examples found in the community (e.g., local business, First Nations governance authorities, not-for-profit organizations, public sector entities).

outcomes.statement: Analyze the relationship between assets, liabilities and owners’ equity within the accounting equation.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 3: Accounting Equation (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 1, 2

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define assets, liabilities and owners’ equity (capital).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Classify and sort examples of assets, liabilities and owners’ equity.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain the accounting equation relationship (i.e., a = l + oe).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Manipulate and solve problems using the accounting equation.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine how business transactions affect the accounting equation and apply to calculations.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Analyze the preservation of equality (e.g., increasing assets impacts liabilities and owners’ equity) within the accounting equation.

outcomes.statement: Utilize transactions and apply T-accounts in order to understand the concept of an account.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 4: T-accounts (Core) · Suggested Time: 10-12 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 3

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Relate the left and right of the T-account location to the accounting equation.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Label debit (left) and credit (right) as left and right of the T-account location.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify the location (l/r) of the elements (i.e., assets, liabilities, owners’ equity) of the accounting equation and how those elements correlate to the normal balance of an account.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Implement the use of normal balance in each sub-element of owners’ equity (i.e., capital [CR], drawings [DR], revenue [CR] and expenses [DR]).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Interpret how the normal balance side of a T-account relates to the increase and decrease of an account balance.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Recognize and apply the concept of double entry accounting by assigning the amounts of a transaction into one debit and one credit part.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Analyze transactions into debits and credits using a pair of T-accounts.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Analyze a full set of business transactions and record in a ledger of T-accounts.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Calculate the final balance of a T-account.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Prove equality between normal debit balances and normal credit balances by totaling accounts to confirm the accounting equation.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Discuss how capital, drawings, revenue and expenses relate to owners’ equity.

outcomes.statement: Explore how journals simplify and organize transactions in accounting.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 5: Journals (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-8 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 4

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify the information contained in source documents.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Justify the importance of a journal as a permanent legal entity or legal document as it connects to Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAPs).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify columns (i.e., general debit, general credit, special amount columns) of a combination journal.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze and record business transactions into a journal or journals referencing a chart of accounts.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Prove the total of debit columns equals the total of credit columns.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Prove cash by determining that the amount of cash in the journal agrees with the accounting records (e.g., cheque stub).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Analyze, explain and correct discrepancies when preparing a series of accounting proofs such as slide, divide by 9, and double/half.

outcomes.statement: Summarize transactions of an account by updating ledgers to obtain current balance.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 6: Ledgers (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-8 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 5

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Create a chart of accounts and sort assets (100), liabilities (200), capital (300), revenue (400) and expenses (500) into numerical order for a service business organized as a proprietorship.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify the columns (e.g., date, name, account, number, account number, entry, balance) of a ledger form and open a ledger for each account.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss the need for a ledger (i.e., balance of accounts) when a journal is already done.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Post amounts from the general debit and credit columns into individual accounts in the general ledger.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Post totals from the special amount columns to individual accounts.

outcomes.statement: Create a worksheet to summarize data in order to generate financial statements.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 7: Worksheets (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-7 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 6

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Prove the ledger by preparing a trial balance in the worksheet which includes listing all account titles and balances from the general ledgers into correct debit and credit columns.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Calculate and record adjustments in the worksheet in accordance with the Generally Accepted Accounting Principle (GAAP) matching principle.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Extend the revenue and expense accounts into the income statement from the trial balance and adjustments column.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Extend the assets, liabilities, capital, and drawing accounts to the balance sheet column from the trial balance and adjustment column.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Total the columns of the income statement and calculate net income/net loss with proving totals.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Analyze the relationship between sales and expenses (i.e., net income or net loss) on the worksheet.

outcomes.statement: Prepare and interpret financial statements (income statement and balance sheet) for an accounting period.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 8: Financial Statements (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-8 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 7

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss how recording and reporting financial information affects business owners’ ability to make accurate business decisions.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Consider the inquiry questions: How are financial statements used to aid decision makers? What information must be present on a financial statement (e.g., adequate disclosure)?

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss the purpose of income statements and balance sheets.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Compile the income statement listing the heading, business name, date, account titles and appropriate debit and credit amounts.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Calculate the net income or loss by comparing the revenue and expenses to ensure the net income/loss on the income statement is consistent with the worksheet.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Recognize that a balance sheet reports the financial condition of a business on a specific date by detailing the assets, liabilities and capital.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Compile a balance sheet listing business name, date, account titles and appropriate amounts for the assets and liabilities using the amounts from the worksheet’s balance sheet columns.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Calculate the capital for a balance sheet ensuring that total assets equal total liabilities and capital.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Critique a presentation of financial statements from the perspective of a member of the board of directors or from the perspective of a potential investor.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Assess the viability of a business based on a simulated balance sheet.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Analyze examples of publicly available financial statements.

outcomes.statement: Generate adjusting and closing entries in relation to the appropriate accounting period.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 9: Adjusting and Closing Entries (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-7 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 8

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe how the matching principle justifies the need for adjusting and closing entries.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Record adjusting entries in the general or combination journal for all prepaid expenses (e.g., supplies, insurance, advertising).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Transfer the adjusting entries from the general or combination journal to the ledger by posting them to appropriate ledger account.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Distinguish between permanent and temporary accounts.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify the new account income summary as a temporary account.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Define and discuss the purpose of closing entries (e.g., update accounts, transferring net income/loss to owners’ equity account).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Calculate and prepare closing entries by journalizing each entry and posting them to the ledger to bring temporary accounts to zero.

outcomes.statement: Explore the final step of the accounting cycle.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 10: Post-Closing Trial Balance (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 9

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define post-closing trial balance and its purpose.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Prove the equality between debits and credits of the permanent accounts.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Rationalize why no temporary accounts will be in the post-closing trial balance.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Recognize the end-of-the month permanent account balances are new balances for the next month.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine the inquiry question: Why is it important to complete the post-closing trial balance at the end of a fiscal period?

outcomes.statement: Examine accounting practices through application of the accounting cycle for service business scenarios.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 11: Accounting Cycle Project (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-10 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 10

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Apply the accounting cycle (i.e., analyze originating transaction data, journalize, post, prepare worksheets, prepare financial statements, journalize and post adjusting and closing entries, prepare post-closing trial balance) to a service business scenario.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Apply error finding techniques within aspects of the accounting cycle and identify appropriate corrections.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss and justify decisions made to solve problems that arise during the accounting cycle.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze decisions for given scenarios utilizing the accounting cycle.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze the financial situation of a service business based on the financial statements.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Compose questions to help accountants interpret and analyze financial statements.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Compare post-closing trial balances for two different accounting cycles and examine changes that occurred during the accounting period.

outcomes.statement: Justify the importance of wellness practices for employers and employees.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 12: Employee Wellness (Core) · Suggested Time: 1-2 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research practices that impact employee productivity, profit and retention.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify factors (e.g., snacks, atmosphere, movement opportunities) that influence employee wellness.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine the impact that sitting at a desk or computer has on physical and mental wellness.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Perform stretches designed for employees that are working at a desk or computer for extended periods.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Design a company policy regarding employee wellness.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify ergonomic risk factors and plan an ergonomic work station.

outcomes.statement: Investigate career opportunities in the accounting industry in Saskatchewan and Canada.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 13A: Career Opportunities in Accounting (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify occupations in the accounting industry (e.g., public accounting, industry, government).

indicators.label: b
c
indicators.text: Reflect upon one’s suitability or non-suitability for a specific occupation in the accounting industry.

outcomes.statement: Investigate career opportunities in the accounting industry.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 13B: Career Opportunities in Accounting (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-5 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 13A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research different specializations in the accounting field such as business analyst, controller, financial accounting, managerial accounting and forensic accounting.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Reflect upon one’s suitability or non-suitability for a specific occupation in the accounting industry.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss how accounting professionals apply and adhere to different accounting standards depending on the type of entity (e.g., publicly accountable enterprise [IFRS], private enterprise [ASPE], not for profit organization [NPO], public sector entity [PSAB]) in which they are employed.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Design interview questions that could be used for an accounting position.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Critique skills and interests that would enhance career choices (e.g., a focus on accounting practices specific to the agricultural community).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss how economic conditions may affect job prospects in the accounting industry.

outcomes.statement: Evaluate the operation and viability of a merchandising business from an accounting perspective.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 14 : Introduction to Merchandising (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 11

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate the difference between a service business and a merchandising business.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Analyze local, provincial, national and international examples of merchandising (buying and selling) between producer, manufacturer, wholesaler, retailer and consumer.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Evaluate business decisions related to import/export costs, product sustainability, local vs international merchandise and the impact those decisions have on the financial profits/loss of a business.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify examples of merchandising businesses within the community and examine the viability of the business.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Interview an owner of a merchandising business in the community to discuss operational information.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain the difference between the acquisition price and the selling price of a product.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss the meaning of markup, margin and markdown.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explain purchases and their related accounts as being the main record of costs of the merchandise for resale in a periodic inventory system.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Design a proposal for a home-based or online merchandising business, including components such as cost price, profit, overhead, selling price, salaries, delivery, advertising, income tax benefits, primary or secondary source revenue, supplier and markdown.

outcomes.statement: Explain the purpose and application of the Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAPs).
outcomes.printedWith: Module 15: Accounting Standards and Business Ethics (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 2

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss how Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAPs) and accounting standards are applied to accounting cycles and to business transactions.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Collaborate with peers to discuss inquiry questions such as: Why do GAAPs and accounting standards exist? How are the GAAPs applied? What would happen in the absence of any standards?

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine the relationship between personal, professional and business ethics and how it relates to GAAPs and the accounting standards.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss why different parts of accounting handbook exist (e.g., International Financial Reporting Standards [IFRS], Accounting Standards for Private Enterprises [ASPE], Not-for-profit organizations [NPO], Public Sector Accounting Board [PSAB]).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate accounting examples of current events that involve a breach in ethics or failure to adhere to accounting standards.

outcomes.statement: Explore the importance of inventory and its accurate value within a merchandising business.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 16: Merchandising Inventory Accounts (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-6 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 14

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define merchandising inventory.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Classify and assign a number to the different types of accounts used in a merchandising business such as merchandise inventory, purchases, sales and cost of goods sold to the chart of accounts.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine the inquiry questions: Why is inventory reported on the balance sheet as the amount paid for the item, not the selling price? Why is the cost of goods sold reported on the income statement?

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the relationship between beginning inventory (e.g., cost of goods on hand) and ending inventory.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Calculate the balance of merchandise inventory in a merchandising business.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Differentiate between perpetual inventory and periodic inventory, considering cost, ease of handling, computerization and labour hours.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Analyze the implications of inventory surplus or deficits in a business (e.g., cash flow, expenses, loss).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Calculate the cost of goods sold.

outcomes.statement: Assess sales and purchase accounts for a merchandising business.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 17: Sales and Purchases Accounts (Core) · Suggested Time: 9-12 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 16

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Distinguish between cash and purchase transactions.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Analyze sales tax as a liability in a business and how it is calculated on sales transactions.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Assess discounts and how they apply to purchases (e.g., 2/10 n/30 – 2% off if paid within 10 days or net 30) in a merchandising business.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze the effect that sales returns and discounts have on original sales transactions.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Implement contra accounts to record returns and allowances transactions.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Analyze a sales invoice to see if all relevant components including seller, buyer, date, quantity, date, amount, item, tax, terms and total are noted.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Implement the use of special journals (e.g., purchases, cash payments, sales, cash receipts, departmental journals).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Organize transactions into the appropriate sales or purchase journals.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Distinguish between the general ledger and the subsidiary ledgers.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Discuss how the controlling accounts receivable and the controlling accounts payable account summarize all accounts from the subsidiary ledgers.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Produce a schedule of accounts payable and accounts receivable ensuring the total matches the appropriate controlling account.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Post-sales on account transactions, totals, merchandise purchases, cash receipts and cash payments to the appropriate ledger or column.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Critique how cash on delivery (COD), on account, charge, discounts and returns all impact the sales revenue of a merchandising business.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Explain how sales and related accounts are the main source of revenue in a merchandising business.

indicators.label: o
indicators.text: Classify purchases and related accounts (e.g., source documents, invoice, returns and allowances, discounts) as well as invoice and transportation costs (e.g., freight-in, free on board destination).

indicators.label: p
indicators.text: Explain purchases and its related accounts as being the main record of costs of the merchandise for resale in a periodic inventory system.

indicators.label: q
indicators.text: Apply generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) to sales and purchases.

outcomes.statement: Implement steps 1-3 of the accounting cycle for a merchandising business.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 18: Steps 1-3 of Accounting cycle for Merchandising Business (Core) · Suggested Time: 15-20 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 17

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Review and summarize the eight steps in the accounting cycle (i.e., analyze originating transaction data, journalize, post, prepare worksheets, prepare financial statements, journalize and post adjusting and closing entries, prepare post-closing trial balance) for a merchandising business.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Distinguish differences in the accounting cycle for a merchandising business versus a service business.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify what source documents include (e.g., till tape, invoices, memos, cash receipts, cheque stubs) in a merchandising business.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Justify that no entry should be made unless it has a supporting document as related to the GAAP objectivity principle.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze each source document and journalize appropriately for a merchandising business.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Execute a multi-journal system and/or an expanded combination journal (e.g., sales, purchases, cash receipts, cash payment) for a scenario/simulation of a merchandising business.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Post values to the general ledger and subsidiary ledgers such as accounts receivable and accounts payable.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Total and prove journal(s) debit columns equal credit columns.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Examine ways to prove the accuracy of posting (e.g., schedule of accounts payable, schedule of accounts receivable).

outcomes.statement: Implement steps 4-8 of the accounting cycle for a merchandising business.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 19: Steps 4-8 of Accounting Cycle for Merchandising Business (Core) · Suggested Time: 15-18 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 18

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Prove the accuracy of the general ledger for a merchandising business by preparing a trial balance.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Complete a worksheet by organizing and planning adjustments and sorting account balances into the correct financial statement columns to calculate the net income/loss.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Prepare a balance sheet, income statement and statement of owners' equity for a merchandising business.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine and discuss who reads financial statements and why they do.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Prepare the journal entries for adjusting and closing entries for the end of the accounting period in the general or synoptic/combination journal.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Post the adjusting and closing entries by transferring them from the journals to the general ledger to close the temporary accounts and prepare the business books for the next accounting period.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Prepare a post-closing trial balance to check the equality of the general ledger upon completion of the accounting cycle in a merchandising business.

outcomes.statement: Investigate non-monetary aspects of management accounting.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 20: Introduction to Management Accounting (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 19

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Analyze and describe characteristics of management accounting.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Differentiate between management and financial accounting.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify and explain the management functions of planning, organizing, budgeting, forecasting and decision making.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify and evaluate a range of management styles.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Distinguish the difference among management roles such as manager controller, human resource manager, union-management and operations manager.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify and evaluate skills needed to fulfill management roles.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Design a set of interview questions that could be used to interview for a manager position.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Create a simulation that will evaluate whether or not an individual is an effective manager.

outcomes.statement: Investigate calculating, controlling and reporting costs of doing business.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 21: Cost Accounting (Core) · Suggested Time: 10-12 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 20

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define cost accounting and explain how it relates to management accounting and financial accounting.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Differentiate cost into two categories (i.e., manufacturing costs and nonmanufacturing costs) to be used in management analysis.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Classify direct labour, direct materials and manufacturing overhead as manufacturing costs.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Classify marketing/selling costs and administration costs as non-manufacturing costs.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Debate the importance of labour costs to management accounting.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Assess and describe how opportunity costs and sunk costs become part of the management decision-making process.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Prepare the manufacturing statement, the schedule of cost of goods manufactured statement and the income statement for a merchandising business and manufacturing business and then examine the purpose of each.

outcomes.statement: Evaluate the factors a manager considers when making management decisions.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 22: Fixed and Variable Costs (Core) · Suggested Time: 10-12 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 21

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss factors such as prices of products, volume of sales or production, per unit variable costs, total fixed costs and mix of products sold that a manager considers when making management decisions.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Distinguish costs as being fixed or variable and describe how a manager may use this information.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Determine a mixed costs analysis using the high-low method and the scatter graph method.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Compare an income statement detailing the contribution margin to the traditional income statement and explain how changes in sales levels affect contribution margin and net income.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Create an income statement detailing the contribution margin.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Define the breakeven point to be when sales revenue is equal to total costs.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Calculate the breakeven point in units and sales and discuss how managers would use the breakeven point.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Examine how cost-volume-profit (CVP) analysis connects the relationship of product prices, volume or activity levels, variable costs per unit and total fixed costs.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Apply the CVP equations (e.g., breakeven sales volume = fixed costs ÷ contribution margin) to analyze various scenarios to determine their application to the contribution approach of an income statement.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Analyze various scenarios by applying the CVP equations to determine their application to the contribution approach of an income statement.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Define fixed and variable costs and related terms (e.g., cost behaviours, sales revenue contribution margin, contribution approach).

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Compute and explain how changes in sales levels affect contribution margin and net income.

outcomes.statement: Examine how budgets assist in profit planning.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 23: Budgeting for Profit Planning (Core) · Suggested Time: 10-12 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 22

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define the functions, goals, purposes and advantages of a budget and the budgeting process.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Differentiate between the concepts of planning and control when discussing budgets.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify and present the contributions of five types of budgets including sales, purchases, cost of goods manufactured, selling and administrative expense and cash to the master budget as part of the profit planning process.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Organize and construct a budgeted income statement and budgeted balance sheet based on budget information.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Differentiate and describe the variances (e.g., manager’s performance or because of production/ market/ economic conditions) between budgeted and actual data that require further investigation.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Compare and outline the differences between a master budget and a flexible budget using what-if questions to observe changes in net income/loss, using variations in selling price, fixed costs, variable administration expense.

outcomes.statement: Justify how financial statement analysis assists management with decision-making.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 24: Financial Statement Analysis in Management Accounting (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-8 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 23

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine and outline the purpose of financial statement analysis in management accounting.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Review what information financial statements provide and to whom financial statements may be of use.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Analyze financial statements and express trends and changes using comparative balance sheets and comparative income statements.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate how a manager would interpret trends and changes (e.g., a slight increase/ decrease in net sales from one month to another).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze financial statements and express the strengths and weaknesses of a business using ratios (e.g., current, quick or acid test, inventory turnover, debt and equity, return on owners’ equity, markup and return on sales).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine the performance earnings and efficiency analysis and describe how they support management decision-making.

indicators.label: e

indicators.text: List different types of businesses such as merchandising, manufacturing, service and e-commerce.

outcomes.statement: Analyze how financial statements are used when making business decisions related to bad debt.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Generate a list of who (e.g., insurance agencies, Canada Revenue Agency, financial institutions) needs access to financial statements and discuss the purpose of granting access.

indicators.label: b

indicators.text: Discuss how bad debts, depreciation, and inventory valuations assist in assuring that assets are represented as accurately as possible on financial statements.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Assess the impact of the GAAPs (e.g., historical cost, adequate disclosure, matching revenue with expenses, consistent reporting) on what is reported on financial statements.

- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?

- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?

- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

outcomes.statement: Analyze the diversity of Saskatchewan’s agriculture industry.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 1A: Agriculture Today - Diversity (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe personal perception of the agriculture industry in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Differentiate between domestic (i.e., within Canada) and international (i.e., export or trade) markets.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss ways (i.e., primary production and value-added) that agricultural products are sold on domestic and international markets.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Justify the role of Saskatchewan’s agriculture industry in serving both domestic and international markets.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research agricultural products and/or services produced in Saskatchewan for both types of markets.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify agricultural products imported and exported by Saskatchewan and classify each as primary production or value-added.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Investigate the presence and impact of the three categories of agriculture, known as the three Fs (i.e., food, fuel and fibre) within the agriculture industry in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Assess differences in agricultural practices and commodities produced in various regions of Saskatchewan including within First Nations and Métis communities.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Analyze the roles (e.g., farmers, landlords and agribusiness entrepreneurs) of First Nations and Métis peoples in Saskatchewan agriculture.

indicators.label: j

outcomes.statement: Analyze the significance of Saskatchewan’s agriculture industry.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 1B: Agriculture Today - Significance (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-7 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 1A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research the economic, environmental, cultural and social significance of Saskatchewan’s agriculture industry locally, provincially, nationally and globally.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Chart the growth of various aspects of the agriculture industry in Saskatchewan over the past 25 years, using measures such as metric tonnes (e.g., crops), acres (e.g., farm size), kilograms (e.g., milk), cash receipts (e.g., livestock), numbers (e.g., farms or producers) and Gross Domestic Product.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate factors (e.g., family members/owners incorporating for tax reasons) that have contributed to the establishment and growth of largescale farming operations in the province.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze the growth of agriculture enterprises among First Nations communities in recent decades and the factors (e.g., signing of The 1992 Treaty Land Entitlement [TLE] Framework Agreement) that have contributed to the growth.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine challenges (e.g., access to capital and financing, and limited agricultural knowledge and skill) faced by First Nations and Métis communities in establishing and growing farming operations and agribusiness enterprises in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Assess provincial and federal legislation that apply to farmland ownership in Saskatchewan and Canada.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Predict the impact of changes in the provincial, national and global population (i.e., growth and decline) on Saskatchewan agriculture.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Investigate other factors (e.g., climate change, activity in global markets and legislation) that may impact agriculture in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Identify current events, trends and issues affecting the agriculture industry in Saskatchewan and Canada.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Investigate innovations in agriculture that are attributed to Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Trace the impact of the multiplier effect on an agriculture product (e.g., food product) from the selling price to the consumer to the selling price by the producer.

outcomes.statement: Investigate agribusiness activity and enterprises throughout the agricultural supply chain.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 2: Agricultural Supply Chain (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-6 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 1B

indicators.label: a
b
indicators.text: Examine the kinds of activities typically associated with each stage of the supply chain for several agriculture products destined for domestic and global markets.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Assess examples of agribusiness enterprises that support activities at every stage of the agricultural supply chain.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate factors (e.g., inputs to the product or service, processes and techniques, human resources, safety and environmental standards and rules and regulations) which may influence or affect agribusiness enterprises at each stage of the agricultural supply chain.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine the effect of events (e.g., pandemic, trade wars, transportation issues, inclement weather and labour strikes) on various stages of the agricultural supply chain.

outcomes.statement: Analyze the role of agribusiness within the agriculture industry.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 3: Agribusiness (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 2

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine the term agribusiness.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the evolution of agriculture to agribusiness and describe the growing interdependence between agriculture (e.g., farmers and producers) and other businesses that support the industry.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify agribusiness enterprises and activities within the local area and/or Saskatchewan and classify according to the stage(s) of the agricultural supply chain they support.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe factors (e.g., physical resources [e.g., soil, water and climate], transportation, human resources, population and educational institutions) that have contributed to the establishment of agribusiness enterprises within the local area and/or other parts of Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore opportunities and challenges currently faced by agribusiness enterprises in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Debate the opinion that the family farm is disappearing in Saskatchewan and Canada.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Assess the role of agribusiness in supporting growth of the agriculture industry in Saskatchewan and the economies of Saskatchewan and Canada.

outcomes.statement: Examine the importance of public trust in the agriculture industry.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 4: Public Trust (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 3

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine consumer expectations (e.g., safety, affordability, ethical production and traceability) of food produced by the agriculture industry in Saskatchewan and Canada.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe the concept of public trust within the context of Saskatchewan agriculture.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain principles of public trust such as transparency of industry practices, continuous improvement of practices, evidence-based decisions and collaboration with relevant experts.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the potential impact (e.g., counter-productive public policy and regulatory changes) on the industry of negative consumer perceptions of agriculture.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identity sources (e.g., social media, newspaper, television and word of mouth) often accessed by the public for information on the agriculture industry.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Assess the importance of, and ways to determine, the credibility of a source of information.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Research standards set by the Hazard Analysis Critical Control Point (HACCP) and International Standards Organization (ISO) food safety management systems.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Examine the role of the Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) in the Canadian agriculture industry.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Investigate the advantages of, and processes for, obtaining HACCP, ISO and CFIA certifications.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Research current provincial and federal government strategies and programs for fostering public trust in agriculture.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Explore the mandates as well as current and past initiatives of a variety of organizations (e.g., Farm & Food Care Saskatchewan, Agriculture in the Classroom and 4-H Saskatchewan) in fostering public trust in agriculture.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Reflect on the role that individuals and agribusiness enterprises throughout the agricultural supply chain can play in supporting and building public trust in the agriculture industry.

outcomes.statement: Assess the role of technology and innovation in supporting and growing Saskatchewan’s agriculture industry.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 5: Technology and Innovation (Core) · Suggested Time: 10-15 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 2

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore innovation and its impact on agribusiness.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Debate the risks (e.g., cost and wasting resources) and rewards (e.g., reducing costs and providing a better-quality product) often associated with innovation.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss reasons (e.g., global competition, efficiencies, safety and cost savings) for the research, development and implementation of innovative ideas and practices.

indicators.label: d
e
indicators.text: Examine examples of innovative technologies (e.g., drones, autonomous tractors and robots) and other innovations (e.g., production cost insurance, business risk management programs and urban farms) used in agribusiness today.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify benefits realized by the agriculture industry through research, development and implementation of innovative ideas and practices.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Research programs and services offered by organizations (e.g., Prairie Agricultural Machinery Institute [PAMI], Innovation Saskatchewan, Saskatchewan Cattlemen’s Association, Crop Development Centre [CDC], Vaccine and Infections Disease Organization [VIDO], the Food Centre, the AgKnowledge Centre and Synchotron) that support the research, development and implementation of technology in Saskatchewan’s agriculture industry.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Debate issues (e.g., technology use agreements [e.g., for seed], right to repair [R2R] movement, energy use, ethics and safety, use of antibiotics in livestock and environmental concerns) related to the use of various innovative technologies and practices in agriculture.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Predict and describe the future impact of innovative ideas and practices on agribusiness in Saskatchewan and Canda.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Identify a problem or issue that currently exists in the agricultural supply chain and propose an innovative solution to the problem.

outcomes.statement: Develop effective information gathering and communication skills commonly used in agribusiness.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 6: Information and Effective Communication for Agribusiness (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-7 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 3

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine the importance of effective communication skills (e.g., speaking, public speaking, writing, listening and reading) for those employed in agribusiness.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Reflect on personal ability to communicate effectively in a variety of situations.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Assess the role that negotiation plays in effective communication within agribusiness.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify strategies for negotiating better business deals within agribusiness.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Role-play and analyze situations that demonstrate effective and/or ineffective negotiation skills within an agriculture context.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Assess the importance of access to reliable information through all stages of the supply chain.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine types of information needed at every stage of the supply chain for a variety of agricultural products.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss ways to determine the credibility of a source of information.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Research sources of credible information that support decision-making at every stage of the supply chain.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Identify communication tools (e.g., software applications; video conferencing and videotelephony; text messaging; electronic mail; blogging and videologging [vlogging]; print and broadcast media; and social media), the skills required to use them effectively, and when and why they might be used in agriculture.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Justify the increasing involvement of farmers or producers in communications and conversations (e.g., with regulators, government and consumers) around food and production practices.

outcomes.statement: Examine a variety of marketing strategies used in agribusiness.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 7: Marketing (Core) · Suggested Time: 7-10 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 6

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of a good buyer-seller relationship for agribusiness success.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research strategies (e.g., building trust and competitive pricing) for developing and maintaining strong buyer-seller relationships.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe the interchangeability and interdependency of buyer-seller roles (e.g., farmer/producer as buyer and seller, and grocery store owner as buyer and seller) within agribusiness.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify the four Ps of marketing (i.e., product, price, place and promotion) known as the Marketing Mix.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore factors to be considered for each of the components of the Marketing Mix.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine the advantages and disadvantages of traditional (e.g., print and radio) and digital (i.e., online) marketing strategies as part of the place and promotion components of the Marketing Mix.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Assess the application of the Marketing Mix for a variety of agribusiness enterprises within the community or province.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify local, provincial, national and international markets for a variety of Saskatchewan agricultural products or services.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Analyze statistics related to the exporting of Saskatchewan agricultural products and services.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Describe the basic steps in marketing an agricultural commodity, product or service within the community, province or country and around the world.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Identify organizations (e.g., Saskatchewan Trade & Export Partnership) that assist provincial businesses, including agribusiness enterprises, in accessing global marketing opportunities.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Analyze the marketing strategies used by a variety of agribusiness enterprises.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Examine factors (e.g., cultural differences, language barriers, currency exchange and different time zones) that need to be considered, and ways to effectively deal with them, when marketing to customers globally.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Design a marketing strategy for an agriculture product or service of choice that includes adjustments for external factors such as changes in supply in demand or increases in production costs.

outcomes.statement: Assess rules and regulations that apply to the agriculture industry in Saskatchewan and Canada.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 8: Quality Assurance and Agriculture Policy (Core) · Suggested Time: 10-15 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 4

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Assess the importance (e.g., product quality and safety) of rules and regulations throughout the supply chain.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe what quality assurance means within the context of agriculture.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify rules and regulations (i.e., agriculture policy) that apply to the agriculture industry in Saskatchewan and Canada today.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Research post-colonial legislation and regulations that impacted, and continue to impact, agricultural activity among First Nations and Métis peoples.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine the alignment of current Saskatchewan and Canadian agriculture policy with First Nations and Métis worldviews (e.g., stewardship of the land).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain the role of municipal, band, provincial and federal governments in establishing and enforcing rules and regulations for the agriculture industry.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Classify rules and regulations for the agriculture industry according to the level of government (i.e., municipal, band, provincial and federal) that is responsible for implementing them.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Reflect on individual responsibility for knowing and complying with rules and regulations applicable to the agriculture industry for those involved in it.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Discuss the role that producers and consumers can play in influencing the development and introduction of rules and regulations in the agriculture industry.

indicators.label: j
k
indicators.text: Predict potential repercussions of events such as an outbreak of food poisoning or other foodborne illness, an anthrax outbreak among cattle herds, an outbreak of clubroot disease in canola crops, rail blockades and protests that are indicative of, or could lead to, a lack of quality assurance in the agriculture industry.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Research the mandate of a variety of agricultural organizations such as the Saskatchewan Food Processors’ Association, the Prairie Machinery Manufacturers’ Association and commodity associations as well as federal and provincial government agencies such as Agriculture and Agri-food Canada, Canadian Food Inspection Agency, Saskatchewan Agriculture and Food, Health Canada, Canadian Renewable Fuels Association, Saskatchewan Health and Public Health in maintaining product quality and safety.

outcomes.statement: Analyze opportunities for a successful career in agribusiness.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 9: Careers in Agribusiness (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 3

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research and describe the diverse opportunities (e.g., farm and livestock management, food science, agricultural and rural policy, foreign trade, entrepreneurship, commodity marketing and economic development) related to the field of agribusiness.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify current and forecasted career opportunities and employment trends, including labour surpluses or shortages, in the field of agribusiness in Saskatchewan, Canada and the world.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the availability of, and eligibility requirements for, employment programs (e.g., Seasonal Agricultural Worker Program or Temporary Foreign Worker) that attempt to fill vacancies in Canadian primary agriculture.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of such employment programs from both the employer and worker perspectives.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Debate the statement, “Growing up on a farm is necessary for a successful career in agribusiness.”

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine opportunities (e.g., independence, increased self-confidence and pride in ownership) and challenges (e.g., stress, anxiety, business succession, and mental health and well-being) associated with being an agribusiness owner.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Reflect on personal interests, skills, abilities and traits that could lead to a one or more personal career options in agribusiness.

indicators.label: h

outcomes.statement: Assess opportunities for diversification in agriculture.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 10: Agricultural Diversification (Optional) · Suggested Time: 7-10 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 2

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine types of risks (e.g., operational and financial) agribusiness owners may face.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Define the terms diversification and risk management.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss the relationship between risk management and diversification within the context of agriculture.

indicators.label: d
e
indicators.text: Assess the benefits (e.g., better livelihood for producers/farmers, increased variety of products in the marketplace and increased employment opportunities) and challenges (e.g., capital costs, financing and skillset required) associated with various agricultural diversification strategies.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe ways to analyze the success of a diversification strategy following its implementation.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify the purpose of Business Risk Management (BRM) programs (e.g., AgriStability, AgriRecovery and AgriInvest).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Investigate features of, and eligibility and application requirements for, BRM programs.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Analyze a variety of given agribusiness scenarios, propose potential solutions for diversification and defend the best solution for each scenario.

outcomes.statement: Examine strategies for promoting and supporting safety and efficiency in the agribusiness workplace.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 11: Safety in the Agribusiness Workplace (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 9

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of workplace safety (e.g., to self and others, the business and society).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Assess the impact of a workplace injury on individuals (e.g., self and others) and the business.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Analyze the effect that costs of injury and equipment damage (e.g., down time, repair costs and insurance premiums) have on agribusiness profit margins.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Research employer, supervisor and employee responsibilities pertaining to occupational health and safety standards in the workplace as required by Saskatchewan and Canadian law.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify sections of the Saskatchewan Employment Act that apply to owners, employers, contractors, supervisors, suppliers, self-employed persons and workers as it relates to agribusiness operations.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Assess when coverage from the Saskatchewan Workers’ Compensation Board is optional and when it is mandatory.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explain the benefits to employers and employees of the Saskatchewan Workers Compensation Act and the Meredith Principles.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Research the financial penalties for failure to comply with the Saskatchewan Occupational Health and Safety Regulations.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Examine what a workplace hazard is.

indicators.label: j
k
indicators.text: List examples of potential workplace hazards for each of the four categories within a variety of agribusiness workplaces.

outcomes.statement: Analyze processes for selecting and developing an agribusiness enterprise.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 12: Agribusiness Opportunities (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-7 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 3

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research local, provincial and national resources (e.g., industry organizations, government agencies, websites and financial institutions) that can assist with identifying and developing an agribusiness enterprise.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of accessing these resources for informed decision making.

indicators.label: c
d
indicators.text: Describe the concept of economic viability.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify factors (e.g., public trust, environment and economic) that affect agriculture and agribusiness in the local or regional area.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Differentiate among resources (e.g., technical, human and financial) required by a variety of agribusiness opportunities such as a tire shop, food processor, greenhouse, berry farm or trucking firm.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine the role of market research in developing an agribusiness enterprise.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Assess various methods (e.g., consumer polls, online surveys and focus groups) for conducting market research.

outcomes.statement: Prepare for and present a business pitch for an agribusiness idea or concept.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 13: Planning an Agribusiness Enterprise (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-8 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Modules 11, 12

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of planning before launching a start-up.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Develop questions that should be answered when planning a start-up, such as:
- What is the business idea?
- What need or want does it fill, or what problem does it solve?
- Who are the targeted customers?
- How much money and other resources will be required for start-up?
- How will money and other resources be obtained?
- What other resources are needed?

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the business model canvas and how it can be used to visualize and outline a business idea or concept.

indicators.label: d
e
indicators.text: Outline an agribusiness idea or concept using the business model canvas.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine characteristics (e.g., short and concise, tells a story and pays attention to details) of an effective and compelling business pitch.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Propose, and develop answers for, questions that may be asked by investors or potential supporters during a business pitch, such as:
- How big is the market for your idea?
- Who are your competitors and what are their market shares?
- What is your competitive advantage?
- What is unique about your idea?
- How much money are you prepared to invest yourself?
- What other sources of finance do you have access to?

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Pitch the agribusiness idea or concept to trusted supporters.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Reflect on feedback received from trusted supporters.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Adjust the plan based on feedback received.

outcomes.statement: Prepare for the work placement.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 80: Work Study Preparation (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate, Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 9

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III – Occupational Health and Safety in The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019:
- the right to know – the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate – in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,
- the right to refuse – work that you believe is unusually dangerous.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent, teacher or other school staff, employer) involved in the work placement.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the business/organization to become familiar with its operations.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: In collaboration with all partners, develop personal and learning goals for the work placement.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents needed for the work placement (e.g., personal career documentation such as a resume or portfolio, permission forms, logs, self- and employer evaluation forms).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop a list of questions that could potentially be asked by the employer/work placement in an interview situation as well as answers to the questions.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Participate in an interview with the employer prior to beginning the work placement.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Reflect upon one’s performance during the interview.

outcomes.statement: Participate in a work placement experience.

indicators.text: Apply relevant skills and abilities during the work placement experience.

indicators.label: b
c

outcomes.statement: Relate one’s work placement experience to personal and career goals.

indicators.label: a
b

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Prepare a letter, note, card or other communication for the work placement employer, expressing appreciation.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Develop and/or revise personal and career goals based on the work placement experience.

outcomes.statement: Develop an awareness of the agriculture industry.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 1: Agriculture Industry Overview (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore the history of the agriculture industry in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify the different sectors (e.g., crops, livestock, fisheries, apiculture and fruit farming) of the agriculture industry.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate the percentage of residents of Saskatchewan who are employed in the agriculture industry.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify the types (e.g., seeding, application, harvesting and tillage) and specific examples (e.g., air seeder, sprayer and combine) of equipment used in agriculture.

indicators.text: Research and create a representation (e.g., timeline and infographic) of important dates in the history of the development of agricultural equipment (e.g., tractors and ploughs).

indicators.label: f

outcomes.statement: Apply safety standards to prevent injuries in the agricultural equipment technician workspace.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 2A: Personal Safety (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-8 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss worker and employee rights and responsibilities as they relate to workplace safety and how they can prevent injuries.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify common safety hazard categories and hierarchy of control common to the agriculture equipment service industry.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Assess and mitigate the risks (e.g., slips, trips, falls, burns) and potential safety hazards (e.g., exposure to chemicals, gasoline, diesel) in the agricultural technician workspace.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Research the benefits of completing the different certifications and programs offered by Work Safe Sask, Sask Safety Council, Motor Safety Association, Agricultural Health and Safety Network, Sask Prevention and the Ministry of Labour Relations and Workplace Safety.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify and explore basic safety procedures (e.g., storage and maintenance of tools, clean workspace and caution when working at high heights and around large equipment) as they apply to an agricultural equipment technician.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Develop a list of rules for workplace safety including proper personal protective equipment (PPE), sanitation, neat and tidy work area and reporting workplace accidents and safety incidents.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify the dangers of working in a confined space (e.g., sprayer tank, combine grain tank and barn manure tank or pit).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Demonstrate the utilization and maintenance of protective devices on equipment.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Perform proper lockout and de-energizing of equipment before beginning inspections or repairs.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Identify the advantages and disadvantages of using each category of industry standard personal protective equipment (PPE) for respiratory, hearing, sight and body protection such as masks, ear plugs or earmuff, safety goggles and shields, gloves, footwear and aprons.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Demonstrate PPE cleaning procedures.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Describe hazards from the misuse of oxy-acetylene welding equipment (e.g., tanks, hoses and gauges) and take measures to avoid unintentional injuries caused by flashback and backfire.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Locate and demonstrate the correct use of safety equipment (e.g., eye wash station, shower, first aid station, shop ventilation, fire extinguishers and caging devices) in the workplace.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Post and maintain emergency phone numbers in a visible location.

indicators.label: o
indicators.text: Discuss appropriate actions in the event of an injury in the workplace, including whom to contact, how to report and first-aid procedures.

indicators.text: Investigate Occupational Health and Safety (OH&S) regulations for the storage of hazardous wastes.

indicators.label: d

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Select and use appropriate tools to manipulate fasteners.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explain the importance of torque values and tightening sequence of specific fasteners.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Adjust and utilize torque wrenches to properly tighten fasteners.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Utilize a tap and die set to complete thread repair of damaged fasteners.

indicators.label: j

indicators.label: k
