indicators.text: Lift and lower agricultural equipment in a safe manner using the appropriate lifting devices.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss the limitations of the human body in lifting materials or equipment and the ergonomic best practices to avoid injury.

outcomes.statement: Investigate basic agricultural equipment maintenance procedures.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 9A: Introductory Agricultural Equipment Maintenance (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-8 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore the safety procedures identified by the manufacturer related to agricultural equipment maintenance.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe common procedures for periodic inspection and testing of agricultural equipment.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Select lubricants and filters for different agricultural equipment and service conditions according to manufacturers’ specifications.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Locate and follow manufacturer’s lubrication and maintenance schedules.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the benefits of using a regular maintenance schedule for agricultural equipment.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe the service intervals, specifications and maintenance requirements to maintain a manufacturer’s warranty.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Recognize, inspect and adjust basic components (e.g., tires, bearings, belts, fuel, air filters, fluid levels and lights) of agricultural equipment that require periodic inspection and/or lubrication.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify, replace or repair and confirm the repair of minor broken parts.

outcomes.statement: Perform appropriate advanced agricultural equipment maintenance procedures safely and correctly.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 9B: Advanced Agricultural Equipment Maintenance (Core) · Suggested Time: 10-20 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 9A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Follow the manufacturer’s safety guidelines when performing advanced agricultural equipment maintenance procedures, including maintaining a clean and organized work area.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe and demonstrate processes used to identify faults in the components of agricultural equipment.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Conduct a visual inspection of agricultural equipment including tire pressure and condition, lights, fluid levels, condition of hoses, belts, pulleys and battery.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Carry out drivetrain (e.g., differential, engine, transmission and transfer case) lubricant and filter changes following manufacturer’s specifications.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Demonstrate manufacturer recommended system maintenance such as checking spark plugs, positive crankcase ventilation valves and valve adjustments.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Inspect and replace faulty bearings and seals while following safe work processes.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Inspect, repair and confirm the repair of a driveline with worn and faulty parts while following safe work processes.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Investigate the types of interactive diagnostic tests of agricultural equipment such as dynamometer test, engine cylinder cut-out test and emission system fault codes.

outcomes.statement: Explore the processes involved in the diagnosis, service and repair of agricultural equipment tracks, tires and wheels.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 10: Tracks, Tires and Wheels (Optional) · Suggested Time: 5-10 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify safe work practices (e.g., lifting heavy parts, proper inflation process and recognition of cut and pinch points) when working with agricultural equipment tracks, tires and wheels, including maintaining a clean and organized work area.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain how track and tire condition affects the handling, fuel economy and safety characteristics of agricultural equipment.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Compare the advantages and disadvantages of using tracks or tires on agricultural equipment.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe the design, construction and purpose of different tracks, tires and wheels including tire sidewall information.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify common physical and mechanical issues in the operation of agricultural equipment tracks.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Evaluate track and tire condition (e.g., tread depth, rubber condition and wear patterns) and explain causes and effects of rubber damage, wear and defects.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explain the purpose of and when track and tire service (e.g., tire rotation and balancing and track replacement) is required.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explain the parameters (e.g., caster, camber and toe) that affect wheel alignment and how misalignment can affect agricultural equipment handling and tire wear.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Inspect tracks for wear and proper adjustment as per the manufacturer’s specifications and discuss how improper adjustment can cause safety concerns.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Inspect lug nuts for proper torque as per the manufacturer’s specifications and discuss how improper torque and mounting can cause safety concerns.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Describe the design, construction and hazards associated with tires mounted on a split rim (locking ring).

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Follow correct environmental procedures for recycling and disposal of tires.

outcomes.statement: Investigate diagnostic service processes for agricultural equipment storage batteries.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 11: Storage Batteries (Optional) · Suggested Time: 2-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Follow the manufacturer’s safe work practices when working with storage batteries, including maintaining a clean and organized work area.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify the manufacturer’s requirements for the voltage, size, shape and quantity of batteries required for specific agricultural equipment.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe the construction and operation of common types (e.g., absorbent glass mat [AGM] and lead acid) of agricultural equipment storage batteries.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify cold cranking amperes (CCA) and reserve capacity minutes of storage batteries.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Perform service tests (e.g., check voltage and load) on storage batteries.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Follow safe procedures including connection order when performing battery replacement, boosting and charging operations.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe and diagnose common battery failures (e.g., frozen, sulfated and short circuits).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Follow correct environmental procedures for recycling and disposal of storage batteries.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Identify emergency procedures for first aid and cleanup of ruptured batteries.

outcomes.statement: Locate agricultural equipment service information utilizing appropriate tools and sources.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 12: Agricultural Equipment Service Information and Tools (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-8 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Summarize the type of information available from common agricultural equipment service information sources (e.g., apps, computers, diagnostic charts, manuals, scan tools and technical bulletins).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of proper communication with parts personnel.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore the use of parts codes and acronyms used in an electronic service tool (EST).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Determine correct service information such as torque specifications, wiring diagrams and disassembly/assembly procedures from appropriate sources.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Demonstrate care in handling computers, manuals and scan tools.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Analyze vehicle identification numbers (VIN) and engine emission compliance labels.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss the strategies (e.g., contacting the manufacturer engineers and online forums) used by technicians to gather information that is not readily available from service material.

outcomes.statement: Investigate common agricultural equipment diagnosis and repair processes.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 13: Agricultural Equipment Diagnosis and Repair Processes (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-10 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify and follow manufacturer and industry safe work practices when diagnosing and repairing agricultural equipment, including maintaining a clean and organized work area.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify common steps (e.g., identify, diagnose, repair and confirm the repair) of agricultural equipment repair processes.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe common practices and procedures (e.g., diagnosing, torquing, measuring, lifting and cutting) involved in agricultural equipment repair.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Use service information to identify proper processes for repairing a specific problem.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe the importance of accurate service records for the dealership business processes.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Assess the components of single and multi-segment work orders for different types of repairs.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Follow the path of a work order and its connections to various roles and departments in an agricultural equipment dealership.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Complete a work order for different scenarios indicating the complaint, cause and corrections required.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Identify and document required components, create a parts list and cost estimate for a specific repair or modification.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Describe repair processes for identified issues or modifications.

outcomes.statement: Explore the function and operation of electrical circuits.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 14A: Fundamentals of Agricultural Equipment Electrical Systems (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-10 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Follow safe work practices (e.g., avoid sharp material and hot parts or tools) when working with electrical circuits, including maintaining a clean and organized work area.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe major electrical concepts including basic atomic structure and conductor, insulator and semi-conductor materials.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Define current, resistance and voltage and state their units of measurement.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the factors (e.g., wiring, connection quality and corrosion) that affect resistance and their effect on current and voltage.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Differentiate between AC and DC circuits and identify where they are used in electrical circuits in agricultural equipment.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Distinguish between the characteristics of series, parallel and series-parallel electrical circuits.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify different types of switches and their purpose.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explain the purpose of a controller area network binary unit system (CANBUS).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Classify common types of electric motors.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Diagnose, repair and confirm the repair of electrical circuits by soldering, splicing and taping wires and connections.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Assess the quality of and adjust electrical repairs.

outcomes.statement: Examine agricultural equipment electrical systems.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 14B: Advanced Agricultural Equipment Electrical Systems (Optional) · Suggested Time: 5-10 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 14A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify and follow safe work practices (e.g., ground static electricity, avoid the presence of water and disconnect the batteries) when working with agricultural equipment electrical systems, including maintaining a clean and organized work area.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore the use of electrical and electronic components (e.g., sensors, actuators and switches) in agricultural equipment.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Perform mechanical adjustments (e.g., camera, headlight and sensor alignments) to agricultural equipment electrical system components according to manufacturer’s specifications.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe wiring terminology and principles of electrical wiring.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify and select appropriate wire gauge, connectors and circuit protection devices like fuses when working on electrical systems.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine electrical system schematic diagrams and service manuals to help diagnose electrical problems.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Perform common electrical tests (e.g., current, parasitic draw, resistance, voltage and voltage drop) using electrical testing equipment like a multimeter.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Provide examples of common faults (e.g., open circuit, short circuit and burned-out fuse or bulb) that may occur in agricultural equipment electrical circuits.

outcomes.statement: Investigate agricultural equipment computer systems.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 15: Agricultural Equipment Computer Systems (Optional) · Suggested Time: 5-10 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 14A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify and follow safe work practices in dangerous situations (e.g., hot components, pinch points, shock hazards and static electricity discharge) when working with agricultural equipment computer systems and their components, including maintaining a clean and organized work area.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the operation of computer-controlled fuel systems.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Retrieve fault codes from the memory of an agricultural equipment computer system using an electronic service tool (EST) or onboard diagnostic system.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe the diagnosis and repair of agricultural equipment computer systems following the appropriate fault code diagnostics.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore how to download software updates on agricultural equipment computer systems.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the operation, diagnosis and repair of small engines.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 16: Small Engines (Optional) · Suggested Time: 10-15 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify and follow safe work practices in dangerous situations (e.g., shock hazards, hot and sharp surfaces and moving parts) when working with small engines, including maintaining a clean and organized work area.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the working principles of an internal combustion engine.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Differentiate between the operation of 2-stroke and 4-stroke engines.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain the construction and function of the 5 C’s (i.e., camshaft, connecting rod, crankshaft, cylinder block and cylinder head) of major engine subassemblies

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe how improper cooling and lubrication can cause engine failure.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify specialized measuring equipment used to measure specific engine parts (e.g., pistons, cylinders and cam shaft).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Define and determine engine measurements (e.g., clearance, out of round and taper) that are used to assess an engine.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explain how repair manuals are used to disassemble, repair and reassemble engines.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Demonstrate how to disassemble and reassemble an operational small engine.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Verify correct assembly by following manufacturer’s procedures to start, run and stop a small engine.

outcomes.statement: Explore the construction and operation of multicylinder engines.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 17: Industrial Engine Theory (Optional) · Suggested Time: 10-15 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 16

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate common agricultural engine configurations (e.g., inline and Vtype).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Define and determine agricultural engine measurements (e.g., displacement, compression ratio and clearance).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Differentiate between common valve train configurations (e.g., in block and single or dual overhead camshaft) in agricultural engines.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe the components and function of major, multi-cylinder engine subassemblies (e.g., cooling, exhaust, fuel and lubrication systems).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain the variations (e.g., cam lift, piston shape and ring design) of internal engine components.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Compare the air flow of naturally aspirated and forced air turbocharged diesel engines.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Compare how fuel is supplied and ignited in spark ignition gasoline engines and compression ignition diesel engines.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Describe the advantages and disadvantages of different fuel sources used in agricultural engines.

outcomes.statement: Examine engine charging systems.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 18: Charging Systems (Optional) · Suggested Time: 5-10 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 14A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify and follow safe work practices (e.g., disconnect battery, prevent grounding of live wires, and be aware of sharp surfaces and cleaning agents) when working with agricultural equipment charging systems, including maintaining a clean and organized work area.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Find and identify components (e.g., alternator, batteries and voltage regulator) of an engine charging system.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe the function and operation of an engine charging system and its components.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Use appropriate equipment like a multimeter or battery load tester to test engine charging systems.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Diagnose, repair and confirm the repair of common charging systems faults (e.g., alternator failure, damaged or loose belts and poor connections) following manufacturer recommendations.

outcomes.statement: Investigate engine starting systems.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 19: Starting Systems (Optional) · Suggested Time: 5-10 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 14A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Follow safe work practices (e.g., disconnect battery, prevent grounding of live wires, and be aware of sharp surfaces and cleaning agents) when working with engine starting systems, including maintaining a clean and organized work area.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify and find the components (e.g., battery, ignition switch, starter motor, solenoid, starter relay and safety lockout switch) of an engine starting system.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss the function and operation of an engine starting system.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe the operation of a starter including the starter activation and drive mechanisms.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify common faults and symptoms associated with engine starting system malfunctions.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Perform tests on engine starting systems using appropriate equipment like multimeters.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss how to use voltage drop to test a starter.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Diagnose, repair and confirm the repair of common starting system faults (e.g., control circuit failure, starter failure and poor connections).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Perform safety checks to ensure equipment does not move unintentionally when performing starter system tests.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the diagnosis, service and repair of engine fuel delivery systems.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 20: Fuel Delivery Systems (Optional) · Suggested Time: 5-10 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify and follow safe work practices (e.g., handle and store fuel safely, and be aware of pressurized fuel and fire hazards) when working with fuel delivery systems, including maintaining a clean and organized work area.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the operation of fuel delivery systems (e.g., high pressure commonrail, lift-pump, mechanical and unit injectors).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify different fuel types and additives (e.g., anti-gel and lubricant) used in agricultural engines.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe the benefits of using fuel additives.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Use appropriate equipment (e.g., fuel pressure gauge) to test fuel delivery systems.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Perform fuel delivery system scheduled maintenance (e.g., fuel filter change and system flush).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Diagnose, repair, and confirm the repair of common fuel delivery system faults (e.g., faulty filters, clogged injectors, leaks and lift-pump replacement).

outcomes.statement: Explore agricultural equipment intake, exhaust and emission systems.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 21: Intake, Exhaust and Emission Systems (Optional) · Suggested Time: 5-10 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify and follow safe work practices (e.g., be aware of hot surfaces and use of pipe bending equipment) when working with intake and exhaust systems, including maintaining a clean and organized work area.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe the components and structure of agriculture equipment intake systems.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of the air intake system to the performance of the engine.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Summarize the regulations governing emission control of diesel engines.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify exhaust system components such as exhaust gas recirculation (EGR), selective catalytic reduction (SCR) system and diesel particulate filter (DPF).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain the purpose of the components such as diesel nitrogen oxide (NOx) sensors, DPF, mixing chambers and diesel engine fluid (DEF) injectors of the emission control system in diesel engines.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe the common issues (e.g., putting DEF into the diesel tank, contamination and improper storage) related to the use of DEF.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explain how to regenerate a DPF.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Inspect and evaluate exhaust systems for blockage, corrosion, leaks, mounting issues and noise.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Identify the hazards associated with operating engine exhaust systems, including carbon monoxide in enclosed spaces and excessive noise levels.

outcomes.statement: Explore the components and operation of agricultural equipment power trains.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 22: Power Train (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify the components of agricultural equipment power trains.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore the types of transmissions (e.g., mechanical, semi-powershift, powershift, hydrostatic and continuously variable) used in agricultural equipment.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Differentiate between torque and horsepower.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain the theory behind the power output (e.g., speed versus torque) of transmissions.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe the purpose and operation of the power take-off on agricultural equipment.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain how final drives and differentials operate.

outcomes.statement: Investigate agricultural equipment steering systems.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 23: Steering Systems (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify and follow safe work practices in dangerous situations (e.g., dangers of welding or heating steering linkage components) when working with agricultural equipment steering systems, including maintaining a clean and organized work area.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Compare the operation and components of linkage and hydrostatic steering systems.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain the parameters camber, caster and toe that affect wheel alignment.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe how misalignment can affect agricultural equipment handling and tire wear.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe how wear or damage to steering components can affect handling, steering control and wheel alignment.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Inspect and assess steering components for corrosion, damage, excessive play and wear.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss how improper torquing can be a safety issue when replacing steering components.

outcomes.statement: Examine the component parts and operation of agricultural equipment hydraulic systems.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 24: Agricultural Equipment Hydraulic Systems (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-10 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify and follow safe work practices (e.g., avoid contact with pressurized hydraulic fluids and brake fluids contacting painted surfaces) when working with hydraulic systems, including maintaining a clean and organized work area.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the difference between pneumatic and hydraulic systems.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe the uses of pneumatic systems.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify the properties of different hydraulic fluids (e.g., brake, power steering, transmission and lifting systems) including the three main varieties (e.g., petroleum, mineral and synthetic).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain why one hydraulic fluid cannot be used for all applications including why an application-specific additive package may be required by a manufacturer.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Demonstrate the proper disposal of used hydraulic fluids.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Summarize potential environmental concerns of hydraulic fluids.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify the parts (e.g., reservoir, pump, valves and actuator) of a hydraulic system.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Describe the different types of fittings including thread style, function and uses.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Explain how Pascal’s law applies to hydraulic systems.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Investigate common hydraulic system component failures (e.g., filter, hose and pump) recognizing to never use a part of the body to detect a hydraulic leak. (e.g., never use your hand to run along a pressurized line).

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Identify the advantages of a hydrostatic drive.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Explain how a hydrostatic drive works.

outcomes.statement: Investigate agricultural equipment brake systems.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 25: Brake Systems (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-10 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 24

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify and follow safe work practices in dangerous situations (e.g., contact with asbestos dust from brake components and contact of brake fluid with eyes and painted surfaces) when working with agricultural equipment brake systems, including maintaining a clean and organized work area.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: List the properties, testing procedures and manufacturer suggested maintenance of different types of agricultural equipment brake fluids.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain the construction and inspection of brake components (e.g., brake hoses, lines, wheel cylinders, calipers, drums and hardware).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe how principles of friction apply to a drum brake system.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss factors that affect agricultural equipment brake performance.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe the purpose, construction and operation of electric, hydraulic and mechanical brake systems including emergency and park brake systems.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify common brake problems and how to repair them.

outcomes.statement: Explore agricultural equipment heating and cooling systems.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 26: Heating and Cooling Systems (Optional) · Suggested Time: 5-10 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify and follow safe work practices (e.g., check coolant temperature and pressure) when working with cooling systems, including maintaining a clean and organized work area.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Demonstrate the proper disposal of used coolants and explain potential environmental concerns of antifreeze disposal.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify the role of antifreeze in a cooling system.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain how cooling systems remove and dissipate heat from engines.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe the function of the components (e.g., pump, reservoir, thermostat and radiator) of a liquid cooling system.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Compare the operation of compound cooling systems.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Investigate common cooling system maintenance procedures (e.g., checking fluid levels and flushing the system) and tests (e.g., visual inspection, coolant and pressure tests and leak detection).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Fill coolant systems according to specifications and purge air where required.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Identify the risks of removing a radiator cap from a hot or overheated cooling system.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Describe the function and operation of a heating system to heat, cool and ventilate agricultural equipment cabs.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Examine regulations and legislation that govern the use of air conditioning systems.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Explain the basics of how an air conditioning system works.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the diagnosis, service and repair of agricultural equipment heating and ventilation systems.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 27: Heating and Ventilation Systems (Optional) · Suggested Time: 8-10 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 26

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify and follow safe work practices (e.g., check coolant pressure and temperature and watch for pressurized refrigerants and moving components) when working with agricultural equipment heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC) systems, including maintaining a clean and organized work area.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Demonstrate the proper disposal of used coolants.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain the potential environmental concerns of coolant disposal.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify how the cooling and heating systems are connected.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Perform common HVAC system tests (e.g., visual inspection, coolant and pressure tests and leak detection) and maintenance procedures (e.g., flushing the heater core and checking fluid levels).

indicators.label: f

outcomes.statement: Prepare for the work placement.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 80A: Work Study Preparation (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate, Advanced · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III – Occupational Health and Safety in The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019:
- the right to know - the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate - in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,
- the right to refuse – work that you believe is unusually dangerous

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent, teacher or other school staff, employer) involved in the work placement

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the business/organization to become familiar with its operations.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: In collaboration with all partners, develop personal and learning goals for the work placement.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents needed for the work placement (e.g., personal career documentation such as a resume or portfolio, permission forms, logs, self- and employer evaluation forms).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop a list of questions that could potentially be asked by the employer/work placement in an interview situation as well as answers to the questions.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Participate in an interview with the employer prior to beginning the work placement.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Reflect upon one’s performance during the interview.

outcomes.statement: Explore the role of injury prevention and safety in agriculture production.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 2A: Introduction to Farm Safety (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-8 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 1

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify the types and frequency of common farm preventable injuries by analyzing industry statistics.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe the hierarchy of controls to control hazards and mitigate risks in various agriculture workspaces and environments.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Analyze and describe the effect of lost production time due to equipment damage or personal injury during critical times of the year (e.g., seeding, harvest, calving).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze the effect that costs of equipment damage have on production profit margins (e.g., down time, repair costs, insurance costs).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore ways to mitigate risk of damage to equipment (e.g., maintenance schedule, pre-use inspections, scheduled inspections, understanding manufacturer's recommendations and reporting damage).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify the positive and negative effects to using each category (e.g., respiratory, hearing, vision, skin and body) of industry standard personal protective equipment.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify sections of the Saskatchewan Employment Act that apply to owners, employers, contractors, supervisors, suppliers, self-employed persons and workers as it relates to agriculture production operations.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify when an Occupational Health and Safety (OH&S) program is required by law for an agriculture production operation.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Describe the worker's three rights: the right to know, the right to participate and the right to refuse unsafe work.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Research the benefits of completing certifications and programs offered by Work Safe Sask (Mental Health and Wellness, Occupational Health and Safety and Young Career Worker Readiness), Sask Safety Council (Online Agriculture Training System - OATS and Career Safety Education), Motor Safety Association (Introduction to Workplace Safety), Agricultural Health and Safety Network (Respiratory Health in Ag), Sask Prevention (Farm Safety) and the Ministry of Labour Relations and Workplace Safety (Farm Safety).

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Describe basic response plans for common types of emergencies in agriculture operations (e.g., fire, medical aid, entrapment, violent threat, severe storms).

outcomes.statement: Investigate holistic approaches to positive psychological health and safety.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 4A: Psychological Health and Safety - Personal (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine how psychological health forms part of a person's physical, mental, emotional and spiritual well-being.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Analyze the factors (e.g., loss of a loved one, divorce, poor farm year caused by drought and imbalances in chemical, neurological, hormonal and biological systems) that may contribute to mental illness.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate the impact of social media, culture, lack of community resources and an unsupportive social network on mental health.

indicators.label: d
e
indicators.text: Examine the effects that experiences (e.g., residential schools and inter-generational trauma and farm accident) can have on individuals and communities.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify risky behaviours (e.g., alcohol, drugs, gang affiliation and toxic relationships) that can impact positive psychological health.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Analyze how Western, Indigenous, traditional, complementary and alternative approaches to health care can contribute to a holistic perspective of psychological health.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss examples of misconceptions and stigmas associated with mental illness within society.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Identify feelings (e.g., embarrassment, shame and resentment) and behaviours (e.g., abandonment, exclusion and rejection) resulting from societal stigma.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Discuss valuable skills (e.g., positive self-perception, effective communication, stress management and a positive social network) for maintaining positive psychological health.

outcomes.printedWith: Module 5A: Psychological Health and Safety - Workplace (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 4A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe how life/work balance can impact personal wellness.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore the prevalence of mental illness in agricultural producers in Canada.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research how personal financial stress may impact productivity.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe unavoidable stresses (e.g., harvest time, calving season, weather events and relationship challenges) in agriculture production.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the benefits of monitoring and maintaining positive psychological health.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explore practical strategies when poor psychological health prevents an individual from accomplishing farm tasks.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Research sources of support (e.g., websites, telehealth and community centers) for producers experiencing poor psychological health including trauma.

outcomes.statement: Investigate employer and employee psychological health and safety in the workplace.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 6A: Psychological Health and Safety - Employer and Employee (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 5A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore accommodations (e.g., flexible hours, job sharing and modifications to the work environment and duties) that can be requested by employees of businesses in an agriculture setting (e.g., farming operations, chemical companies and grain elevators) to support mental health during peak operating efficiency.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss barriers (e.g., lack of awareness of accommodations, lack of confidence in requesting help, where to find supports, social stigma, fear of reprisal and fear of rejection) that employees face in disclosing a mental health problem or illness and/or requesting accommodations.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe and suggest possible solutions for unavoidable stresses during peak operating times (e.g., harvest time, calving season and weather events) that employers face in providing accommodation requests.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss practical ways that employees can contribute to a psychologically healthy and safe workplace.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research employers' duties and responsibilities to support workplace mental health as outlined in The Saskatchewan Employment Act.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine employers' duty to accommodate employee requests as outlined in the Canadian Human Rights Code.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the history of Indigenous agriculture.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 7A: History of Indigenous Agriculture (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-8 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine the importance of the relationship First Nations and Métis peoples have with the land.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss Indigenous perspectives on agriculture and their connections to the land with an Elder or Knowledge Keeper.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate the impact of settlers on Indigenous agricultural practices.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the agriculture clauses found in the numbered treaties from 1871-1921.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore the difficulties Indigenous farmers experienced through the creation of the Indian Act of 1876. (e.g., the pass and permit system from the late 1800s up to and including 1951).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research the significance of traditional farming methods (e.g., Three Sisters crop model and planting a fish with corn seed) developed by First Nations and Métis communities.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Investigate the importance of the role of bison for First Nations and Métis peoples.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explore the impact the mass elimination of bison had on Indigenous communities.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Describe the inclusion of agriculture (e.g., livestock and farming implements) in the numbered treaties.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Discuss the importance to the First Nations peoples of agriculture being included in the numbered treaties.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Explain the role of livestock (e.g., oxen, horses and cattle) in early Indigenous farming practices.

outcomes.statement: Explore Indigenous contributions to agriculture production.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 7B: Indigenous Contributions in Agriculture (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-8 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 7A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Analyze how working with horses can benefit the rediscovery of the First Nations traditional role of horses.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify plants that were domesticated by First Nations peoples as a crop for a specific purpose (e.g., wild rice, corn, potatoes and tomatoes).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of agricultural stewardship.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe traditional Indigenous agricultural practices (e.g., companion planting, composting and rain gardening) that are used today to improve agricultural sustainability.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss traditional and current Indigenous perspectives on connections to the land and agriculture with an Elder or Knowledge Keeper.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain the role of the four sacred medicines (i.e., tobacco, sage, sweetgrass and cedar) in Indigenous culture.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the current use of agriculture by Indigenous communities in Saskatchewan.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 7C: Contemporary Indigenous Agriculture (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-8 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 7B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore agricultural commodities produced in First Nations communities of Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Analyze the opportunities for growth that agriculture provides First Nations communities.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore programs that facilitate the development of agricultural enterprises among First Nations communities.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Research current agricultural practices (e.g., Treaty Land Sharing Network) that honour treaty rights.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss Indigenous perspectives on the current and future use of agriculture in communities with an Elder or Knowledge Keeper.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explore The Treaty Land Entitlement Framework Agreement and the impact it can have on indigenous agriculture.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explore the barriers (e.g., Treaty and government policies) that exist for Indigenous farmers that limit their farming operations on reserves.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify current programs specific to Indigenous agriculture.

outcomes.statement: Explore how livestock and crop production information is gathered and interpreted.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 8: Information Gathering (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-6 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the need for reliable information in all production sectors.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Determine the reliability of a source of gathered information.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Locate, organize and clarify information in a variety of formats (e.g., spreadsheets, concept webs and graphs).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Interpret animal health labels (e.g., medications) and crop input product information (e.g., product labels on pharmaceuticals, fertilizers and pesticides).

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Identify available government and private sector services in the production of livestock and crops.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explore sources of information on livestock and crop production (e.g., Saskatchewan Ministry of Agriculture and The Western Producer).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Read technical information from an information management system (IMS).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Analyze livestock and crop production information from various sources (e.g., blogs/vlogs, Saskatchewan Soil Information System [SKSIS] and Community Collaborative Rain, Hail and Snow Network [CoCoRHS]).

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Explore programs and services that do not align with First Nations policy and cannot be used by First Nations peoples.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the importance of water stewardship in sustainable agriculture production.

indicators.text: Explain the rationale for choosing a type of ranching, size of operation and breed of livestock for a given farm location.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore the biosecurity and food safety requirements (e.g., ProAction, VBP+ and Start Clean Stay Clean) for livestock production.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine aspects of livestock nutrition programs including sources of feed, prepared rations, feed storage, method of feeding, grazing methods and sources of water.

indicators.label: g

indicators.text: Analyze the suitability of farm locations for a chosen species of livestock and size of operation.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate livestock management practices (e.g., percentage as meat processing, crossbreeding, show and aging livestock and introduction of new animals to the herd or operation) including the ability to handle waste (e.g., manure and carcasses) and herd protection measures (e.g., herd dogs, donkeys and structures).

outcomes.statement: Prepare for the work placement.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 80A: Work Study Preparation (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate, Advanced · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III - Occupational Health and Safety in n The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019.
- the right to know - the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate - in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,
- the right to refuse - work that you believe is unusually dangerous

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent, teacher or other school staff, employer) involved in the work placement.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the business/organization to become familiar with its operations.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: In collaboration with all partners, develop personal and learning goals for the work placement.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents needed for the work placement (e.g., personal career documentation such as a resume or portfolio, permission forms, logs, self- and employer evaluation forms).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop a list of questions that could potentially be asked by the employer/work placement in an interview situation as well as answers to the questions.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Participate in an interview with the employer prior to beginning the work placement.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Reflect upon one's performance during the interview.

outcomes.statement: Examine the relationship between stewardship and sustainability.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 1: Stewardship and Sustainability (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define the term sustainability.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe the purpose and components of each of the four pillars of sustainability (i.e., social, human, economic, environmental).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe what sustainability means in agriculture.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain the concept of stewardship, including who has responsibility for stewardship.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Reflect on what it means to be a good steward.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the relationship between sustainability and stewardship.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Research sustainability and stewardship according to the Seventh Generation Principle.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Propose personal and collective actions that might support the Seventh Generation Principle.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the importance of food and food security.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 2: Food and Food Security (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 1

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore the emotional and physical importance of food, considering factors such as food abundance, food choices and lack of food.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Differentiate between hunger and malnutrition.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain the United Nations’ definition of food security.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze global disparities in food security, considering the differences between developed and developing countries and the challenges faced by each.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine the concept of sustainable food systems and their role in ensuring long-term food security, considering factors such as environmental sustainability, social equity and economic viability.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Defend food security as a basic human right.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Assess the four pillars of food security in relation to availability, access (i.e., affordability), utilization (i.e., cultural relevance) and stability.

indicators.label: h
i
indicators.text: Examine the impact of factors such as income, employment and culture on food insecurity for individuals, families and communities.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Research factors that influence food insecurity internationally (e.g., lack of access to farming lands; conflict, violence and wars; unfair trade rules; natural disasters; inability to adopt modern technology).

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Differentiate between chronic and transitory food insecurity.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Describe actions one might undertake as an individual stakeholder in the food system to enhance food security.

outcomes.statement: Explore solutions to local and global food insecurity.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 3: Local and Global Food Security (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 2

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of food security.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into the impact of food insecurity on Canadians, considering factors such as regional differences and vulnerable population groups.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research grassroots approaches to alleviating food insecurity in Canada (e.g., community fridges, food banks, food drives, community gardens).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate the current global state of food insecurity, including geographic variations and root causes.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Compare the current state of food insecurity in Canada to the global state of food insecurity.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research the prevalence and significance of conflict as a factor in situations of international food insecurity and hunger.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Investigate contemporary and historical examples of food used as a weapon in conflict.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify organizations working to alleviate food insecurity (e.g., Canadian Foodgrains Bank, World Vision, Red Cross) and their responses to global food insecurity.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Investigate the role of trade policies and globalization in influencing food security, including the impact of trade barriers, subsidies, and market volatility on local and global food systems.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Reflect on personal and collective responsibility for addressing local and global food security.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Discuss the roles that individuals, organizations and governments at the local, provincial, First Nations and federal levels can play in alleviating food insecurity.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Identify approaches for improving food security in the local community or region.

outcomes.statement: Explore the importance of food sovereignty.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 4: Food Sovereignty (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-6 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 2

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore the importance of food sovereignty.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Assess the relationship between food sovereignty and food security.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the historic role of trade as an element of food sovereignty in pre-European contact Indigenous societies in what is now Canada.

indicators.label: d
e
indicators.text: Identify challenges and opportunities faced by newcomers and First Nations, Métis and Inuit peoples and communities in achieving food sovereignty.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine successful case studies and initiatives that promote food sovereignty at local, regional, and national levels, highlighting innovative approaches and best practices.

indicators.label: g
h
indicators.text: Investigate the role of trade as it relates to food sovereignty.

outcomes.statement: Examine the impact of colonization and government policies and practices on Indigenous food sovereignty.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 5: Indigenous Food Sovereignty (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-7 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 4

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore traditional Indigenous food sourcing practices.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Compare food sourcing practices of traditional Indigenous, early settler and present-day communities.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate the importance of country foods and wild-harvested foods in traditional and contemporary Indigenous communities.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate the historical and current impact of the Indian Act on Indigenous agricultural practices in Canada.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe the impact of government policies, including the reserve system, and the Peasant Farm Policy, and practices, including the pass system and home farm program, on historical and contemporary Indigenous agricultural practices.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Summarize the impact of prairie colonization and the reserve system on Indigenous food sovereignty.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Investigate agricultural and food sourcing initiatives currently underway on various Saskatchewan First Nations to achieve food sovereignty.

outcomes.statement: Investigate sustainable food systems.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 6: Food Systems (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-7 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 3

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the concept of a food system.

indicators.label: b
c
d
indicators.text: Describe the interconnectedness of food systems on a local, provincial, national and global scale.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Compare the operation of food systems within different regions of Canada.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify primary production and value-added agricultural products produced in various regions of Saskatchewan, including the local area.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify characteristics of a sustainable food system.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Investigate factors that may challenge the sustainability of a food system.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Propose solutions to issues currently challenging the sustainability of food systems.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Analyze the impact of consumer behavior and food choices on food systems, exploring topics such as food marketing and dietary trends.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Reflect on personal that actions support local sustainable food systems (e.g., eating and buying local, cooking more, composting).

outcomes.statement: Examine the importance of food literacy.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 7: Food Literacy (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-6 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 6

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define the term food literacy.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Assess the benefits to self and others (e.g., family, community) of being food literate.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Analyze the impact of cultural, social, and economic factors on food literacy, considering how factors such as socioeconomic status, cultural traditions, and food marketing influence food choices and behaviors.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine the role of Health Canada, the Canadian Food Inspection Agency and Agriculture and Agri-food Canada in establishing policies, regulations and standards related to the safety and nutritional quality of all food sold in Canada.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine the role of education and awareness in promoting sustainable food practices, including initiatives aimed at fostering food literacy, promoting responsible consumption, and reducing food waste.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the relationship between a healthy diet, a nutritional food supply and nutritional well-being, and the health and productivity of Canadians.

indicators.label: g
h
indicators.text: Explain the reasons for food labelling in Canada.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Assess personal knowledge of food labelling information.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Differentiate between information for health and nutritional purposes and information for marketing purposes found on food packaging in Canada.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Identify how food labels could be misleading through the application of marketing tactics.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Examine the role of media and digital technologies in shaping food literacy, discussing the influence of food advertisements, social media, and online resources on consumer behavior and food choices.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Define the concept of food miles/food kilometres.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Identify the origin of an imported food item (e.g., fresh fruit, spice, coffee), the food miles/kilometres associated with that item and potential modes of transportation used to get it to its destination.

indicators.label: o
indicators.text: Articulate the limitations of using only food miles/kilometres as the measure for deciding what is a good food choice.

indicators.label: p
indicators.text: Compare Canada’s reliance on imported versus domestic foods.

indicators.label: q
indicators.text: Identify food traceability requirements and methods used in Canada.

indicators.label: r
indicators.text: Assess the importance of food traceability.

indicators.label: s
indicators.text: Debate the merits of shopping for local and Canadian food.

indicators.label: t
indicators.text: Appraise personal food literacy skills and understanding.

indicators.label: u
indicators.text: Develop a plan for becoming more food literate.

outcomes.statement: Assess the environmental, economic and social impacts of food loss and food waste.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 8: Food Loss and Food Waste (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 7

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Differentiate between food loss and food waste.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research factors that can contribute to food loss (e.g., pests attacking a crop, animal deaths, transportation issues) and food waste (e.g., purchasing or preparing more food than can be consumed, inadequate storage).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research traditional Indigenous approaches to food efficiency, food waste and food loss.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify measures the Canadian agriculture industry takes to reduce or prevent food loss, including protection from loss to pests, spoilage and advances in processing and transportation.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Define the term upcycling as it pertains to by-products of food and reduction of food waste.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate the redirection of unusable and unwanted food from the human food stream into food for animals.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Compare Canadian food waste and food loss data to that of a country in the developing world and speculate on reasons for differences.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of curbing food loss and food waste to help address global food insecurity.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Explain the difference between “best before” and “expiry” date labels on purchased foods.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Develop a plan for reducing personal food waste (e.g., shopping with a grocery list, finding new ways to use leftovers, meal planning, freezing foods).

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Investigate organizations dedicated to reducing food waste in Saskatchewan and Canada.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Propose actions (e.g., donating unsold fresh goods to local charities, educating consumers on ways to cut household food waste, implementing employee education programs) that retailers such as grocery stores, bakeries and restaurants can take to curb food waste.

outcomes.statement: Examine the influence of media and marketing on consumer food choices.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 9: Media and Marketing (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify sources (e.g., social media, newspaper, television, word of mouth) available to the Canadian public for information on the agriculture and food industry.

indicators.label: b

indicators.label: d

indicators.label: e

indicators.label: f
g
h

outcomes.statement: Assess the sustainability of agricultural practices in Saskatchewan.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 10: Sustainable Agriculture in Saskatchewan (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-7 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 3

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Differentiate between primary production (i.e., raw agricultural products such as cereal grains or vegetables) and value-added agricultural products (e.g., fruits made into pies or jams, meats made into jerky).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore the origins and uses of agricultural by-products (e.g., poultry feathers for pillows, canola meal for livestock feed, flax straw and hemp for building materials, straw from cereal grains for bedding for animals or ethanol production).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Assess statistics related to Saskatchewan’s exporting and importing of both primary and value-added agricultural products.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate the importance and application of standards and regulations for export, import and trade in agricultural products within Canadian and international contexts.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Compare Indigenous approaches to food production within First Nations communities in Saskatchewan pre- and post-contact.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine factors (e.g., religious, social, cultural, ecological and economic) that influence agricultural practices.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe the relationship between sustainable agriculture and sustainable food systems.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of soil health and sustainable soil management practices.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Examine current practices that have improved the sustainability of agriculture in the province (e.g., no till seeding and variable rate technology).

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Research innovations in sustainable agriculture practices that are attributed to Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Identify emerging sustainability actions being undertaken voluntarily by Saskatchewan food producers.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Explore factors (e.g., availability of cultivated farmland, innovations in crop varieties) that have helped to position Saskatchewan as a major global supplier of food.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Examine the impact of scale of operations (i.e., small garden plots, 5 acre plots, 10,000 acre plots) on food production in Saskatchewan, including social, economic and environmental factors.

outcomes.statement: Assess the impact of technology and innovation on agricultural production in Saskatchewan.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 11: Technology and Innovation (Core) · Suggested Time: 8-10 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 10

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the role of research and development in agricultural innovation.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Differentiate between natural selection, traditional plant breeding and scientific genetic manipulation in crops.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate the role of data analytics and farm management software in decision-making processes, including yield prediction, disease monitoring, and real-time monitoring of crop and soil conditions.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Research the history of technology and innovation, including automation, in Saskatchewan agriculture.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate current application of innovative machine technology and crop and plant science biotechnology in Saskatchewan agriculture.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine the current state and emerging opportunities associated with digital agriculture in Saskatchewan and Canada.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Summarize reasons for innovation in Saskatchewan’s agriculture sector.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Describe the relationship between agriculture biotechnology and food system sustainability.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Investigate the purpose of, and benefits derived from, Saskatchewan’s Global Institute for Food Security.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the importance of digital agriculture to sustainable food systems.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 12: Digital Agriculture (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 11

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe the characteristics of digitally assisted precision agriculture.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain potential environmental and economic benefits of digitally assisted precision agriculture.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research current technological innovations used in digitally assisted precision agriculture, such as Global Positioning Systems [GPS], precision machinery and drones.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore emerging trends and future directions in digital agriculture, such as artificial intelligence, robotics, and autonomous farming systems, and their potential impacts on farm productivity.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Assess how various types of digital farm data informs the management of small areas within fields (e.g., effective application of fertilizers, pesticides, tillage and irrigation water).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss issues (e.g., ownership, security, control) related to farming data.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Research challenges and opportunities encountered by a farming operation that implements digitally assisted precision agriculture.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Assess the role of digitally assisted precision agriculture in supporting sustainable food systems.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate factors (e.g., consumer demand for healthier food choices, sensationalized claims in marketing and media, convenience, changing cultural demographics, environmental impact) that contribute to changing food consumption preferences of Saskatchewan residents.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research changes in the types of food products available locally over the past decade and quarter century.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate influences (e.g., diverse cultures, food trends, health needs) on product availability in Saskatchewan grocery stores.

indicators.label: d
e

indicators.label: f

outcomes.statement: Assess the importance of animal health and well-being to sustainable food systems.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 15: Animal Health and Well-being (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 10

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Differentiate between animal health and animal well-being.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss animal welfare as a human responsibility.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss the concept of biosecurity and its role in preventing the introduction and spread of diseases in livestock populations.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine the Five Freedoms (i.e., freedom from hunger and thirst; freedom from discomfort; freedom from pain, injury, and disease; freedom to express normal and natural behavior [e.g., having sufficient space]; and freedom from fear and distress) as the globally recognized gold standard in animal welfare.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss how voluntary and mandatory assurance systems (e.g., Verified Beef Production Plus and proAction), can assure consumers that animal welfare standards are being maintained.

indicators.label: f
g

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Assess essential elements (e.g., adequate ventilation and space, proper drainage, access to food and water) of animal welfare during transportation of livestock.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Explain the importance of animal health in supporting sustainable food systems.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Evaluate current federal and provincial laws and regulations for animal health and welfare. (e.g., Federal Health of Animals Act, Saskatchewan Animal Protection Act and Regulations 2018, Saskatchewan Animal Health Act 2019).

outcomes.statement: Prepare for the work placement.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 80A: Work Study Preparation (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate, Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 10

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III - Occupational Health and Safety in n The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019.
- the right to know - the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate - in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,
- the right to refuse - work that you believe is unusually dangerous.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent, teacher or other school staff, employer) involved in the work placement.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the business/organization to become familiar with its operations.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: In collaboration with all partners, develop personal and learning goals for the work placement.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents needed for the work placement (e.g., personal career documentation such as a resume or portfolio, permission forms, logs, self- and employer evaluation forms).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop a list of questions that could potentially be asked by the employer/work placement in an interview situation as well as answers to the questions.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Participate in an interview with the employer prior to beginning the work placement.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Reflect upon one's performance during the interview.
