indicators.text: Articulate what musical, elements, techniques, tools, language and practices were used to create the composition.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss legal and ethical arts practices when composing or arranging (e.g., copyright, plagiarism).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Use technology (e.g., recording or notation) to generate or complement musical material.

outcomes.statement: Apply complex skills, practices and techniques accurately and consistently during ensemble rehearsal and performance.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Respond to changes in function and role of sections within an ensemble.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Demonstrate the ability to perform specific tasks particular to the instrument in the ensemble.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Individually attend to melodic phrasing, rhythmic accuracy and articulation in the preparation and performance of music.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Play in tune with good balance and tone and know the intonation tendencies of one’s instrument.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Demonstrate knowledge of the skills, attitudes and techniques necessary for ensemble performance.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Employ rehearsal techniques (e.g., making notes, respectfully providing and applying feedback, making and trying out musical decisions).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Demonstrate leadership as a performer by modelling and/or offering assistance, ideas and guidance to other performers during rehearsal/practice.

outcomes.statement: Incorporate, independently, constructive criticism and reflection on personal and group performance.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine own musical expressions, in real time and/or using recording technology, in order to improve through critical self-reflection (e.g., create inquiry questions such as What can I do to get better? How could I change this performance, arrangement or composition?).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Reflect on the input of others (e.g., peers, teacher, adjudicator).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify main areas of focus for musical growth and set and monitor specific musical goals.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine and recommend various solutions to common musical challenges and goals.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe the development of personal musical skills and knowledge.

outcomes.statement: Explore and analyze the impact and role of music in own life and consider and plan for continuing engagement in music.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Engage with local, Saskatchewan and Canadian musicians, including Indigenous musicians, to expand learning opportunities.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Extend understanding of First Nations and Métis music and cultures through dialogue with local Elders or Knowledge Keepers.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Broaden musical experience and interests through active participation (e.g., trying different instruments, attending concerts, joining other ensembles).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Research and describe the benefits of participating in diverse musical and other arts activities (e.g., community ensembles, drum groups, live performances, jams).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine the role and impact of music in own lives (e.g., mental health, peer group relationships, social change) and recognize the value of music as a life-long source of enjoyment and personal fulfilment.

outcomes.statement: Listen and respond, independently, to musical expressions of self and others, conducting critical analysis using musical terminology.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Create a list of specific criteria to use in assessing performances.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Critique own performance.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Critique performance of others and provide feedback (e.g., What is going well? What could be improved?) using appropriate musical terminology.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Apply attained knowledge to improve personal and ensemble performance.

outcomes.statement: Analyze the historical, cultural and social contexts of repertoire.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Internalize and convey the intent of the piece.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Compare music from diverse periods, worldviews or contexts (e.g., common themes such as nationalism, social movements, historical events such as revolutions).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the historical, cultural and social contexts of composers’ works and share with others.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discover, practice and perform music from various time periods, decades, genres, styles and worldviews.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss where the wind band fits in the spectrum of performance music.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Develop an understanding of cultural appropriation in music and respect and follow related protocols.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explore how evolving technology and media have influenced and changed how music is created, produced, distributed and shared (e.g., instrument evolution, recording, printing press, online music sites).

outcomes.statement: Investigate diverse Canadian and international music literature including established and historically under-represented composers.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine the work of both established and historically under-represented composers (e.g., inclusive of Saskatchewan, Canadian, Indigenous, minority, gender and sexually diverse composers).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Study and perform wind band works composed by living composers (e.g., inclusive of Saskatchewan, Canadian, Indigenous, minority, gender and sexually diverse composers).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Connect composers’ personal experiences to the literature where appropriate.

outcomes.statement: Evaluate the quality of repertoire.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine and play a range of repertoire (e.g., traditional wind band, composers of diverse genders, Indigenous, self-published, young composers, variety of genres and styles).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine and play repertoire that utilizes a variety of compositional techniques and devices.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Develop criteria to use in determining quality of repertoire.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze and determine the quality of repertoire based on criteria developed.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze and discuss characteristics of high-quality repertoire representative of various worldviews (e.g., traditional wind band, gender and sexually diverse composers, Indigenous, self-published, young composers, variety of compositional techniques and devices).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Design a well-rounded concert program and provide a rationale for choices (e.g., diversity of genres and styles).

outcomes.statement: Examine how traditional and contemporary First Nations and Métis instrumental music has been preserved or changed over time.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research and engage with Elders and local Métis and First Nations musicians and composers to discuss how music varies among communities and individuals.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate local protocols and traditional/natural laws related to creating and performing music (e.g., gifting of music, cultural appropriation).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss the historical context of Indigenous music traditions (e.g., forced relocations, banning of traditional music in Saskatchewan and elsewhere).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss examples of contemporary First Nations and Métis instrumentalists including how music has changed over time.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss how music has changed according to values and beliefs of the time and place (e.g., treaty education outcome SI12 - investigate the values and beliefs of self, family, community, and society in relation to the importance of honouring the spirit and intent of treaties).

courses.name: Biology 20, 30
courses.problem: No outcomes are published on the site for this curriculum.

outcomes.statement: Create and carry out a plan to explore one or more topics of personal interest relevant to Biology 30 in depth.
outcomes.printedWith: DM, SI, TPS

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Design a scientific investigation related to a topic of study in Biology 30 that includes a testable question, a hypothesis, an experimental design that will test the hypothesis and detailed procedures for collecting and analyzing data. (STSE, S)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Carry out an experiment following established scientific protocols to investigate a question of interest related to one or more of the topics of Biology 30. (S, A, K, STSE)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Assemble and reflect on a portfolio that demonstrates an understanding of a topic of interest related to biology. (S, A)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Design, construct and evaluate the effectiveness of a device, model or technique that demonstrates the scientific principles underlying concept related to a Biology 30 topic. (STSE, S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Debate an issued related to biology, including developing materials to support the arguments for and arguments against a position. (A, K, S)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Share the results of student-directed research through a display, presentation, performance, demonstration, song, game, commercial, fine art representation, video or research paper. (S)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Construct a tool (e.g., rubric, checklist, self-evaluation form or peer-evaluation form) to assess the process and products involved in a student-directed study. (S, A)

outcomes.statement: Explore how scientific understandings of life and its characteristics change in light of new evidence.
outcomes.printedWith: CP, DM

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain what characteristics you use to define what is or what is not considered living. (A, K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Distinguish among scientific, First Nations, Métis, Inuit and other cultural perspectives with respect to the question of what constitutes life. (STSE, A)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore how scientific definitions of life have changed over time as a result of advances in technologies and scientific understanding. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Debate whether or not entities such as viruses, viroids and prions should be considered alive. (S, STSE)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Recognize the contribution of scientists (e.g., Francesco Redi, Louis Pasteur, Stanley Miller, Harold Urey and Lynn Margulis) whose experiments contributed to a wider understanding of life from a biological perspective. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine the impact of the cell theory and advances in microscopy on past and current scientific definitions of life. (K, STSE, A)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Create a representation of historical events related to the study of life. (K, S)

outcomes.statement: Examine the significance of evolution as a key unifying theme in biology through the principles, processes and patterns of biological evolution.
outcomes.printedWith: SI, DM

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify common misconceptions (e.g., individuals evolve, natural selection is evolution, evolution is random and evolution is a theory) regarding biological evolution. (K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Outline the key principles (e.g., descent with modification, fitness as a result of adaptations and struggle for existence) and processes (e.g., natural selection, genetic drift and selective breeding) of biological evolution. (K, STSE, A)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate how humans use selective breeding (i.e., artificial selection) to enhance desirable characteristics in organisms. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain the importance of the concept of the last universal common ancestor (LUCA) in understanding evolutionary relationships among organisms. (K, A)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Interpret cladograms and phylogenetic trees to determine evolutionary relationships among organisms. (S)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify historical perspectives and key contributions to the field of evolutionary biology by scientists such as Jean-Baptiste Lamarck, Thomas Robert Malthus, Charles Darwin, Alfred Russel Wallace, Alfred Wegener, f. Theodosius Dobzhansky, Lynn Margulis, Stephen Jay Gould, and E. O. Wilson. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss how Darwin's observations informed the development of the theory of natural selection as a mechanism of evolution. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Recognize how the principles of natural selection occur at the level of the individual and may result in the evolution of the population. (K)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Examine how particular selective pressures (e.g., competition, predation, changes in climate, parasitism and pollution) acting on an individual can influence a population over time. (K, S)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Explain how geographic, temporal and behavioural isolation can influence speciation. (K)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Identify concepts (e.g., gradualism versus punctuated equilibrium, convergent evolution, divergent evolution, coevolution, adaptive radiation, mass-extinction and the evolutionary arms race) that are only evident when examining evolution over a multitude of generations extending to geological time. (K)

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Examine how scientists use the fossil record, radioactive dating, comparative embryology and homologous and analogous structures as evidence of biological evolution. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Explore human evolution in relationship to other primates, considering the Out of Africa hypothesis and the agricultural revolution. (STSE, A, K)

outcomes.statement: Investigate cell structure and processes, including energy transfer and transport of materials, in unicellular and multicellular organisms which are representative of each kingdom.
outcomes.printedWith: SI, TPS

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Pose questions regarding the diverse ways in which organisms perform life's processes such as locomotion, reproduction, acquiring energy and responding to stimuli. (S)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Analyze the processes (e.g., chemosynthesis, photosynthesis and cellular respiration) through which organisms from each kingdom synthesize energy in the form of adenosine triphosphate (ATP). (K)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe how biologically important molecules work together to form complex structures (e.g., cell membranes, ribosomes and deoxyribonucleic acid [DNA]). (K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Compare the structure and composition (e.g., chitin, cellulose and peptidoglycan) of cell walls in a variety of organisms. (K)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Design and carry out a plan to gather evidence of how unicellular organisms, such as yeast or paramecia, exhibit characteristics of living things. (STSE, A, S, K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research how structural and biochemical adaptations enable some archaeans (e.g., halophiles, thermophiles and methanogens) to live in extreme environments. (S, K)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Observe and compare structures (e.g., pseudopods, cilia and flagella) and processes that enable locomotion in unicellular organisms such as amoeba, paramecium, dinoflagellates and euglena. (K, S)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Research how advances in tools (e.g., light microscopes, transmission electron microscopes and scanning electron microscopes) and techniques (e.g., culturing cells and cell fractionation) have enabled scientists to develop deeper understandings of cell structure and processes. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Design, construct and evaluate the function of a model to demonstrate passive and active transport of materials at the interface of the cell membrane. (A, STSE, S)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Demonstrate how osmotic pressure helps maintain homeostasis in cells. (K, S)

outcomes.statement: Compare the anatomies, physiologies and behaviours of multicellular organisms including protists, fungi, plants and animals.
outcomes.printedWith: SI

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Compare the anatomical structures and functions of organisms using microscopy, simulations and/or dissections where appropriate. (K, S, A)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss the ethical implications of using model organisms (e.g., Aspergillus nidulans, slime moulds, C. elegans, Arabidopsis, Drosophila and mice) and humans to further scientific understandings of anatomy and physiology. (A, STSE)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research First Nations and Métis perspectives regarding the use of living things for scientific research. (STSE, A)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze the evolutionary costs and benefits of various reproductive strategies evident among multicellular organisms. (K)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore the behavioural, structural and physiological adaptations that enable organisms to defend themselves against threats, such as pathogens, predators and disease. (K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Design and carry out an experiment to determine how multicellular organisms respond to various stimuli (e.g., light, touch, gravity, pheromones and other chemicals). (STSE, K, S, A)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify how multicellular organisms maintain homeostasis through processes such as biofeedback, fluid regulation and thermoregulation. (K)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Compare how multicellular organisms acquire, transport and excrete materials (e.g., nutrients, hormones and wastes) intraorganismally and interorganismally, including through symbiotic relationships (e.g., mutualism, commensalism, and parasitism). (K)

outcomes.statement: Explore how the dynamic nature of biological classification reflects advances in scientific understanding of relationships among organisms.
outcomes.printedWith: SI, CP

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss how classification systems are designed by humans to meet various needs. (STSE, A)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research how First Nations, Métis and Inuit peoples represent their understandings of relationships among living things. (STSE, A)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the contributions of scientists, including Carl Linnaeus, in developing accepted scientific conventions for the naming of organisms. (K, S, STSE)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss how the characteristics of the taxonomic hierarchy represent relationships among organisms. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the challenges associated with classification, including defining taxa and classifying certain organisms, such as protists. (K, A)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Create and use dichotomous keys to gain insights into the challenges of biological classification. (STSE, S)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Demonstrate, using cladograms, how phylogenetic relationships inform our contemporary understanding of biological classification. (K, S)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Critique the strengths and limitations of historical and contemporary systems of classifying living things. (K, A, STSE)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Develop generalizations about the value of biological classification systems. (A, STSE)

outcomes.statement: Explore classical (i.e. Mendelian) and current (i.e. chromosomal) understandings of biological inheritance.
outcomes.printedWith: SI

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Pose questions about why and how offspring only inherit some traits from their parents. (S, A)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore patterns of inheritance by interpreting pedigrees, including your own family tree. (K, A, S)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss the historical development of Mendelian genetics, including why Gregor Mendel is considered the "father of genetics". (STSE, K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of probability in predicting the likelihood of inheriting particular traits. (K)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Distinguish among patterns of inheritance (e.g., dominant and recessive alleles, sex-linked traits, codominance, incomplete dominance, multiple alleles and polygenic inheritance) of heritable traits. (K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Determine an organism's phenotype from its genotype, and where possible, its genotype from its phenotype. (S, K)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Construct Punnett squares for monohybrid crosses using P1 genotypes (i.e., homozygous and heterozygous) to determine genotypic and phenotypic frequencies for F1 and F2 generations. (S)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Describe how gene flow, genetic drift and natural selection influence the frequency of alleles within a population. (K)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Recognize that scientists now understand chromosomes to be the mechanism of Mendel's laws (i.e., law of segregation, law of independent assortment and law of dominance). (STSE, A, K)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Investigate the importance of meiosis, including crossing-over, in creating genetic variation in gametes and non-disjunction in creating chromosomal abnormalities. (K)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Discuss the types of chromosomal mutations (duplication, deletion, inversion, and translocation) that can occur during genetic processes. (K, S)

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Identify, using karyotypes, nondisjunction mutations (e.g., Klinefelter, Down, and Turner syndromes) that can occur during genetic processes. (K, S)

outcomes.statement: Investigate how genetic information is stored, transmitted and expressed at the molecular level.
outcomes.printedWith: SI, CP

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Appreciate how the discovery of the DNA molecule as the chemical basis of inheritance has fundamentally transformed the field of biology. (A, STSE)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the nature of the predominant scientific culture when scientists such as Erwin Chargaff, Rosalind Franklin, Maurice Wilkins, James Watson and Francis Crick were investigating the chemical basis of inheritance. (A, STSE, S)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Assess the importance of the structure of the DNA molecule to its ability to store, transmit and express genetic information. (K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Model molecular genetic processes of DNA replication and protein synthesis (i.e., transcription and translation), including the roles of DNA, mRNA, tRNA and rRNA. (K, S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the types of point mutations (base pair substitution, insertion, deletion) and the effects of these point mutations (missense, nonsense, and neutrality), including the role of reading frame and frameshift effects during additions and deletions of one or two bases. (K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the value of DNA proofreading and repair and its role in preventing genetic mutations. (K)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Assess the role of genetic mutation in the process of evolution. (K)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Describe how environmental and epigenetic factors influence genetic expression. (K)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Model or simulate common techniques (e.g., agarose gel electrophoresis, polymerase chain reaction, DNA sequencing and DNA fingerprinting) used by molecular geneticists. (S, K, A, STSE)

outcomes.statement: Explore the impacts of historical, current and emerging biotechnologies on self, society and the environment.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify examples of historical, current and emerging biotechnologies (e.g., selective breeding, applications of fermentation, genetic engineering, cloning, gene therapy, assistive reproductive technologies and synthetic biology). (K, A, STSE)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore how societal pressures such as food, energy and resource shortages can drive the development of biotechnologies. (A, K, STSE)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research a medical (e.g., 3-D bio printing, personalized medicine, genetic testing and screening and gene therapy) or industrial (e.g., use of recombinant DNA, biofuels and bioremediation) application of biotechnology. (S, STSE)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore potential positive and negative impacts of a specific biotechnology (e.g., the use of stem cells, genetically modified and synthetic organisms and synthetic DNA) on individuals and society. (A, STSE)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore how the use and misuse of antibiotics has led to increased bacterial resistance, including the emergence of superbugs. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Critique how individuals and groups use and misuse scientific information to support their positions regarding biotechnologies such as vaccines. (A, STSE)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Critique the media's role in crafting public perception related to biotechnologies (e.g., vaccines, genetically modified organisms and genetic screening). (STSE, A, S)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Analyze the role of regulation and legislation in providing a level of public safety pertaining to applications of biotechnology. (STSE)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Defend a position related to intellectual property rights in biotechnology such as genome ownership and whether patents should include owning the rights to organisms or parts of organisms. (S, A, STSE)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Examine the Human Genome Project (HGP) as an example of a collaborative scientific endeavour. (A, STSE)

outcomes.statement:
Extend understanding of functions including:
- algebraic functions (polynomial, rational, power)
- transcendental functions (exponential, logarithmic, trigonometric)
- piecewise functions, including absolute value.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, CN, ME, R, T, V]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify functions as algebraic, transcendental, and piecewise from their graphs and from their equations.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify functions as being even, odd, increasing, decreasing, one-to-one, and many-to-one from their graphs and from their equations.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Critique the statement, “The graph of an absolute value function will be located entirely above the x-axis.”

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for determining the domain of a function from its equation and from its graphical representation.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Develop, generalize, explain, and apply strategies for determining the range of a function from its equation and from its graphical representation.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify and express the domain and range of a function using set and interval notation.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Develop, explain, and apply strategies for determining characteristics including symmetry, direction, and end behaviour of functions from their equations and from their graphs.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Analyze rational functions to determine conditions where x intercepts, vertical asymptotes, and holes exist by identifying the values of the domain that produce values which are zero, undefined, or indeterminate.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Critique the statement, “If the denominator of a rational function equals zero at $x = a$, then the rational function has a vertical asymptote at $x = a$.”

outcomes.statement:
Extend understanding of factoring, absolute value, and solving inequalities to include:
- rational expressions
- double inequalities
- absolute value inequalities.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, CN, ME, R]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Extend and apply factoring by greatest common factor (GCF) to include negative and rational exponents.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Extend and apply factoring over the set of rational numbers to the set of real numbers.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Critique the statement, “All polynomials can be factored.”

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Develop, explain, and apply strategies for factoring sum of cubes, difference of cubes, and $x_^n-y_^n$ (where n is a positive integer).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Develop, explain, and apply strategies for solving inequalities containing rational expressions.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Develop, explain, and apply strategies for solving double inequalities.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Develop, explain, and apply strategies for solving rational equations which include absolute value expressions.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop, explain, and apply strategies for solving absolute value inequalities containing rational expressions.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate understanding of limits and continuity.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, CN, ME, PS, R, T, V]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Develop and explain the meaning of a limit.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the difference between the limit of a function and the value of a function.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Critique the statement, “If a function has a limit of L as x approaches a, then as x-values get close to a, the y-values of the function will get progressively closer to L.”

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Determine the value of a limit and express the value using limit notation when given:
- a graph
- an algebraic expression.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze the graph of a function to determine if it is continuous.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Analyze the equation of a function to determine if it continuous.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Develop, explain, and apply strategies for determining if a function is continuous at a given point.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text:
Develop, explain, and apply strategies for determining the type of discontinuity (removable, jump, or infinite) when given:
- a graph
- an algebraic expression.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Develop, explain, and apply strategies (e.g., direct substitution, factoring, simplifying, rationalizing) to determine limits, at real numbers and infinity, of functions including absolute value, root, and piecewise.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Identify the conditions under which a limit does not exist.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate understanding of differentiation based on slope as a rate of change.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, CN, PS, R, V]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify and explain situations in which slope is used to describe a rate of change.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Interpret and explain the difference between average rate of change and instantaneous rate of change.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Solve situational problems involving average rates of change and instantaneous rates of change.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Develop, explain, and apply strategies for determining the slope of the tangent line at a particular point by finding the slopes of secant lines.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Develop, explain, and apply the following definition of a derivative: $\lim_{h→0}{f(x+h)-f(x)}/h$

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Develop, explain, and apply rules of differentiation:
- power
- product
- quotient
- chain.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Apply two or more differentiation rules to a function.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Critique the statement, “It is possible to differentiate any function with the rules that we have studied.”

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Identify the value(s) of x where a function is not differentiable.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Critique the statement, “If a function is continuous, then it is differentiable.”

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Develop, explain, and apply the process of implicit differentiation.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Determine the equation of the tangent line and normal line at a specific point on a function.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Express derivatives using a variety of notations such as $f'(x)$, $y'$, $d/d_\x$, and $d_\y/d_\x$.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Critique the statement, “The $f'(x)$ notation for the derivative is superior to the $d_\y/d_\x$ notation.”

outcomes.statement: Extend understanding of curve sketching by applying differentiation and limits.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, CN, V]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Develop, explain, and apply strategies for finding higher order derivatives and their notations.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Develop, explain, and apply strategies for using the first derivative to determine:
- critical points
- increasing and decreasing intervals.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Develop, explain, and apply strategies for using the second derivative to determine:
- points of inflection
- concavity intervals.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe the difference between relative and absolute extrema.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Apply the first and second derivatives to determine relative and absolute extrema.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Analyze graphical representations of $f(x)$ to identify critical point(s), increasing and decreasing intervals, point(s) of inflection, and concavity intervals.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify characteristics of $f(x)$ when given the graph of the first derivative and/or second derivative.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify characteristics of $f(x)$ when given descriptions of the first derivative and/or second derivative.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Apply understanding of limits to determine vertical and horizontal asymptotes.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Sketch the graph of a function with and without the use of technology.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Critique the statement, “An absolute maximum or minimum value occurs at $x=a$, if and only if $f'(a) = 0$.”

outcomes.statement:
Demonstrate understanding of the application of derivatives to solve problems including:
- optimization
- rates of change
- related rates.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, CN, ME, PS, V]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Solve situational problems involving optimization as they apply to topics such as area, volume, and cost.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Solve situational problems involving rates of change as they apply to topics such as business, motion, and science.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Solve situational problems involving related rates by the application of implicit differentiation.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Critique the statement, “If the rate of change of the radius of a circle doubles, then the rate of change of the area will also double.”

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate understanding of transcendental function derivatives and their applications.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, CN, R, T, V]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Develop an understanding of e using limits.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Utilize the squeeze theorem to evaluate limits involving trigonometric functions.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Develop, explain, and apply strategies to determine derivatives of the following transcendental functions:
- exponential and logarithmic functions using any base
- sine and cosine functions.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Apply first and second derivatives to sketch graphs of:
- exponential and logarithmic functions using any base
- sine and cosine functions
- composite transcendental functions.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Critique the statement, “A function and its derivative are always different.”

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Solve situational problems involving the derivatives of transcendental functions.

outcomes.statement:
Demonstrate understanding of indefinite and definite integration:
- by sight
- by substitution
- as used in the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.
outcomes.printedWith: [C, CN, ME, PS, T, V]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Distinguish between indefinite and definite integration.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Critique the statement, “If a function can be differentiated, then it can be integrated.”

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Determine indefinite integrals by sight.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Determine indefinite integrals by substitution.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Apply the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus to evaluate definite integrals by sight and by substitution.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Solve situational questions involving integration.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Critique the statement, “The integral of $f'(x)dx$ equals $f(x)$.”

indicators.label: h
indicators.text:
Develop, explain, and apply strategies for determining the area bounded by:
- a curve and the x-axis over [a,b]
- two curves.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Critique the statement, “To integrate any power, we apply in reverse the power rule for differentiation.”

courses.name: Career and Work Exploration 10, 20, A30, B30

outcomes.statement: Investigate the career/life development process.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 1: An Introduction to Career Development (Core) · Suggested Time: 1-2 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss career/life development as a non-linear and life-long process.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Differentiate between job, occupation and career.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe the three levels (i.e., awareness, exploration and experiential) of the career/life development process.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Reflect on the career journey to date for self and a trusted adult.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss potential future experiences that will have an impact on one’s lifelong career journey.

outcomes.statement: Explore transferable skills.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 2: Transferable Skills (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the term transferable skills and provide examples of transferable skills within the context of specific occupations or jobs.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Compare the skills described by the Employability Skills and the skills described by the Essential Skills taxonomies which were developed by the Conference Board of Canada and Human Resources and Service Development Canada respectively.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Compare transferable skills to soft skills.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Showcase one’s transferable and soft skills in a personal career portfolio.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore volunteer activities within the community and discuss the opportunities they provide for enhancing one’s transferable skills.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss opportunities to enhance one’s transferable skills through leisure activities.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Analyze local and provincial employment advertisements found in a variety of sources (e.g., online, print and social media) for common job requirements, including skills.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explore and discuss ways to develop and improve upon one’s skill set while still in high school.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Describe how skills developed in high school can be transferred or applied to the workplace.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Discuss how transferable skills might evolve and change throughout one’s career journey.

outcomes.statement: Construct a personal career portfolio.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 3: Career Portfolios (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-10 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 2

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Reflect upon personal accomplishments, strengths, talents, skills, traits, abilities, interests, education and training as the basis for the development and organization of one’s career artifacts.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Generate a list of the types of artifacts (e.g., certificates, examples of school work/projects, photographs, videos, blogs, vlogs, personal web sites, awards, resume, cover letter and micro-credentials) that showcase one’s accomplishments, strengths, talents, skills, traits, abilities, interests, education and training.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of organizing one’s career artifacts in a print or online/digital portfolio.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss common steps (e.g., collecting, reflecting and selecting) for determining artifacts that should be included in a career portfolio.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the benefits of having separate personal and career portfolios for school, career goals, personal life and work.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Develop one’s career portfolio that includes a resume, cover letter and other relevant artifacts.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Reflect on the content within one’s career portfolio to answer questions such as:
- Who am I?
- What are my strengths and weaknesses?
- How have I demonstrated my talents, skills and abilities?
- What are some of my accomplishments both in and out of school?
- What are my interests?

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Describe the process and rationale for editing or modifying career artifacts (e.g., documents such as a cover letter or resume) to suit the needs of a specific job application.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Explore how on-line platforms and social media tools can be used to develop and/or organize career artifacts.

outcomes.statement: Explore types of work.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 4: Types of Work (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 1

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Differentiate between types of work such as full-time, part-time, seasonal, contract, gig, casual, shift, self-employment, entrepreneurship and volunteer.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss when and why individuals might engage in each type of work.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Generate a list of jobs in one’s community and classify them according to the types of work.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss how being employed or volunteering supports positive mental health and engaged citizenship.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Reflect on questions such as:
- Why do people work?
- Why do people choose a particular occupation?
- What are my career goals and how will I achieve them?
- Why do I want to or not want to pursue a particular career?

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research the concept of non-traditional careers and provide examples relevant to one’s community, province and country.

outcomes.statement: Explore the potential impact of networking on one’s career journey.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 5: Recognizing Networks (Optional) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 1

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define networking.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Differentiate among personal, social and career networks.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Describe one’s personal, social and career networks by answering questions such as:
- Whom do I know?
- What do I do outside of school?
- What opportunities exist or could exist because of these networks?

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Recognize how networking can impact one’s career opportunities and support one’s career journey.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss how online and social media activity as well as one’s digital identity can positively and negatively impact such things as employment status, employability and career opportunities.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify potential allies (e.g., people, groups, businesses, post-secondary institutions and training institutions) that could be a part of one’s network to support at least one career development interest.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe ways (e.g., volunteering, job shadows and informational interviews) to build and expand networks.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: List the advantages and disadvantages of networking with a variety of allies.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Discuss the mutual benefits of contributing to and receiving support from a network.

outcomes.statement: Access and assess sources of career information.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 6: Sources of Career Information (Core) · Suggested Time: 1-2 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 1

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss how to determine if a source of career information is considered credible.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research sources of career information found within one’s school.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify a variety of sources of career information (e.g., online job sites, social media sites, local career centres, regional colleges, post-secondary institutions, online career planning programs, government agencies, newcomer centres, print publications, peers and adults) and how they can support career development.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Compare the types of career information available through a variety of sources.

outcomes.statement: Explore industry sectors.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 7: Industry Sectors (Core) · Suggested Time: 1-2 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 1 and 2

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research various ways of classifying and organizing occupations, including the National Occupational Classification (NOC) tool and the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: List the main industry sectors at the local, provincial and national levels.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Provide examples of occupations and job opportunities within each sector at all three levels.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss how political, environmental, economic, technological and other factors can impact industry sectors.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify transferable skills that are common to many industry sectors.

outcomes.statement: Examine several career pathways.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 8: Career Pathways (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-8 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define the term career pathway.

indicators.label: b
c
indicators.text: List potential work opportunities within one’s community, province or country that are available through the transition to work pathway.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Research career laddering within the workforce and on-the-job training opportunities associated with the transition to work pathway.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research the prominence of entrepreneurship or self-employment within one’s community, province and country.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: List sources of information and support (e.g., Women Entrepreneurs of Saskatchewan, economic development offices and tribal councils) for entrepreneurs.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: List occupations that require education or training beyond high school.

indicators.label: h
i
indicators.text: Research the process for becoming a journeyperson in the province of Saskatchewan, including the apprenticeship and tradesperson routes.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Research potential local, provincial, national and global opportunities associated with a travel or gap year.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Discuss reasons for taking a travel or gap year upon graduation from high school.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Justify the viability of taking a travel or gap year, considering factors such as the impact on one’s finances.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Discuss the role of lifelong learning regardless of one’s chosen career pathway.

outcomes.statement: Analyze how a variety of factors influence career decisions and planning.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 9: Self-Awareness and Career Choices (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-8 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Complete personal inventories to determine one’s values, learning styles, interests, personality, emotional intelligence, strengths, multiple intelligences and/or virtues.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Reflect on how results from personal inventories connect to perceptions of self and potential career opportunities.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate work placement opportunities in one’s community based on the results from personal inventories.

outcomes.statement: Analyze one’s compatibility for a variety of occupations.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 10: Career Awareness (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 9

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Complete inventories (e.g., personality, values, interests, beliefs and attitudes) using career development software/tools to understand one’s profile.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Compare one’s personal survey results to potential occupational matches across industry sectors locally, provincially and nationally.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore occupational matches identified in personal survey results.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Reflect upon one’s compatibility for a variety of occupations as well as current and projected labour market information to develop a plan for transitioning through and beyond high school.

outcomes.statement: Outline potential career plans.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 11: Career Planning (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-6 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 10

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the relationship between one’s lifestyle and occupational choice(s).

indicators.label: b
c
indicators.text: Explore educational requirements associated with a variety of occupations.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Plan one’s career journey for the next ten years considering a minimum of three industry sectors of interest.

outcomes.statement: Interpret Labour Market Information (LMI).
outcomes.printedWith: Module 12: Labour Market Information (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 7

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe labour market information (LMI).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research trends (e.g., new collar jobs, aging workforce, skills and labour shortage, automation, use of artificial intelligence, gig economy, sharing economy, skills mismatch, rapid change, lack of digital literacy and birthrate) and their potential impact on employment opportunities.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore and interpret labour market information for one’s local community, province and country.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine current labour market trends and issues and the potential impact on self and society.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore labour market information and identify short-, medium- and long-term opportunities in one’s local community, province, and country.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Predict trends that may impact jobs of the future.

outcomes.statement: Explore skills, tools and strategies that support the job search process.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 13: Job Search (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research sources of employment/job postings locally, provincially and nationally.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research how employers accept, review and analyze applicants’ resumes using processes such as online submissions/uploading documents, keyword searching, and automatic tracking systems.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss the process for accurately completing an application form.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Complete sample job application forms for a variety of positions.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate the hidden job market and recommend ways to access it.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the concept of unconscious bias and how it might impact a job search.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Develop a list of questions that are commonly asked in a job interview and develop responses to them.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Demonstrate effective interview skills through role-playing scenarios or mock interviews conducted by community professionals that include common parts of an interview (e.g., introduction, interviewer’s questions, interviewee’s questions and closing).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Analyze one’s performance during role-playing or mock interviews and suggest areas for improvement.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Role-play what to do and what not to do at a job interview.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Discuss how networking, interviews, application forms, letters of application, resumes and personal career portfolios can support a job search.

outcomes.statement: Analyze fair and cooperative workplace practices and procedures.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 14A: Employment Standards A (Core) · Suggested Time: 1-2 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe individual’s rights and responsibilities with respect to fair treatment in the workplace as outlined by the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the Saskatchewan Human Rights Code.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: List fair workplace practices covered by The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions new employees should ask employers before beginning work, and role-play appropriate ways to ask them. Questions may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- What is my wage?
- How and when will I be paid?
- What deductions will be made from my pay cheque?
- Who is my supervisor?

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss and suggest ways to address conflict situations that may occur in the workplace.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Propose resolutions to workplace conflict as represented in a variety of scenarios.

outcomes.statement: Analyze employment standards for Saskatchewan workers.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 14B: Employment Standards B (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-4 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 14A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss ways that various agencies (e.g., Employment and Social Development Canada, the Saskatchewan Human Rights Commission, Saskatchewan Labour Relations Board, the Saskatchewan Ministry of Labour Relations and Workplace Safety, Saskatchewan Federation of Labour and unions) support fair workplace practices in Saskatchewan and Canada.

indicators.label: b
c
indicators.text: Research the processes for filing formal complaints related to employment standards and discrimination in the workplace.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify employment standards that pertain to an occupation of interest or to one’s present place of employment.

outcomes.statement: Compare the impact of federal and provincial legislation on workers in Saskatchewan.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 14C: Employment Standards C (Optional) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 14B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: List examples of industries (e.g., inter-provincial and international services such as railways, pipelines, shipping and shipping services; radio and television broadcasting; air transport; banks; most grain elevators, flour and seed mills; uranium mining and processing; and most federal crown corporations and the federal public service) that are federally regulated by the Canada Labour Code.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: List examples of industries that are provincially regulated by The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019.

indicators.label: c
d
indicators.text: Role-play scenarios that demonstrate ways of managing anger and negotiating and resolving conflict in the workplace.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Develop an employment contract that outlines working conditions for a specific workplace.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss ways to address workplace disputes such as a worker not being paid overtime.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: List community agencies that can provide information about employment standards.

outcomes.statement: Analyze the importance of rights and responsibilities in relation to workplace safety.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 15A: Workplace Safety – Rights and Responsibilities (Core) · Suggested Time: 1-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III – Occupational Health and Safety in The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019:
- the right to know - the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate - in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,
- the right to refuse - work that you believe is unusually dangerous.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research employer and worker responsibilities with respect to health and safety standards as required by law in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss steps that can be taken to refuse potentially unsafe work.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Role-play scenarios to demonstrate how to properly refuse potentially unsafe work.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain the purpose of The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019 and associated Regulations, and how they affect safe workplace practices.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate how workers can participate in and support health and safety activities in the workplace. (e.g., Occupational Health and Safety Committees, professional development, training and following safety procedures).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of reporting workplace incidents, dangerous occurrences, injuries, or illnesses immediately and the proper procedure to do so.

indicators.text: Discuss steps that can be taken to refuse potentially unsafe work.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Role-play scenarios to demonstrate how to properly refuse potentially unsafe work.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain the purpose of The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019 and associated Regulations, and how they affect safe workplace practices.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate how workers can participate in and support health and safety activities in the workplace. (e.g., Occupational Health and Safety Committees, professional development, training and following safety procedures).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of reporting workplace incidents, dangerous occurrences, injuries, or illnesses immediately and the proper procedure to do so.

outcomes.statement: Explore workplace hazards and injury prevention.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 16A: Workplace Safety – Hazards and Injury Prevention (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 15A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss how a workplace injury might affect the injured worker and others such as the employer, supervisor, work colleagues, family and friends.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Differentiate between a workplace hazard and risk.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Differentiate among the four Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) hazard categories including physical (e.g., heavy lifting, repetitive motion, slipping/tripping, working at heights, working alone, cuts and burns), chemical (e.g., chemicals, fumes, vapours and gases), biological (e.g., viruses, fungi, bacteria, mold; bodily fluids; sewage; animal/pet waste; and influenza), and psychological (e.g., harassment and bullying, stress, fatigue and shift work).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Provide examples of potential workplace hazards in the five major categories.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe employers’ and employees’ rights and responsibilities pertaining to workplace hazards and how they can work together to prevent workplace hazards.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of proper orientation, training, appropriate supervision, workplace inspections and following safe work practices, and provide examples of each for a variety of industries.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify potential safety hazards in a variety of environments including home, school, and workplace.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explore safety statistics related to young workers in the workplace in Saskatchewan and Canada and compare the statistics to those of workers in other age brackets.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Describe current prevention programs or agencies (e.g., Mission Zero, Work Safe Saskatchewan and Saskatchewan Safety Council) in Saskatchewan that are designed to raise awareness of and prevent workplace incidents.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Explain health and safety regulations common to a specific occupation of interest.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Identify employer responsibilities in relation to safety hazards.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Discuss the need for health and safety legislation and regulations.

outcomes.statement: Explore the Workplace Hazardous Materials Information System (WHMIS).
outcomes.printedWith: Module 17A: Workplace Safety – Workplace Hazardous Materials Information System (WHMIS) (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-5 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 16A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss what the Workplace Hazardous Materials Information System (WHMIS) is and its purpose and scope in the workplace.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Differentiate between general education and workplace training in regards to WHMIS 2015.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss factors that determine the required level of workplace specific training in WHMIS 2015.

indicators.label: d
e
indicators.text: Define the four parts of WHMIS 2015 (i.e., hazard identification and product classification; labels with warning symbols; Safety Data Sheets (SDS); and worker education and worksite specific training) that help workers handle hazardous materials safely.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify the roles and responsibilities of the employer, worker, and supplier in relation to the safe handling of hazardous materials.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe the two main types of WHMIS 2015 labels (i.e., supplier and workplace).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Differentiate between the supplier label and workplace label.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Identify hazard classes and categories.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Describe the purpose and contents of current hazard pictograms.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Identify the 16 sections of a Safety Data Sheet (SDS).

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Describe the usefulness of Safety Data Sheets (SDS) in helping to control hazardous materials.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Role-play a variety of scenarios that require one to evaluate hazardous materials and respond appropriately.

outcomes.statement: Explore psychological health and safety in the workplace.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 18A: Workplace Safety – Psychological Health and Safety (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 15B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define life/work balance and how it relates to maintaining personal wellness.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the prevalence of mental illness in Canada and the resulting impact on the workplace.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research how areas of stress, including personal financial stress, impact productivity in the workplace.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the benefits of a psychologically healthy and safe workplace to employees and employers.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research employers’ responsibility for establishing a psychologically healthy and safe workplace.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe practical ways that employees can contribute to a psychologically healthy and safe workplace.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Research employers’ duties and responsibilities about workplace mental health as outlined in The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Research accommodations (e.g., modification of work duties, flexible hours, job sharing and modifications to the work environment) that employees experiencing mental health problems or issues can request.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Research employers’ ‘duty to accommodate’ as outlined in the Canadian Human Rights Code.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Discuss barriers (e.g., lack of awareness that accommodations may be possible, lack of awareness of where to find supports and lack of confidence in requesting accommodations) that employees face in disclosing a mental health problem or illness and/or in requesting accommodations.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Research sources of support (e.g., Human Resources Department, union, Saskatchewan Health Authority, Canadian Mental Health Association, Mental Health Commission of Canada and Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety) for those experiencing mental health problems or issues in the workplace.

outcomes.statement: Examine how personal, cultural and societal beliefs affect relationships in the workplace.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 19: Diversity in the Workplace (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-4 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss how workplace relationships can benefit when diversity is acknowledged, accepted and incorporated in the workplace.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate the cultural diversity within one’s community and the impact on local workplaces.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss how discrimination based on factors such as ancestry, nationality, creed, gender diversity, sexual orientation, age, religion and disability can affect the workplace.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate issues faced by underrepresented groups (e.g., persons with disabilities; ethnic or cultural groups; and lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, and Two-spirit persons) face in the workplace.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the benefits of an open discussion to establish workplace standards and norms that foster respect, mutual understanding and inclusion within the workplace.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Reflect on personal beliefs and unconscious bias, and their potential impact on relationships in the workplace.

outcomes.statement: Examine fair and ethical practices and privacy rights in the workplace.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 20: Workplace Ethics and Privacy (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the impact of ethical (e.g., responsibility, honesty and confidentiality) and unethical (e.g., conflict of interest, abuse of substances, sexual harassment, bullying, theft, falsifying documents and reports, and misrepresentation) behaviours on the workplace.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the evolution of unions in Saskatchewan and Canada.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate the role of unions in the workplace.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss common expectations for union members in the workplace.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss advantages and disadvantages of being employed in a workplace where workers are unionized.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate the term harassment and discuss the potential effects of harassment on mental health and wellbeing.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss ways to deal with harassment of self or others in the workplace.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Compare the code of ethics for school with a code of ethics for a workplace.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Compare employers’ and employees’ expectations with respect to fair and ethical workplace practices.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Research employee and employer rights and responsibilities that foster a culture of privacy in the workplace.

outcomes.statement: Analyze components of a pay stub.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 21: Understanding Earnings (Core) · Suggested Time: 1-2 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Differentiate among the various types of pay periods for employees such as weekly, bi-weekly, semi-monthly and monthly, and discuss their impact on personal budgeting.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss methods of payment such as direct deposit, cash and cheque.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify the information that must be listed on a pay stub or statement of earnings as required by law (i.e., Part II Employment Standards in The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Differentiate among deductions that are required (i.e., income tax, Canadian Pension Plan and Employment Insurance), allowable (e.g., employee contributions to pension plans; charitable donations voluntarily made by an employee; and volunteer employee purchases from the employer for goods, services or merchandise) and illegal (e.g., deductions for alleged theft, damages, breakages and poor quality work).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Calculate gross pay for various earning situations such as contract, hourly and commission.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify strategies for dealing with a payroll error.

outcomes.statement: Explore factors that contribute to a successful work placement experience.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 80A: Work Study Preparation A (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Modules 3, 9

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent or guardian, teacher or other school staff and employer) involved in the work placement.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the business/organization to become familiar with its operations.

indicators.label: c
d
indicators.text: Identify safety hazards that could potentially be encountered during the work placement experience.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Compose a list of questions related to workplace hazards and safety to ask of the work placement employer such as:
- What physical, chemical, ergonomic or biological hazards should I be aware of in my work placement?
- When will I receive job safety training and orientation before I begin work?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear or other clothing am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify employment standards (e.g., use of a uniform) that may pertain to one’s work placement.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Reflect on one’s right to know, right to participate and right to refuse while in the work placement.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop personal and learning goals for the work placement in consultation with the parent or guardian, teacher or other school staff member and employer.

outcomes.statement: Explore factors that contribute to a successful work placement experience.

outcomes.statement:
Examine the significance of God's covenantal relationship with humanity through the stories of:
- Moses
- David
- selected prophets of the Old Testament.
outcomes.printedWith: [SH, KG]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Interpret lessons learned about hearing and heeding the call of God through the stories of:
- Moses (e.g., God commissions us to do His work)
- David (e.g., the smallest or seemingly least can be great with God) prophets of the Old Testament (e.g., Miriam – courageously live and celebrate your faith in God, Jonah - you cannot run from the call of God, Samuel - sometimes we need others to help us discern God is calling us).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Give examples of how individuals within the Catholic community, including oneself, respond to the revelation of God's commitment through covenant.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain the significance of the name of God revealed to Moses (i.e., "I am"), and collaborate to examine the significance of other key faith experiences of Moses.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify ways the story of Moses foreshadows the story of Jesus including Passover for the Paschal mystery.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Examine Catholic perspectives on the Davidic covenant such as:
- David's rise to and loss of power (e.g., trust in God)
- the role of Jerusalem in salvation history (e.g., capital city uniting the northern and southern tribes of Israel)
- the importance of the Temple in salvation history (e.g., physical reminder of the covenants with Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses and David giving added significance to Mt. 12:6).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify how David fulfills the roles of priest, prophet and king, and discuss one's own call to such roles within the covenant.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine connections between David and the Messiah as presented through various prophets (e.g., Samuel, Isaiah, Jeremiah).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Represent how the prophets play the role of bridge from Moses to Messiah within salvation history.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text:
Discuss various ways the prophets describe the Eucharistic covenant of the Messiah such as:
- new covenant (e.g., Jeremiah)
- everlasting covenant (e.g., Isaiah)
- covenant of peace (e.g., Ezekiel).

outcomes.statement: Examine the history of the development of the four Gospels and consider implications for faith formation.
outcomes.printedWith: [KG]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Outline and explain the three stages of Gospel formation including:
- life and teaching of Jesus Christ
- oral tradition
- written Gospels.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain why the Gospels were not written immediately following the death and resurrection of Jesus (e.g., expectation of impending Second Coming, prevalence of oral tradition, literacy rates, etc.).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss the influence of oral teachings (i.e., stage two of Gospel formation) on the written Gospels (i.e., stage three of Gospel formation).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the impact on personal faith of skepticism concerning the historical accuracy of the Gospels (e.g., accuracy of oral traditions, limited historical documents on the life and teaching of Jesus).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify the target audiences of all four Gospels and discuss implications for the writing style, content, and sequencing of the Good News according to each of the four evangelists (i.e., Matthew, Mark, Luke and John).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Discuss how understanding Gospel formation and intent influences the development of faith using examples such as:
- the development of the synoptic gospels
- the theory of a potential Q-source
- presence of unique content within John's Gospel
- conflicting interpretations of scripture (e.g., contextualists vs. Bible literalists).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explain key uses of the Gospels after they were written (e.g., prayer, liturgy, catechesis, evangelization) and examine their influence on communal and personal faith development.

outcomes.statement: Contrast the Mosaic Law perspective on morality and sin with a contemporary Christian perspective of relationship building with God.
outcomes.printedWith: [SH, DHP, CH]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the place of the Ten Commandments within Mosaic Law.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss the shift in understanding the Ten Commandments as laws (e.g., enforced by scribes and Pharisees) to a relationship with God in the spirit of the law (e.g., Jesus as fulfillment of the law).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Contrast how each of the Ten Commandments was understood from a legal perspective and a contemporary relational context through discussions such as:
- keep holy the Sabbath (e.g., adherence to Sabbath laws moving towards relationship building with God)
- honour mother and father (e.g., moving from honouring parents towards honouring parents and other elders within the community)
- do not commit adultery (e.g., rules and punishment pertaining to extra-marital sex moving towards personal responsibility for sexual morality)
- do not covet (e.g., person as possession moving towards recognition of the dignity of the person).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Distinguish the difference between merely avoiding evil and doing good using examples from Mosaic law and relational perspectives (e.g., the parable of the Good Samaritan).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Discuss legalistic and relational considerations in making a moral judgement including:
- the moral object (i.e., action)
- the moral intention (i.e., motive)
- the moral circumstance (i.e., context and consequence).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Collaborate with peers to represent the Catholic teaching that a good intention can never justify an evil act.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss examples of diminished responsibility for immoral acts (e.g., conditions for mortal sin).

outcomes.statement: Express Catholic perspectives on forgiveness, mercy, generosity, justice and joy within the ongoing nature of salvation history.
outcomes.printedWith: [SH, SSM]

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Examine Catholic connections between:
- original sin and forgiveness, mercy, generosity, justice and joy
- personal sin and forgiveness, mercy, generosity, justice and joy

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
