indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Recognize that a material's chemical and physical properties are dependent on the type of bonds and the forces between atoms, molecules or ions. (K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify and describe some properties (e.g., melting point, solubility, thermal conductivity, electrical conductivity, hardness, heat capacity, tensile strength, surface tension, reactivity with acids and bases, flammability, flame tests and odour) of ionic and molecular compounds, metals and network covalent substances. (S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Design and carry out a procedure to compare several physical and chemical properties of various materials (e.g., sugar, salt, sand, paradichlorobenzene [mothballs], paraffin and beeswax). (S, STSE, A)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Construct a classification system of student-tested materials according to one or more properties. (S, STSE, A)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Determine which intermolecular force is dominant in a student-tested material, based on test results and knowledge of intermolecular forces. (K, S)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Place new substances into a student-constructed classification system based on their properties. (S, A)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Recognize the limitations of personal and scientific classification schemes. (STSE, K, A)

outcomes.statement: Explore the nature and classification of organic compounds, and their uses in modern materials.
outcomes.printedWith: SI, DM

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Pose questions about the prevalence and diversity of organic compounds in daily life. (STSE, A)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain how the valence structure of carbon leads to the large number and diversity of organic compounds in nature. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe and compare the advantages of using different models (e.g., molecular, structural, condensed-structural, space-filled, 2-dimensional and 3-dimensional) to represent organic molecules. (K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Write the molecular and structural formula and provide the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) name for a representative sample of straight-chain alkanes, alkenes and alkynes, with up to 10 carbon atoms in the molecule. (K, S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Provide the IUPAC names, and illustrate, using diagrams, molecular modelling kits and/or digital technology, the structural formulas of a variety of branched- and straight-chain hydrocarbons. (S, K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of isomerization, including geometric and optical isomerization, in materials science and biological applications. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify various classes of organic compounds based on functional groups including cyclics, aromatics, alcohols, aldehydes, ketones, ethers, esters, organic acids and halocarbons. (S, K)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Describe applications of the various classes of organic compounds, including compounds (e.g., carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, nucleic acids) important to biological systems. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Research how First Nations and Métis people used organic compounds as medicines and to make soap and cleaning products. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Provide examples of consumer and industrial products that are derived from the refining of fossil fuels. (STSE)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Research some societal benefits and environmental impacts related to the petrochemical industry. (STSE)

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Describe processes of polymerization and explain the significance of some natural and synthetic polymers. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Design and carry out a procedure to synthesize an organic compound (e.g., soap, esters and polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) polymer slime). (STSE)

outcomes.statement: Determine the suitability of materials for use in specific applications.
outcomes.printedWith: DM, TPS

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Determine the properties of a material that make it suitable to meet the specifications for a particular product (e.g., catalysts and solvents for oil extraction and refining, metals in equipment for mining, bulletproof fabric, nanotechnologies, superconductors and instant adhesives). (STSE)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Evaluate the risks and benefits to society and the environment of a product (real or imagined) throughout its life cycle, from raw materials to production, use and disposal. (STSE, A)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Suggest a range of suitable applications for a material based on its chemical and physical properties. (STSE, K, A)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore how First Nations and Métis people used their understanding of material properties to determine their use (e.g., different species of wood used for burning, smoking and creating structures for housing and transportation). (STSE, K)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research First Nations and Métis beliefs regarding the ethical treatment of Mother Earth with respect to the gathering, creating, using and disposing of materials. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify criteria (e.g., cost, availability, ethics, transportation cost and source of material) used to guide the choice of materials for a specific application. (STSE, A)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Justify the use of the material chosen for a specific application based on student-selected criteria. (STSE, A)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Investigate the potential of modern materials (e.g., graphene, aerogels, polymers and carbon nanotubes) to change the way we live. (STSE)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Analyze how a product (e.g., sporting equipment, vehicle, clothing or building material) has evolved in response to the development of new materials. (STSE, A)

outcomes.statement: Consider, qualitatively and quantitatively, the characteristics and applications of equilibrium systems in chemical reactions.
outcomes.printedWith: SI, DM, TPS

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss why most chemical reactions do not proceed to completion. (K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss the criteria (e.g., closed system, constancy of properties and equal rates of forward and reverse reactions) that characterize an equilibrium system. (K)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Analyze graphs of the concentrations of reactants and products with respect to time in chemical reactions which approach equilibrium, chemical reactions which achieve equilibrium and chemical reactions which undergo a change in equilibrium. (K, S)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Write the equilibrium constant (Keq) expression for a variety of chemical reactions. (K, S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Recognize that equilibrium constant (Keq) values are dependent upon pressure (for gases only) and temperature but are independent of concentration and the presence of a catalyst. (K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain why solid and liquid phases have no effect on the value of an equilibrium constant. (K)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Interpret Keq values to determine whether the concentration of products, reactants or neither is favoured once equilibrium has been reached. (S)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Perform calculations involving Keq and the equilibrium concentrations of reactants and products. (S)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Solve problems related to chemical equilibrium, using Initial concentration, Change in concentration and Equilibrium concentration (ICE) charts. (K, S)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Predict the shifts in equilibrium caused by changes in temperature, pressure, volume, concentration or the addition of a catalyst, using Le Chatelier's principle. (S)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Construct a model or design an experiment that demonstrates the concepts of equilibrium and/or Le Chatelier's principle. (STSE, S)

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Describe the Haber process, its historical significance and societal impacts. (STSE, K, A)

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Describe ways in which industry manipulates chemical reactions to change the equilibrium point to make processes economically viable. (STSE, K, A)

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Examine how the concepts of reversible reactions and equilibrium apply to biological systems. (STSE)

outcomes.statement: Analyze aqueous solution equilibria including solubility-product constants.
outcomes.printedWith: SI

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss conditions necessary for the establishment of equilibrium in aqueous solutions. (K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Analyze how temperature and the common ion effect influence the solubility of substances in aqueous solution. (K, S)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Predict the changes in solution equilibrium caused by changes in temperature, pressure, volume, concentration or the addition of a catalyst, using Le Chatelier's principle. (S)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Research applications of solution equilibria in Saskatchewan agriculture, resource extraction, manufacturing and chemical industries. (STSE, K, A)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Construct solubility graphs from student collected data to demonstrate the effect of temperature on the change in solubility of chemical compounds in water. (K, S)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Interpret solubility curves of selected substances. (K, S)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Calculate the solubility product constant (Ksp) for saturated solutions, given solute concentrations. (K, S)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Calculate the solubility of substances in aqueous solutions, given Ksp. (K, S)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Predict whether a precipitate will occur in a double replacement reaction when given the initial concentration of reactants and solubility product constant (Ksp) values of the products. (S, K)

outcomes.statement: Observe and analyze phenomena related to acid-base reactions and equilibrium.
outcomes.printedWith: SI, DM

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify examples of acid-base reactions in the manufacture and use of consumer products (e.g., foods, cosmetics, pharmaceuticals and cleaners), industrial processes (e.g., resource extraction and refining, mine tailings), agricultural processes (e.g., fertilizer and pesticide application) and First Nations and Métis practices such as tanning hides. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss the historical development and limitations of theories, including Arrhenius, Brønsted-Lowry and Lewis, which explain the behaviour of acids and bases. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify conjugate acids and bases formed in acid-base reactions using Brønsted-Lowry theory, including substances which are amphiprotic (amphoteric). (S, K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Differentiate between strength (strong versus weak) and concentration (concentrated versus dilute) when referring to acids and bases. (S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Classify strong and weak acids and bases using the magnitude of Ka and Kb. (S, K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the relationship between [H+]/[H3O+] and [OH-] in the dissociation of water, to explain Kw and perform relevant calculations. (K, S)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Solve problems involving pH, pOH, [H+]/[H3O+], [OH-], Kw, Ka and Kb. (S)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explain how acid-base indicators function chemically, using Le Chatelier's principle. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Estimate the pH of solutions using acid-base indicator solutions and indicator papers. (S, K)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Design and carry out an experiment to differentiate between weak and strong acids using indicators. (S, K)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Perform acid-base titrations and relevant calculations for multiple ratios of [H+]/[H3O+] to [OH-], including those for reactions that either reach the endpoint/equivalence point or represent over-titration. (S)

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Interpret pH titration curves for various combinations and strengths of acids and bases, by identifying endpoints and choosing appropriate indicators. (STSE, S)

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Discuss the role of acid-base buffering as an aspect of maintaining homeostasis in biological systems. (K)

outcomes.statement: Investigate the chemistry of oxidation and reduction (redox) reactions.
outcomes.printedWith: SI, TPS

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Compare the characteristics of oxidation-reduction (redox) reactions with other types of chemical reactions. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Define oxidation and reduction and oxidizing and reducing agents in terms of electron transfer. (K)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Write and balance redox equations using the half reaction and oxidation number method. (K, S)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Create a reduction potential series based on student-collected data. (STSE, S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Illustrate and label the parts of electrochemical and electrolytic cells and explain how they work, including half-reactions, flow of ions and flow of electrons. (K, S)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Differentiate between electrochemical and electrolytic cells in terms of spontaneity, direction of electron flow, energy, charge on electrodes and chemical change. (K, S)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Predict the electric potential and spontaneity of various redox reactions using reduction potentials. (K, S)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Design, construct, and evaluate a prototype of a working battery that meets specific student-identified criteria such as powering a small electric device. (STSE, S)

outcomes.statement: Examine applications of electrochemistry and their impact on society and the environment.
outcomes.printedWith: SI, DM

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Provide examples of oxidation-reduction (redox) reactions that occur in nature and in technological processes. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Evaluate the economic importance of electrochemical technologies and processes. (STSE, K, A)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate the impact of the electrochemical industry on the environment, including disposal of raw materials, batteries and mine tailings. (STSE, A)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Design and carry out experiments which illustrate the processes of electrolysis and electroplating. (S, K)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate the process of corrosion and its prevention (e.g., painting and coating, cathodic protection, alloys, sacrificial anodes and avoiding incompatible metals). (STSE, K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine the role of oxidation and reduction in biological processes (e.g., photosynthesis, respiration and the action of antioxidants). (STSE, K)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Research the role of oxidation and reduction in First Nations and Métis practices (e.g., drying and smoking meat for preservation). (STSE, K)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explain how electrical energy is produced in hydrogen fuel cells and various types (e.g., lead-acid, nickel-cadmium, alkaline and lithium-ion) of batteries. (STSE, K, A)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Research and discuss the issue of storage of electrical energy as a barrier to large scale adoption of renewable energy resources. (STSE, K, A)

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate basic fundamentals of vocal technique.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Sing with breath support (e.g., practise appropriate breathing technique and recognize how it helps support sound production and vocal health).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe and demonstrate quality singing in response to given criteria and considering cultural context.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Hear and match pitch and discern accuracy of notes.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of vocal warm ups and regular practise.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine different ranges (i.e., alto, bass, baritone, tenor, soprano) on a choral score.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify own range, with teacher guidance, and recognize that voice range may change over time.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Recognize, experiment with, and demonstrate different vocal registration (e.g., head voice, chest voice, falsetto, speaking voice).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Demonstrate understanding of fundamentals of tone production (e.g., breath management, supported projection, characteristic tone quality across the ranges, vowel sounds).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Discuss basic principles of vocal anatomy (e.g., vocal bands/folds, how to produce a sound, sound source, articulators and resonators).

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Discuss and demonstrate the difference between pronunciation (e.g., the act of speaking words correctly), enunciation (e.g., the art of speaking words clearly and concisely) and diction (e.g., the "choice of words" used in writing, speaking or singing).

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Demonstrate and articulate the importance of proper posture and body alignment for singing.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Demonstrate choral blend through vowel unity and understand the role it plays in intonation.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Identify factors and apply techniques for maintaining vocal health.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate skills (e.g., intonation, pitch breathing, alignment) and practices necessary for ensemble singing.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Demonstrate ensemble skills such as:
- adjusting dynamics
- blending vowels
- placing consonants
- adjusting vibrato
- maintaining own part.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Demonstrate personal and interpersonal skills necessary for ensemble music making including:
- etiquette
- rehearsal protocols
- leadership.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Recognize opportunities for applying interpretation abilities (e.g., inflection, tone, emulating instrumental sounds).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Maintain accurate pitch when singing harmony.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Demonstrate fluency and growth in vocal techniques and musicality when singing advanced vocal ensemble repertoire.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Apply processes (e.g., focusing on a specific part, experimenting with phrasing, running through from start to finish, working on sections, isolating variables, making group choices), with teacher guidance, for collective practice, rehearsal and performance.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine various musical functions in a song (e.g., melody, harmony, bass line).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Incorporate movement in ensemble work (e.g., use movement to experience music concepts) recognizing how singing involves the whole body.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Demonstrate ability to respond to the conductor.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate ability to interpret music using various visual (e.g., standard and/or non-standard notation, written musical scores, graphic score) and aural music systems.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Demonstrate ability to respond to notation systems such as letter names, solfege, scale degrees and aural cues when singing in the context of the repertoire studied.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Demonstrate ability to read, notate, understand and interpret written musical scores and various notation systems.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Sight sing a short passage (e.g., at a lower difficulty level than the repertoire studied).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Demonstrate ability to learn music through aural transmission.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Interpret expressive terms and music symbols within the context of the repertoire (e.g., tempo, dynamics, form, style, articulation, graphic symbols).

outcomes.statement: Experiment with processes for improvising, arranging and composing.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate ways that music elements (e.g., tempo, rhythm) can be used to express musical ideas.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Take creative risks when creating and refining work.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Embellish, ornament or improvise on a melody.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Experiment with stylistically appropriate group improvisation (e.g., with chords/harmonic background).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore and examine composition and arranging techniques (e.g., What is the composer doing musically in relation to the text? What is a compositional hook?).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Compose, arrange or improvise a short phrase (e.g., create a vocal warm up).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Reflect on individual and group compositions and arrangements, identifying strengths and challenges encountered.

outcomes.statement: Identify and experiment with stylistic practices of various vocal and choral music traditions.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify and experiment with vocal characteristics and stylistic features that are typical in diverse music genres (e.g., spirituals, jazz, blues, opera).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Sing (e.g., warm up, excerpt, repertoire, short folk song) in a minimum of two languages.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Incorporate stylistic features reflective of the socio-cultural contexts of the choral repertoire being studied.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the role of choral music in the context of various cultures, places and eras.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Connect with community choirs (e.g., Ukrainian, German) to discuss the influence of culture, time or place on repertoire choices and performances.

outcomes.statement: Prepare for the work placement.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 80A: Work Study Preparation (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate, Advanced · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III – Occupational Act, 2019:
- the right to know – the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate – in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,
- the right to refuse – work that you believe is unusually dangerous.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent, teacher or other school staff, employer) involved in the work placement.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the business/organization to become familiar with its operations.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: In collaboration with all partners, develop personal and learning goals for the work placement.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents needed for the work placement (e.g., personal career documentation such as a resume or portfolio, permission forms, logs, self- and employer evaluation forms).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop a list of questions that could potentially be asked by the employer/work placement in an interview situation as well as answers to the questions.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Participate in an interview with the employer prior to beginning the work placement.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Reflect upon one’s performance during the interview.

outcomes.statement: Examine historical influences on the modern food service industry.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 1: The Food Service Industry (Core) (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the circumstances that led to the creation of the food service industry at the time of the French Revolution.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss historical (e.g., King Henry IV, Antonin Carême and Auguste Escoffier) and contemporary (e.g., food network, convenience food, food blogs and fast food) influences on the food service industry.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine how current food service industry terminology is based on terminology (e.g., sous chef) and practices (e.g., brigade system) used at the time of the French Revolution.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Differentiate between a classic kitchen brigade system (e.g., chef de cuisine, chef de partie, saucier, garde-manger and pâtissier) and a modern (e.g., executive chef, sous-chef, line cook and pastry chef) kitchen brigade.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify the duties of common back-of-the-house (e.g., executive chef, sous chef, station chef and line cook) and front-of-the-house (e.g., maitre d’, server and food runner) roles in food service operations.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research the effects of technological developments (e.g., tools, electricity, electronics and computers) on the food service industry.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine how innovative technologies (e.g., food preservation and storage techniques), consumer concerns (e.g., food safety and nutrition) and new foods (e.g., convenience foods) influence the modern food service industry.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify the types of establishments (e.g., institutional kitchens, work camps, hotels, hospitals, bakeries, home-based and mobile food vendors) related to employment opportunities in the food service industry.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Discuss the role of the food service industry in the community.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Examine cultural, economic, technological, social and environmental factors that influence the food service industry in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Describe how current food trends impact the food service industry.

outcomes.statement: Examine the importance of professionalism in the food service industry.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 2: Professionalism in the Food Service Industry (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-4 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
b
indicators.text: Research expectations for employee and employer professionalism in the food service industry.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss working conditions and employment standards common to the food service industry.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify common worker injuries reported within the food service industry.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify types of workplace harassment and related resolution procedures (e.g., provincial labour mediation and conciliation services).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe the rights and responsibilities of employees and employers, including the right to refuse process.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Recognize and apply safe and fair work practices including freedom from violence, harassment and bullying.

outcomes.statement: Apply kitchen safety and sanitation practices.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 3A: Kitchen Safety and Sanitation (Core) · Suggested Time: 8-12 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of safety in a commercial kitchen.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the purpose of food safety standards and regulations, including the role of public health inspectors.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify potential worker safety hazards in a commercial kitchen.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Research injuries (e.g., strained muscles, cuts and lacerations, slips, falls and pepper burns) common among workers in commercial kitchens.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Identify industry standard personal protective equipment (PPE) such as safety goggles, gloves, footwear, masks, headwear and protective clothing.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe ways to reduce and prevent injury to self and others from unsafe work acts or environments.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Demonstrate personal hygiene (e.g., hand washing and hair restraint) and safe dress (e.g., closed-toe shoes, apron and gloves) when working in a commercial kitchen.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Explain the importance of sanitation in a commercial kitchen.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Discuss practices to maintain a safe and sanitary kitchen, including prevention of pest infestation.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Maintain a clean and sanitary work area, including surfaces (e.g., floors, walls and tables) tools and equipment.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Practise safe and hygienic washing of dishes, tools and cookware, either manually or using a dishwasher.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of reporting workplace incidents or injuries immediately and the proper procedure to do so.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Identify common causes of commercial kitchen fires.

indicators.label: o
indicators.text: Examine procedures for preventing and dealing with commercial kitchen fires.

indicators.label: p
indicators.text: Review the fire evacuation plan for the work area and building.

indicators.label: q
indicators.text: Research Workplace Hazardous Materials Information System (WHMIS) standards that apply to a commercial kitchen.

outcomes.statement: Examine appropriate procedures to ensure food safety in the kitchen.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 4A: Food Safety (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 3A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify the causes of food contamination (e.g., biological, chemical and physical) that can occur in a commercial kitchen.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: List examples of biological (e.g., bacteria and viruses), chemical (e.g., cleaners and disinfectants) and physical (e.g., glass or metal fragments) contaminants.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify causes of food-borne illnesses (e.g., food poisoning and food allergies).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Differentiate between direct contamination and cross-contamination.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss common food safety steps (e.g., clean, separate, cook and chill) to reduce food contamination.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Differentiate date labelling (e.g., best-before, packaged on and expiration) on pre-packaged foods.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explain the importance of kitchen sanitation and personal hygiene in the prevention of food contamination and food-borne illnesses.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Examine safe and sanitary practices to dispose of kitchen waste.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Discuss the role of municipal, provincial and national food safety legislation and regulations.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Demonstrate appropriate food safety standards when receiving, selecting, handling, preparing, serving and storing food.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate appropriate measurement techniques used in commercial cooking.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 5A: Kitchen Measurement (Core) · Suggested Time: 1-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify measurements (e.g., weight, volume and count) common to the commercial cooking.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe measurements traditionally used in commercial cooking including weight (e.g., As purchased – AP and Edible portion – EP), volume, count, dry and wet measurement.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify measurement tools (e.g., measuring spoons, measuring cups, thermometers and kitchen scales) common to a commercial kitchen.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Differentiate between imperial and metric systems of measurement.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Convert recipe measurements from imperial to metric (e.g., teaspoon to millilitres and pounds to grams) and metric to imperial.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Measure ingredients using liquid, dry and displacement methods.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Demonstrate proper scaling techniques.

outcomes.statement: Prepare for the work placement.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 80A: Work Study Preparation (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate, Advanced · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III – Occupational Health and Safety in The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019:
- the right to know - the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate - in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,
- the right to refuse – work that you believe is unusually dangerous

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent, teacher or other school staff, employer) involved in the work placement.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the business/organization to become familiar with its operations.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: In collaboration with all partners, develop personal and learning goals for the work placement.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents needed for the work placement (e.g., personal career documentation such as a resume or portfolio, permission forms, logs, self- and employer evaluation forms).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop a list of questions that could potentially be asked by the employer/work placement in an interview situation as well as answers to the questions.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Participate in an interview with the employer prior to beginning the work placement.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Reflect upon one’s performance during the interview.

indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

outcomes.statement: Apply various problem-solving strategies to solve programming problems throughout Computer Science 20.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore the computational thinking concepts of decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction and algorithm design.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Provide examples of the importance of computational thinking in many fields (e.g., physics, biology, mathematics, geology, linguistics, psychology and economics).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Generalize a specific solution to a problem to solve multiple problems of similar type (e.g., moving a character in a grid world to the origin regardless of its initial position).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Design algorithms that allow computers and humans to solve problems effectively.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Use flowcharts, pseudocode and/or visual programming environments to model the logic of algorithms.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Analyze and implement programs with the goal of improving code to achieve the most elegant solution.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss the advantages of subdividing a problem into smaller components.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Analyze existing code to predict output, and verify the prediction if possible.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Discuss the strenghts and limitations of visual programming environments versus text-based languages.

outcomes.statement: Use common coding techniques to enhance code elegance and troubleshoot errors throughout Computer Science 20.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss and implement appropriate coding style (e.g., indentation and comments) and naming conventions for the programming language used in Computer Science 20.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss the concept of elegance in coding.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Improve the elegance of existing code by simplifying, improving efficiency and enhancing code readability.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Create internal documentation (e.g., inline comments and header comments) for a program.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss different types of errors (e.g., syntax, semantic and runtime) and their impacts on program execution.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify and correct errors in a program.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Use pair programming to write and debug programs, with students experiencing both driver and navigator roles.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop testing procedures, such as outputting values during execution, to debug programs.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Implement exception handling to validate user input.

outcomes.statement: Utilize different data types, including integer, floating point, Boolean and string, to solve programming problems.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Differentiate between variables and values.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify values of different data types (e.g., integer, floating point, Boolean and string) that can be stored in variables.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Choose and utilize appropriate data types in a program.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain the importance of conventions and rules for naming variables within programming languages.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Distinguish between the concepts of assignment and comparison of variables.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Utilize relational operators, including assignment (=), equivalence (==), not equal (!=), greater than (>) and less than (<), in a program.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Write expressions using math operators (e.g., addition (+), subtraction (-), multiplication (*), division (/), integer division (//) and modulo division (%))

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Provide examples of problems that require data type conversion.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Perform data type conversions (e.g., string to integer, floating point to integer and integer to Boolean).

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Perform data type conversions (e.g., string to integer, floating point to integer and integer to Boolean

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Discuss the implications of using floating point values, with reference to the concept of precision (e.g., calculations with currenct and rounding errors).

outcomes.statement: Investigate how control structures affect program flow.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the necessity of control structures in programming.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Utilize decistion-making structures (e.g., IF, IF-ELSE and SWITCH) to control the order in which instructions execute.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Utilize WHILE and FOR loops to control program flow and to solve problems with an indefinite or definite number of iterations.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Determine which type of looping structure allows for the most elegant solution to a problem.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Solve problems utilizing nested loops.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate the role of logical operators (e.g., AND (&&), OR (||) and NOT(!)) in compound conditional statements.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss operator precedence and how to use parentheses to control the evaluation of Boolean expressions.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explain how to simplify code using control structures and operators.

outcomes.statement: Construct and utilize functions to create reusable pieces of code.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore the benefits of using built-in and user-defined functions.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Incorporate built-in math functions, including random number generation, in programs.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss the concepts of local and global scope and the implication of their use, including scalability problems when using global variables.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Develop user-defined functions that utilize argument passing.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the difference between parameters (variables) and arguments (values) in functions.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Incorporate built-in string functions such as length, substring and concatenation in programs.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss how functions enable programmers to reuse code easily in multiple situations.

outcomes.statement: Investigate one-dimensional arrays and their applications.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Provide examples of the types of problems that can be solved using arrays.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore the advantages of using one-dimensional arrays to manipulate multiple values using loops.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe errors, such as out of bounds errors, which can occur when using arrays.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Write a program that creates, accesses and modifies a one-dimensional array.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate and use built-in array functions (e.g., length and sort) included within a programming language.

outcomes.statement: Explore the underlying technology of computing devices and the internet, and their impacts on society.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate how computing devices function and how the Internet allows connected devices to communicate.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the history of computing devices and the Internet, including key milestones and contributors.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify the units used to measure computing specifications such as data storage capacity, processing speed and transmission speed.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe the role of typical hardware (e.g., CPU, wireless card, RAM, graphics card, SIM card, hard drive and motherboard) found within computing devices.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine the role of technologies (e.g., packets and routing) and protocols (e.g., DNS, IP addresses, HTTP and FTP) that support information transfer on the Internet

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explore the societal impacts of ubiquitous Internet access, cloud computing and connected devices.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explore implications of advances in computing performance.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss limitations of current technologies and predict possible directions of future technologies.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Explore the interactions between humans and computing devices.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the impacts of information technologies on privacy, including digital security practices.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe legal and ethical issues related to the use of computing devices (e.g., social media, advertising, encryption, malicious software and social engineering).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore how issues related to personal rights and privacy such as identity theft, data collection, permanence of information on the Internet and surveillance are affected by technologies.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify the role of different layers (e.g., network, operating system, application and data) of digital security, including the responsibility of users.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the benefits and limitations of user authentication techniques to prevent or allow access to resources

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research data encryption techniques used for storage and transmission.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explore the role of personal responsibility in the context of access and use of confidential information, including intellectual property rights and plagiarism.

outcomes.statement: Explore computer science related career paths in Saskatchewan, Canada and the world.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research and describe career choices and trends in computer science in Saskatchewan, Canada and the world.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research which programming languages are prominent in specific computer science sub-fields such as game, website and mobile development.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify and report on opportunities for experiential learning (e.g., co-op programs, job shadowing and career fairs) in the field of computer science.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Inquire into issues of gender equity and diversity of the computer science workplace, considering questions such as "Why are females and certain cultural groups typically underrepresented in the computer science workplace in Saskatchewan?" and "What steps could be take to encourage more females to pursue computer science related careers?"

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research and report on postsecondary educational programs leading to careers in information systems and computer science (e.g., institutions offering relevant programs, industry certifications, courses of study, entrance requirements, length of programs and costs).

indicators.label: f

outcomes.statement: Develop a coding project and/or research a topic related to computer science of the student's choice.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Create a proposal document for a coding project that includes discussion of the basic premise or problem to be solved, key features and project team members and their roles.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Construct a tool (e.g., rubric, checklist, self-evaluation form or peer-evaluation form) to assess the process and products involved in a student-directed study.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Develop a coding project using the same or a different programming language than those used in Computer Science 20.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine an area of collaborative research between computer science and another field.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research the application of computer science in other fields (e.g., art, trades, sciences, mathematics and medicine).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Inquire into the current state and/or societal implications of a current trend in computing such as hacking, artificial intelligence, robotics, microcontrollers, game design, cryptography, mobile development or intellectual property.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Present the research or project to peers.

outcomes.statement: Implement effective coding practices throughout Computer Science 30.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the rationale for learning and using different programming languages.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Contrast the syntax of the language used in Computer Science 20 with the language used in Computer Science 30, as needed.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Compare the coding conventions of the language used in Computer Science 20 with the language used in Computer Science 30, as needed.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Refactor existing code to increase elegance.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Critique third-party code (e.g., student, teacher or textbook programs) and make suggestions for improvement.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Use interactive debugging techniques involving breakpoints and watch windows.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Access search engines, forums and question and answer sites independently to find solutions to coding problems.

outcomes.statement: Engage in collaborative programming practices.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore collaborative programming practices and models.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Collaborative programming practices and models.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Collaborate with others to plan a solution to a problem.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Develop procedural or object-oriented programs collaboratively.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore version control using shared folders or versioning software.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Develop and follow a common standard of programming style to integrate code from multiple programmers.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Reflect on the advantages and challenges encountered when working collaborative contexts to solve programming problems.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Interact with experts who work collaborative programming environments.

outcomes.statement: Investigate types of data structures and the advantages of organizing data in different ways.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Provide examples of the types of problems that can be solved using two-dimensional arrays, mutable (dynamic) arrays and associative arrays (e.g., hash tables or dictionaries).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Develop a program the utilizes a two-dimensional array.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Solve a problem utilizing a mutable array (e.g., list or ArrayList).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore the use of associative arrays (e.g., hash tables or dictionaries) to store a dataset.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the advantages of using different data structures to solve problems.

outcomes.statement: Create programs that utilize external files.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify the types of problems (e.g., high score list, cookie, preferences or output file) that can be solved by utilizing external data.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Load content from a local or remote file into a program.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Parse the data from an external file to remove extraneous information, if necessary.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Save the state of a program by creating or modifying a file.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of saving data into and external file.

outcomes.statement: Use libraries to simplify solutions to programming problems.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the advantages of using libraries (packages) in programs.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Create a program that imports a package or classes wthin a package.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify the functionality of a library from the documentation or application programming interface (API)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Write a program that utilizes an application programming interface (API)(e.g., social networking, weather data, user authentication, photo sharing and geolocation data)

outcomes.statement: Explore the concepts and principles of object-oriented programming.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate object-oriented programing concepts including classes, objects, attributes and methods.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss how a class can be understood as a programmer-defined data type.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Design and implement a class, and create a program that utilizes instances of this class.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Apply the principle of encapsulation through the creation and use of user-defined objects.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Create a constructor and use it to instantiate an object.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Compare object-oriented and procedural programming paradigms.

outcomes.statement: Explore recursion and investigate sorting algorithms.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Distinguish between iterative and recursive problem-solving techniques and demonstrate how to accomplish a specific task using both approaches.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Create recursive functions and use them in programs to solve problems such as calculating factorials, evaluating exponents, designing fractal images or calculating the Fibonacci sequence.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss the processes (e.g., the stack, stack frames and maximum recursion depth) involved in evaluating recursive functions.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identity the advantages and disadvantages of using recursive problems.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Provide examples of situations where sorting is used to solve problems.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of efficiency in sorting algorithms.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Analyze the execution of insertion, selection and quicksort algorithms using visualizations.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Illustrate the implementation of a sorting algorithm (e.g., selection, insertion, and quicksort) using pseudocode.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Create a program to sort data in an array using one or more sorting algorithms (e.g., selection, insertion, quicksort).

outcomes.statement: Explore number systems and character encoding used in computing.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss how all digital data is stored numerically and how the data type dictates the interpretation of the number.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss the rationale for using various number systems.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Convert between binary (base 2), decimal (base 10) and hexadecimal (base 16) number systems.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze the implications (e.g., rounding error) for precision when storing a floating point value as a binary number.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss how colour values are represented digitally, including RGB and hexadecimal.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss how character encoding systems such as ASCII and Unicode represent text.

outcomes.statement: Create a large-scale computer program to demonstrate proficiency in procedural or object-oriented programming.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Choose a project that is of an appropriate scale and complexity based on the skills and abilities of team members.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify required features and desired features of the project.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Incorporate programming concepts and principles such as data structures, external files, libraries and/or object-oriented programming as required.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Develop elegant code and refine through multiple iterations.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Integrate code from multiple team members as required.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Conduct beta testing with peers and/or external participants as required.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Incorporate feedback from peers and/or external participants as required.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Conduct beta testing with peers and/or external participants as required.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Revise the scale and complexity of the project according to skill, available resources and available time.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Confirm that the project incorporates all required features.

outcomes.statement: Document and reflect on the process of creating a large-scale computer program.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Create a project proposal that includes the basic premise, required features, desired features and project team (e.g., individual, pairs or larger group).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Develop and revise project documents such as team member tasks, change logs, milestone timeline and/or user manuals.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Report on beta testing with peers and/or external participants.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of developing technical supports such as user manuals and training materials.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify how specific programming challenges were resolved.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the challenges and benefits of working with others to develop a large-scale computer program.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine connections between the capstone coding project and related careers.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Present completed capstone project to peers and/or external participants.

outcomes.statement: Apply safety standards to prevent injuries in the construction and carpentry workspace.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 1A: Safety (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss worker and employee rights and responsibilities as they relate to workplace safety and how they can prevent injuries.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify common safety hazard categories and hierarchy of control common to the construction industry.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Assess and mitigate the risks (e.g., slips, trips, falls) and potential safety hazards in the jobsite and shop workspace.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Research the benefits of completing the different certifications and programs offered by Work Safe Sask, Sask Safety Council, Sask Prevention and the Ministry of Labour Relations and Workplace Safety.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore basic safety procedures (e.g., storage and maintenance of tools, clean workspace and caution when working at high heights and power tools) as they apply to the jobsite and shop workspace.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Develop a list of rules for workplace safety including proper personal protective equipment (PPE), sanitation, neat and tidy work area and reporting workplace accidents and safety incidents.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Act consistently to focus on personal tasks while maintaining consciousness of others working in proximity.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Demonstrate the utilization and maintenance of protective devices on equipment.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Perform proper lockout and de-energizing of equipment before beginning inspections or repairs.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Identify the advantages and disadvantages of using each category of industry standard personal protective equipment (PPE) for respiratory, hearing, sight and body protection such as masks, ear plugs, safety goggles and shields.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Demonstrate PPE cleaning procedures.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Demonstrate the correct use of safety equipment (e.g., eye wash station, shower, first aid station, shop ventilation, fire extinguishers and caging devices) in the workplace.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Post and maintain emergency phone numbers in a visible location.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Discuss appropriate actions in the event of an injury in the workplace, including whom to contact, how to report and first-aid procedures.

outcomes.statement: Prepare for the work placement.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 80A: Work Study Preparation (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III – Occupational Health and Safety in The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019:
- the right to know – the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate – in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,
- the right to refuse – work that you believe is unusually dangerous.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent, teacher or other school staff, employer) involved in the work placement.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the business/organization to become familiar with its operations.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: In collaboration with all partners, develop personal and learning goals for the work placement.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents needed for the work placement (e.g., personal career documentation such as a resume or portfolio, permission forms, logs, self- and employer evaluation forms).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop a list of questions that could potentially be asked by the employer/work placement in an interview situation as well as answers to the questions.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Participate in an interview with the employer prior to beginning the work placement.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Reflect upon one’s performance during the interview.

outcomes.statement: Explore design studies and the stages of a design process.

indicators.label: a
b
c
indicators.text:
Examine how the design process is non-linear and recursive, and includes:
- communication of the problem or need by the end user to the designer; and,
- clarification of perception of end user expectation by the designer; or need held by the designer; provided (i.e., test, refine and improve, test again).

indicators.label: d

indicators.label: e

outcomes.statement: Explore common principles and elements of design.

indicators.label: a
b
c

outcomes.statement: Investigate the role of modelling and prototyping in the design process.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 3: The Modelling and Prototyping Process (Optional) · Suggested Time: 7-12 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 2

indicators.label: a
b
indicators.text: Define the term model and explain the purpose for modelling in the design process.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify critical attributes that differentiate a prototype from a model.

indicators.text: Describe situations in which either a model or a prototype is an important aspect of the design process.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Differentiate between a physical and an analytical prototype.

indicators.label: f
g
indicators.text: Speculate on reasons for creating either a comprehensive prototype (e.g., similar in appearance and including most components and attributes of a final product), or a focused prototype (e.g., implementing and testing one or two components and attributes of a final product).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text:
Create a prototype from a given scenario to illustrate a design process, including:
- an annotated sketch of a solution to a design problem;
- two-dimensional and three-dimensional models of the solution to the design problem using digital tools; and,
- a variety of prototypes to test different elements within the design.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Critically evaluate the efficacy of design decisions made within the prototype.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Adapt and refine the design to reflect data gleaned from the testing of prototypes.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Elicit feedback for a prototype using the terminology of the design process.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the engineering design process.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Differentiate among processes for designing:
- a product for personal use (e.g., snowboard, hair dryer, backpack);
- a system (e.g., computer or transportation network, supply chain); and,
- an industrial process (e.g., power generating station, water treatment plant).

indicators.label: b
c
indicators.text: Differentiate between types of engineering challenges to be solved, including structural, mechanical, electrical and systems engineering.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Apply the design process to an engineering challenge scenario, such as building a tower with limited materials or building a bridge to hold maximum weight with minimum material.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Elicit feedback using the appropriate terminology from the design process.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Create a visual representation and narrative description of the engineering design process.

indicators.label: a
b
indicators.text: Differentiate between user-centred design and universal design.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research ways in which design has resulted in exclusion of individuals from accessing objects or spaces.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify individuals, groups and organizations that have advocated for change in design thinking and individual and systemic dispositions toward design.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine ethical and economic reasons for inclusion of universal design in all design processes.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain how universal design facilitates empowerment and self sufficiency among individuals and organizations encountering designed spaces, objects or events.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe ways in which universal design is beneficial to all individuals regardless of life stage or physical abilities.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Create an inventory of universal design features in school and community spaces.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Explore the benefits of universal design applications such as levered doorknobs, taps in sinks and tubs, strategically placed assisted lifts and grab bars, governors on water heaters, adjustable height cupboards and tables, no barrier entries to buildings in single family dwellings and multi-unit residential dwellings.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Propose universal design improvements that would enhance user experiences with a variety of private and public spaces and products.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Suggest considerations required in the design process to develop products and places that are accessible to people with a wide range of abilities, to the greatest extent possible.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Explain why universal design is important to include in all spaces, not just industrial, commercial or publicly accessed buildings and spaces.

indicators.label: a

d

indicators.text:
Critique design solutions using a process that includes the following stages:
- Describe: What do you see (e.g., colour, shape, form)?
- Analyze: What did the producer intend?
- Interpret: Is the product successful in conveying the message or achieving its purpose? Is the product successful using elements and principles of visual design? and,
- Evaluate: What changes would I suggest? What factors need to be considered in assessing the feasibility of the potential changes?

outcomes.statement: Prepare for the work placement.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 80A: Work Study Preparation (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III – Occupational Health and Safety in The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019:
- the right to know – the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate – in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,
- the right to refuse – work that you believe is unusually dangerous.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent, teacher or other school staff, employer) involved in the work placement.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the business/organization to become familiar with its operations.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: In collaboration with all partners, develop personal and learning goals for the work placement.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents needed for the work placement (e.g., personal career documentation such as a resume or portfolio, permission forms, logs, self- and employer evaluation forms).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop a list of questions that could potentially be asked by the employer/work placement in an interview situation as well as answers to the questions.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Participate in an interview with the employer prior to beginning the work placement.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Reflect upon one’s performance during the interview.

outcomes.statement: Investigate inspiration and departure points for dramatic work.

indicators.label: f

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the impact and contributions of contemporary theatre practitioners working within various theatre roles (e.g., writers, dramaturge, performers, directors, stage managers, designers of set/costume/lighting/sound, choreographers of fight/dance, music directors/musicians, technicians).

outcomes.statement: Examine the role of the theatre and artists as potential agents of social change.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Analyze and practically explore a theatre movement that arose in response to social conditions (e.g., Paper Wheat in response to the creation of farming cooperatives in Saskatchewan, Native Earth Performing Arts in response to colonialism, Theatre of the Absurd in Europe and Butoh in Japan in response to WWII, Guerrilla Theatre in response to radical social movements of the 1960s, Bread and Puppets in the 1970s in response to social activism in USA).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Practically explore a current social issue of interest (e.g., treaty education outcome TR12, indicator - analyze how the media currently depicts the treaty relationship and determine the effects this has on public perception, marginalized groups, issues identified in the media) and consider how one might respond through dramatic work.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine how theatre artists use their art form to question the status quo and empower others to influence change (e.g., challenging perspectives on gender equity).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry to examine Saskatchewan theatres and theatre artists (e.g., Gordon Tootoosis Nikaniwin Theatre, SUM Theatre, Persephone Theatre, Globe Theatre, Dancing Sky Theatre, Troupe du Jour, Curtain Razors, Listen to Dis, Deaf Crows, Live Five) whose work addresses local and/or global issues (e.g., food security, water access, health, migration, colonization, reconciliation, climate change, gender and sexual diversity, ethics and technologies, economic disparity, economic, social and environmental sustainability).

outcomes.statement: Research contemporary and/or current theatre practices of First Nations, Inuit and Métis artists in Canada.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss questions concerning the relationship between identity and art-making practices (e.g., Does culture influence the subject matter or themes of dramatic work? How might traditional practices inform the work of specific artists?).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Conduct research on a contemporary First Nations, Inuit or Métis theatre company in Canada and report on such things as company philosophy or focus, subject or themes presented, discipline specific or interdisciplinary approaches and/or the potential influence of local cultural practices.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research (e.g., in person interviews, written information, recorded or online interview) an Indigenous theatre artist and examine what impacts his or her work, considering questions such as What is the role of Indigenous theatre in the local community and society? Is it important to distinguish Indigenous theatre separately from non-Indigenous theatre? Does cultural identity influence the work?

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate effective communication skills.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 1: Communication (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-7 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Compare and contrast various communication styles.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe how professional communication differs from other types of communication (e.g., personal social media posts, personal cell phone use).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe verbal (e.g., calling someone by their first name) and non-verbal communication (e.g., body language, touch, silence, eye contact, shaking hands) that vary among cultures.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore effective communication methods (e.g., paraphrasing, empathetic listening, asking closed questions, asking open-ended questions, clarifying).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain the barriers to effective communication (e.g., vision problems, loud noises, lack of privacy, distractions).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explore augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) tools to reduce barriers to communication.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: List common defense mechanisms (e.g., denial, displacement, passive-aggressiveness, projection, rationalization, suppression) and explain how they interfere with effective communication.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explain how messages can be misinterpreted when conveyed electronically.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Practise using effective communication techniques for telephone conversations and text messages.

outcomes.statement: Describe ways to respect the privacy and confidentiality of care recipients.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 2: Privacy and Confidentiality (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-7 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the importance of maintaining confidentiality in caregiving environments.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe the role and significance of various forms used in caregiving environments such as medical release forms, parental permission forms, incident reports and consent to release information forms.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify situations or types of communication which may compromise the privacy and confidentiality of a care recipient (e.g., taking pictures, using the carbon copy or blind carbon copy function in emails).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine strategies used to protect or respect privacy and confidentiality of care recipients, their families and employees in caregiving environments.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify laws and protocols that regulate privacy and confidentiality in caregiving environments.

outcomes.statement: Discuss characteristics of professional conduct.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 3: Professional Conduct (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-4 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify professional qualities such as being attentive, respectful, resourceful, diligent, responsible and ethical.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine the role of professional organizations in setting and monitoring codes of conduct.

indicators.label: c
d
indicators.text: Discuss professional appearance in various professional caregiving environments.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine the use of personal devices while at work in caregiving roles.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explore the necessity of establishing personal and professional boundaries.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explain what to do if boundaries have been crossed between the care recipient, their family and the caregiver.

outcomes.statement: Research workplace safety principles, practices and relevant legislation required for employees in the workplace.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 4: Workplace Safety (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-7 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None
