outcomes.statement: Analyze the role and contributions of entrepreneurship and intrapreneurship to personal, school and community life.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 1: Introduction to Entrepreneurship (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe what entrepreneurship is and what entrepreneurs do.

indicators.label: b
c
indicators.text: Identify examples of entrepreneurship and entrepreneurs within the local community and province.

indicators.label: d
e
indicators.text: Discuss opportunities and challenges associated with being intrapreneurial and entrepreneurial within the school and community.

indicators.label: f
g
indicators.text: Analyze statistics related to the contributions made by entrepreneurs to the local, provincial and Canadian economics.

outcomes.statement: Investigate factors that define and contribute to entrepreneurial success.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 2: Entrepreneurial Success (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-7 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 1

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Differentiate among for-profit, not-for-profit and social enterprises within the community and province.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss the meaning of success within the contexts of profit, not-for-profit and social enterprises.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine how culture and worldviews, including those of First Nations and Métis people in Saskatchewan, inform the definition of success for an entrepreneurial venture.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Assess entrepreneurial success as defined by the Seventh Generation Principle.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Debate the role of failure in entrepreneurship.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Generate a list of questions that could be asked of entrepreneurs to gain insight into their ventures and to understand what success means to them. Sample questions include:
- How did you come up with your business idea?
- What problem does your business solve?
- What makes your business unique?
- Why did you choose entrepreneurship?
- What is the biggest challenge you have overcome?
- What is your greatest achievement?
- What mistakes have you made in your business, and how did you handle them?
- Do you consider yourself successful as an entrepreneur? Why or why not?
- As an entrepreneur, what advice would you give your younger self?

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Interview or research local and Saskatchewan entrepreneurs to gain insight into the broad range of entrepreneurial ventures within the community and province.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Communicate interview or research findings related to local and Saskatchewan entrepreneurs through a multi-media (e.g., video and presentation), print (e.g., brochure and magazine) or oral presentation.

outcomes.statement: Assess characteristics and skills important for entrepreneurial success.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 3: Entrepreneurial Characteristics and Skills (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 2

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Differentiate between characteristics and skills.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research characteristics (e.g., confidence, passion and motivation) and skills (e.g., leadership, teamwork and networking) common to successful entrepreneurs.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Differentiate between characteristics that are innate and those that are learned and gained through time and experience.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine the relationship among personal financial competence and confidence, personal credit score and entrepreneurial progress and success.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss what it means to have an entrepreneurial mindset.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Debate the statement, “Entrepreneurs are born.”

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine the role of creativity in entrepreneurship.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Describe interpersonal skills (e.g., verbal and non-verbal communication, listening, negotiation, decision-making and assertiveness) that contribute to entrepreneurial success.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Identify traits (e.g., self-doubt, perfectionism and being easily distracted) that may hinder entrepreneurial success.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Reflect on personal characteristics, skills, interest in, and suitability for, entrepreneurship as a career pathway of choice or for intrapreneurship within a company or organization.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Propose ways (e.g., using a team approach, formal and informal education and volunteering) to overcome personal shortcomings necessary for entrepreneurial success.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Commit to a personal plan for utilizing personal characteristics and skills and for overcoming shortcomings necessary for entrepreneurial success.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Recognize and affirm the characteristics and skills possessed by classmates.

outcomes.statement: Examine entrepreneurial opportunities at home, at school and in the community.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 4: Seeking Opportunities (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-6 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 1

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe an entrepreneurial opportunity (i.e., a need, a want or a problem that needs to be solved).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss the view that change causes entrepreneurial opportunities and that entrepreneurial opportunities cause change.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: List potential sources of entrepreneurial opportunities (e.g., technological change, changing demographics, shortages, surpluses and shifts in demand).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Assess the impact of PESTLE factors (i.e., political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental) on entrepreneurial opportunities.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Differentiate between a trend and a fad and their impacts on entrepreneurial opportunities.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Propose ways (e.g., being optimistic, accepting challenges, searching for opportunities and researching) that entrepreneurs discover and take advantage of opportunities.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Differentiate between an opportunity (i.e., the problem) and an idea (i.e., a potential solution).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify potential entrepreneurial opportunities at home, at school and in the community.

outcomes.statement: Assess design thinking as a process for creating successful and meaningful entrepreneurial solutions.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 5: Design Thinking and Entrepreneurship (Core) · Suggested Time: 7-10 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 4

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe design thinking, including its human-centric nature.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research proposed benefits (e.g., increased efficiency and return on investment, increased opportunities for collaboration and reduced risk associated with launching new ideas) associated with using the design thinking process in business.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate how successful companies such as Netflix, Nike and Airbnb have incorporated design thinking into their business strategies.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify the five stages of design thinking (i.e., empathize, define, ideate, prototype and test).

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Explain the non-linear and iterative nature of the design thinking process.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Analyze the role and importance of failure as part of the design thinking process.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Research effective brainstorming techniques (e.g., green light thinking, mind maps, rapid ideation, game storming and step-ladder technique).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Establish norms (e.g., defer all judgment, aim for quantity, build on others’ ideas and involve everyone) for group brainstorming.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Apply the design thinking process to find solutions to real-life or given entrepreneurial scenarios.

outcomes.statement: Investigate Indigenous economic reconciliation as an important contributor to reconciliation in Canada.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 6: Economic Reconciliation (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 4

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe the state of entrepreneurship among First Nations peoples in Saskatchewan and Canada pre- and post-colonization.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research challenges faced, and contributions made, by First Nations and Métis peoples in helping to shape the entrepreneurial landscape of Saskatchewan and Canada.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate the tenets of Indigenous economic reconciliation including its holistic, values-driven approach to attaining community economic prosperity.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the benefits of Indigenous economic reconciliation for all peoples in Canada.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe the concept of economic leakage and the resulting impact on remote, rural, urban and First Nations communities.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate opportunities (e.g., innovation, creating wealth and community issues/problems) that could be addressed by entrepreneurship within the local and/or provincial community.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Define the term urban reserve.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify urban reserves located in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Research the history of urban reserves in Saskatchewan including the impact of the Saskatchewan Treaty Land Entitlement Framework Agreement.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Assess the economic, social and cultural opportunities provided by the establishment of urban reserves in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Reflect on personal and collective responsibility for supporting Indigenous economic reconciliation within the local and broader community.

outcomes.statement: Explore community initiatives, government and community development agencies, and business associations that support entrepreneurship.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 7: Business and Community Development (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-7 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 2

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe networking and its importance for entrepreneurial success.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify potential allies (e.g., family, friends, Elders, tribal councils, postsecondary and training institutions) that could be a part of personal and professional networks to support the development of a new venture within the community.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe ways (e.g., volunteering, job shadows, attending business trade fairs or business functions and informational interviews) to build and expand personal and professional networks within the local business community

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine the mutual benefits of contributing to, and receiving support from, a network.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Propose networking strategies for individuals who are uncomfortable with, or afraid of, the process.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Reflect on personal comfort level with networking.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Construct a plan to develop or grow personal networking skills.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss the value of mentorship in entrepreneurship for both mentors and mentees.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Research the structure, mission and goals of various community development agencies, business associations and agencies (e.g., local and provincial chambers of commerce, Clarence Campeau Development Fund, SK Start-up Institute, Women Entrepreneurs of Saskatchewan, Community Futures Saskatchewan, SaskMétis Economic Development Corporation and Tools and Finance for Aboriginal Business) that support Saskatchewan entrepreneurs.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Examine the relationship between local entrepreneurial success and the growth and sustainability of communities in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Investigate how business ventures evolve and change over time and how the need for, and kinds of, supports also evolve and change.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Identify incentives or initiatives for new and expanding business development available within the local community.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Research the availability of financial support (e.g., grants and loans) for Saskatchewan entrepreneurs including First Nations and Métis people, newcomers, women and youth.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Describe the processes for accessing financial support available to Saskatchewan and Canadian entrepreneurs.

outcomes.statement: Evaluate common types of business structures.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 8: Business Structures (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-7 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 6

indicators.label: a
b
indicators.text: Identify examples of each type of business structure within the local community and province.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Compare the features (e.g., ownership, process for establishing, profitsharing, liability protection and longevity) of various types of business structures.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine the purpose and benefits of succession planning and the impact each type of business structure has on the process.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Summarize the advantages and disadvantages of each type of business structure.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss how attitudes and beliefs (e.g., community and collective wellbeing) shaped by worldviews inform decisions related to business ownership and structures.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Research external factors (e.g., requirements for eligibility to access funding or support from a specific program, and tax and other laws such as the Indian Act) which may impact decisions related to business structures.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify sources of advice and information (e.g., legal, accounting, Chief and Council and other entrepreneurs) related to business structures.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Create scenarios best suited for each type of business structure and justify each choice.

outcomes.statement: Analyze the logistics associated with establishing a business in Saskatchewan.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 9: Establishing a Business in Saskatchewan (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-4 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 8

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research the business licenses and permits typically required at the federal, provincial, municipal and band (e.g., Band Council Resolution or BCR) levels, and the processes for applying for and obtaining them.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate the process for registering a business name (e.g., with Information Services Corporation) in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research requirements for collecting and remitting taxes (e.g., Provincial Sales Tax [PST], Goods and Service [GST] and business income) in Saskatchewan and Canada.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Summarize the process for opening applicable tax accounts (e.g., Provincial Sales Tax [PST], and Goods and Services Tax [GST]), collecting tax and remitting payments.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Assess Saskatchewan employment standards (e.g., employing young workers, minimum wage, overtime and vacation leave) applicable to entrepreneurs who hire employees or use the services of a subcontractor.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Differentiate between mandatory and optional Workers’ Compensation coverage in Saskatchewan and Canada.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify additional types of insurance coverage (e.g., general and professional liability) available to businesses.

outcomes.statement: Analyze the steps for starting a home-based business within the community.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 10: Home-based Businesses (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 9

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define home-based business.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss reasons why individuals start home-based businesses.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the prevalence and types of home-based businesses within the community.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine the advantages (e.g., tax deductions, low overhead and location) and disadvantages (e.g., limited space in the home, issues with neighbours and difficulty separating work from family life) of operating a home-based business.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research factors (e.g., zoning, liability, legal and insurance) that should be considered when establishing a home-based business.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Outline the steps for establishing a home-based business within the community.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify direct sales companies (e.g., skin care, health and wellness, home cleaning products and make-up) that may represent potential home-based business opportunities.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Reflect on personal interests, hobbies and skills that could potentially lead to the development of a home-based business.

outcomes.statement: Assess the importance of social responsibility in entrepreneurship.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 11: Social Responsibility (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-7 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 2

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: List the four components (i.e., environmental, ethical, philanthropic and economic) of social responsibility.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss potential benefits (e.g., stronger brand image and reputation, increased customer loyalty and empowering employees to do good) associated with social responsibility.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research social responsibility according to the guiding principles of wâhkôhtowin, wicihitowin and wîtaskêwin.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify ways (e.g., using alternative energy sources and implementing a recycling program) that businesses can demonstrate environmental responsibility.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe what ethics are, and how personal and societal ethics influence business ethics.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: List examples (e.g., using fair business practises, ethically sourcing materials and offering competitive wages to employees) of ethical business practices.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss ways (e.g., sponsoring a local non-profit annual fundraiser and donating a percentage of earnings to a worthy cause) that an entrepreneur can be philanthropic.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Examine the relationship among economic responsibility and the other components of social responsibility.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Debate the opinion that economic responsibility is the most important component of social responsibility.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Compare the social responsibility efforts of at least two businesses in the same industry.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Develop a social responsibility plan for an existing, proposed or fictitious business.

outcomes.statement: Evaluate opportunities for marketing to local, Saskatchewan, Canadian and global communities.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 12: The Local, Saskatchewan, Canadian and Global Marketplace (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 4

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe the uniqueness of the local area and the businesses, including the goods and services they provide, operating within it.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research Saskatchewan’s major export goods (e.g., agriculture, agri-food, oil and potash) and services (e.g., technology) as well as niche markets filled by unique Saskatchewan goods and services.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify major international customers of Saskatchewan products.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the importance to Saskatchewan of trading, exporting and selling beyond its provincial borders.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify local marketplaces and selling opportunities/services (e.g., trade shows, local farmers’ market, community bulletin boards, buy/sell groups and social media platforms).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Propose instances when entrepreneurs might choose to market their goods or services to potential customers provincially, nationally and globally.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Analyze statistics and trends related to the evolution of electronic commerce (i.e., e-commerce).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Investigate strategies including e-commerce for reaching potential customers beyond the local area.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Identify organizations (e.g., Saskatchewan Trade and Export Partnership [STEP]) that assist Saskatchewan entrepreneurs in accessing global markets.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Research the support and services provided by organizations such as STEP.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Discuss potential positive and negative impacts of factors such as changes in currency values, tariffs, laws/regulations, political unrest, natural disasters and global pandemics on global trade/exports and efforts of individual entrepreneurs to reach global markets.

outcomes.statement: Analyze marketing strategies for managing a brand.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 13A: Marketing Fundamentals A (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-7 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 12

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Differentiate between brand identity and brand image.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify examples of brand names, logos or trademarks, and slogans that contribute to brand identity for a variety of businesses.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate the brand image presented by successful companies.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the purposes of marketing (e.g., selling what a business offers and managing a brand).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Assess the importance of identifying competitors in the marketplace.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Differentiate between direct and indirect competitors.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Define the term competitive intelligence.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Summarize the types of competitor information (e.g., pricing, marketing strategies and market share) that is useful to collect and analyze.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Propose strategies (e.g., posing as a customer, visiting the competitor’s website and reviewing advertisements) for gathering competitive intelligence.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Examine the importance of knowing one’s customers and target market.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Categorize types of customer information (e.g., demographics [e.g., age, gender, income, ethnicity and culture] and psychographic [e.g., attitudes, values and lifestyle]) that is useful to gather and analyze.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Explain the value of a unique selling proposition.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Identify the unique selling propositions presented by several local or other businesses or brands.

outcomes.statement: Examine the interrelatedness of the four Ps of marketing.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 13B: Marketing Fundamentals B (Core) · Suggested Time: 8-10 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 13A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify the four Ps of marketing (i.e., product, price, place and promotion) known as the Marketing Mix.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Differentiate between products that are tangible (e.g., goods) and intangible (e.g., services, ideas or experiences).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Analyze characteristics (e.g., quality, design, features and benefits) considered important for a good product.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Research factors (e.g., input costs, profit, competitive pricing and price sensitivity) that should be considered when pricing a product in the marketplace.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Differentiate between direct (i.e., seller to consumer) and indirect (i.e., seller to a third party such as an importer, wholesaler or retailer) channels for selling and distributing products and services.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Evaluate the impact of technology and e-commerce on a business’ ability to reach potential consumers directly.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Investigate the advantages and disadvantages of direct selling for both buyer and seller.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify ways in which businesses promote their products online and through other mediums using strategies such as coupons, contests, loyalty cards, samples and special events.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Describe the four Ps in action for a business, organization or brand/product of personal interest.

outcomes.statement: Examine the role of market research in effective business planning.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 14: Market Research (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 13B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss reasons (e.g., making informed decisions and avoiding costly mistakes) for conducting market research.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify circumstances (e.g., launching a new business, expanding into a new market or looking for customers) when market research would be beneficial.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore what a trend and industry analyses are and their roles in supporting market research.

indicators.label: d
e
indicators.text: Analyze various scenarios requiring market research to determine when and how one or more methods for collecting data would be effective.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research the availability and use of online (e.g., social media and website) analytics for market research.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine the components and purpose of a SWOT (i.e., Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities and Threats) analysis as a tool for market research.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Prepare SWOT analyses for a variety of entrepreneurship scenarios.

outcomes.statement: Explore the role of human resource management within a business.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 15: Human Resource Management (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 9

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the function and importance of human resource management within a business.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research factors (e.g., the number of employees required currently and in the next few years, training that will be provided, job requirements/descriptions, and how and how much employees will be paid) to be considered in a human resources plan.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the potential impact of generational and cultural gaps within Saskatchewan workplaces.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Strategize ways to effectively manage generational and cultural gaps within the workplace.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify sources (e.g., referrals from friends and employees, hiring from within, employment agencies and social media platforms) for recruiting potential employees.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into the processes commonly used by employers to attract, screen and hire employees.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Assess Saskatchewan and Canadian laws that govern workplace standards pertaining, but not limited, to workplace safety, anti-discrimination, harassment, accessibility and environmental responsibility.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss the relationship among employee satisfaction with their jobs, business success and a business’ reputation.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Propose effective employee retention strategies (e.g., training, bonuses and benefits).

outcomes.statement: Explore financial considerations for a business start-up.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 16A: Financial Records, Planning and Management A (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-7 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 7

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of maintaining accurate and up-to-date financial records throughout the life of a business.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Debate the opinion that financial success equals business success.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore sources (e.g., personal investment, love money, share capital, angel investors, grants, subsidies and bank loans) for funding a business start-up.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Differentiate between start-up and ongoing costs.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine the components of a break-even analysis.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss when (e.g., at start-up or when considering an expansion) a business might conduct a break-even analysis.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Calculate the break-even point for a variety of business scenarios.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Analyze what cash flow is, its importance to the day-to-day operations of a business and how it is commonly reported (i.e., statement of cash flow and cash flow projection).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Differentiate between a positive and a negative cash flow.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Discuss the financial implications of a positive and a negative cash flow.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Explore ways (e.g., using software such as spreadsheets or accounting packages and paper copy) for recording and managing cash flow.

outcomes.statement: Analyze components of a sound financial plan for business.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 16B: Financial Records, Planning and Management B (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-7 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 16A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine formats for basic financial recordkeeping (e.g., using software such as spreadsheets or accounting packages and paper copy).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Analyze prepared balance sheets and income statements to determine how financial statements are used within the context of a business.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Prepare balance sheets and income statements for personal use or for given individual and for business scenarios.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze the conditions of businesses represented by their respective financial statements.

indicators.label: e

outcomes.statement: Assess the importance of positive mental health and well-being for Saskatchewan and Canadian entrepreneurs.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 17A: Mental Health and Well-being (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 1

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the concept of life/work balance as it relates to entrepreneurs.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Analyze the relationship between an entrepreneur’s personal mental health and well-being and the health of their business.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify stressors (e.g., income uncertainty, loneliness and isolation) faced by many entrepreneurs and the resulting impact on self, the business, society and others such as family and friends.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Research statistics related to the mental health and well-being of Canadian entrepreneurs.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze differences in the mental health and well-being challenges faced by various groups of entrepreneurs such as women, newcomers, younger entrepreneurs and individuals who are gender and/or sexually diverse.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate barriers (e.g., cost and stigma) faced by entrepreneurs in seeking mental health services and support.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Suggest strategies (e.g., practising self-care and surrounding oneself with positive influences) for addressing and maintaining positive mental health as an entrepreneur.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explore the impact of mentoring relationships on mental health and wellbeing.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Identify credible sources of mental health support for Saskatchewan and Canadian entrepreneurs.

outcomes.statement: Assess the importance of an occupational health and safety plan within a business.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 17B: Occupational Health and Safety (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 9

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe the general duties of self-employed persons as outlined in the Saskatchewan Employment Act.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify the benefits to employers and employees of the Saskatchewan Workers Compensation Act and the Meredith Principles.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss reasons (e.g., protecting the health and safety of employees, creating a positive work environment and the costs [e.g., to the injured worker and to the business] associated with a workplace injury or incident) for having a safety plan within a business.

indicators.label: d
e
indicators.text: Role-play situations where employees, supervisors and managers effectively deal with health and safety concerns within the workplace.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate employers’ and employees’ rights and responsibilities as they pertain to health and safety in the workplace in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: g

outcomes.statement: Explore entrepreneurship as a career pathway.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 18: Entrepreneurship as a Career Pathway (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 3

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Critique common misconceptions about entrepreneurs, such as:
- Entrepreneurs can be successful only if they have access to lots of money.
- Entrepreneurs set their own hours and vacation schedules.
- Entrepreneurs work alone.
- Entrepreneurs take huge risks to be successful.
- Entrepreneurs are wealthy.
- All it takes is one good idea to be a successful entrepreneur.
- Every entrepreneur needs a post-secondary business degree to be successful.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research typical earnings for entrepreneurs in Saskatchewan and Canada.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss reasons (e.g., media showcasing successful entrepreneurs and increased attention to social entrepreneurship) why entrepreneurship is becoming more widely accepted as a viable career pathway.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Debate the idea that being an entrepreneur is better than working for someone else.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Reflect on personal interest in, and suitability for, entrepreneurship as a career pathway of choice.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Construct a personal plan or a plan for another individual aspiring to be an entrepreneur, considering factors such as
- a supportive network of allies;
- membership in, and support from, professional organizations and associations; and,
- education, training and learning opportunities.

outcomes.statement: Outline a business idea or concept using the business model canvas planning framework.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 19A: Planning a Start-up A (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Modules 5, 11, 14, 15, 16A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of planning before launching a start-up.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Develop a list of questions that should be answered when planning a startup, such as:
- What is the business idea?
- What need or want does it fill, or what problem does it solve?
- Who are the targeted customers?
- How much money and other resources will be required for start-up?
- How will money and other resources be obtained?
- What other resources are needed?

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research what the business model canvas is and how it can be used to outline a business concept.

indicators.label: d
e
indicators.text: Complete a business model canvas for a business idea or concept.

outcomes.statement: Construct a detailed business plan for a proposed start-up.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 19B: Planning a Start-up B (Core) · Suggested Time: 10-15 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 19A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Differentiate between a business model canvas and a business plan.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss reasons (e.g., obtaining financing and planning a start-up or expansion) for preparing a written business plan.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Analyze prepared business plans to identify and describe common components (e.g., executive summary, company description, market analysis, financial projections, operational plan, succession plan and conclusion) of a business plan.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine characteristics (e.g., written in plain, easy-to-understand language; research-based; well-defined market; and, realistic) of an effective and well-written business plan.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Develop a written business plan for a proposed start-up.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Present the business plan to potential investors or supporters.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Reflect on feedback received from potential investors or supporters.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Make required adjustments to the business plan.

outcomes.statement: Execute, conclude and evaluate the success of a short-term startup.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 20A: Executing and Concluding a Start-up A (Optional) · Suggested Time: 10-15 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 19A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of, and processes (e.g., regular reports, maintaining financial reports and collecting data) for, monitoring the operations and progress of the start-up.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Launch and operate the start-up outlined in the business model canvas.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Implement processes for monitoring the operations and progress of the start-up to conclusion.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Reflect on business and personal successes and challenges resulting from the operation of the start-up.

outcomes.statement: Execute, conclude, evaluate the success of, and report on, the start-up.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 20B: Executing and Concluding a Start-up B (Optional) · Suggested Time: 40-60 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 19B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the need for revisiting, updating and revising a business plan throughout the life of a business.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Launch and operate the start-up.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Reflect regularly on business progress and success by answering questions such as:
- What has worked well thus far?
- Are sales goals being met?
- Do we have enough supplies to meet production demands?
- What needs adjustment and why?
- How can productivity be improved?
- What has been accomplished in the business to date?
- Where is the business at financially? Is there a cash-flow problem?
- What have I personally contributed? How else can I contribute?
- What have I learned about business and what it takes to successfully operate a business?
- What have I learned about myself?

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain what a pivot is and why a pivot strategy is important for business success.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Adjust business operations and the business plan as required throughout the life of the business.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Maintain detailed records (e.g., financial and inventory) throughout the life of the business.

indicators.label: g
h
indicators.text: Prepare a final written report (e.g., shareholders’ report) that summarizes operations and success.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Present the final written report to others such as supporters and investors.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Reflect on business and personal successes and challenges resulting from the operation of the start-up.

outcomes.statement: Prepare for the work placement.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 80A: Work Study Preparation (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate, Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 3

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III – Occupational Health and Safety in The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019:
- the right to know – the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate – in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,
- the right to refuse – work that you believe is unusually dangerous.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent, teacher or other school staff and employer) involved in the work placement.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the business/organization to become familiar with its operations.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: In collaboration with all partners, develop personal and learning goals for the work placement.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents needed for the work placement (e.g., personal career documentation such as a resume or portfolio, permission forms, logs, self- and employer evaluation forms).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop a list of questions that could potentially be asked by the employer/work placement in an interview situation as well as answers to the questions.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Participate in an interview with the employer prior to beginning the work placement.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Reflect upon one’s performance during the interview.

outcomes.statement: Analyze and explore environmental science related career paths in Saskatchewan, Canada and the world.
outcomes.printedWith: CP, DM

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Generate a list of occupations that require a background in environmental science. (K, S)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore the connection between topics in Environmental Science 20 and occupations of personal interest. (S, A, STSE)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify which environmental-science related occupations are facing shortages and which are oversubscribed locally, regionally and/or nationally. (STSE, S, K, A)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine the educational qualifications of people involved in environmental-science related jobs. (S, A)

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Compare the roles and responsibilities of various environmental science professionals as they engage with a specific project. (K, STSE, A)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Participate in a workplace-based career development opportunity (e.g., job shadow and career spotlight) related to environmental science. (S, A, STSE)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Participate in a career fair and generate a list of occupations represented that require a background in environmental science.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Conduct a role play and/or model environmental-science related occupations, including perspectives from various stakeholders. (S, A)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Communicate research findings related to environmental - science occupations through a display, brochure, video, presentation software, website or orally. (K, S, A, STSE)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Develop a plan to attain your dream job in the environmental science field. (S, A)

outcomes.statement: Create and carry out a plan to explore one or more topics of personal interest relevant to Environmental Science 20 in depth.
outcomes.printedWith: CP, DM, SI, TPS

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Design a scientific investigation related to a topic of study in Environmental Science 20 that includes a testable question, a hypothesis, an experimental design that will test the hypothesis and detailed procedures for collecting and analyzing data. (STSE, S).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Carry out an experiment following established scientific protocols to investigate a question of interest related to one or more of the topics of Environmental Science 20. (S, A, K, STSE)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Analyze the purpose and benefits of a specific municipal, provincial, territorial or federal policy, legislation, regulation, order, incentive or practice related to the environment and/or sustainability. (S, STSE)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Develop a policy, grounded in environmental science, which addresses an issue of concern to society and/or for the environment. (S, STSE)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Develop an environmental impact assessment of a real or hypothetical development. (S, STSE)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Design, construct and evaluate the effectiveness of a device, model or technique that demonstrates the scientific principles underlying a concept related to Environmental Science 20. (STSE, S)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Develop an action plan, including a desired future state, goals, targets, strategies and performance measures, to address a specific environmental issue. (S, STSE)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Assess the extent to which a global issue (e.g., climate change, water shortages, habitat destruction, invasive species and air pollution) is evident within a local context. (A, STSE)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Debate the applicability of William Forster Lloyd's "tragedy of the commons" to contemporary principles of sustainable development. (S)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Analyze data from sources such as student-developed surveys or research studies, case studies or other statistical methods to make predictions regarding the health of a population and/or ecosystem. (S, STSE, A)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Analyze an issue or case study where humans have greatly affected their environment, including a cost-benefit analysis and ethical implications. (STSE)

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Assemble and reflect on a portfolio that demonstrates an understanding of an environmental science topic of interest to the student. (S, A)

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Develop materials to support the arguments for and against a position related to an environmental science issue. (A, K, S)

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Share the results of student-directed research through a display, presentation, performance, demonstration, song, game, commercial, fine art representation, video or research paper. (S)

indicators.label: o
indicators.text: Construct a tool (e.g., rubric, checklist, self-evaluation form or peer-evaluation form) to assess the process and products involved in a student-directed study. (S, A)

outcomes.statement: Examine the methods, mindsets and purposes of environmental science.
outcomes.printedWith: CP, DM

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Reflect upon how one's connection with the environment is influenced by personal experiences and cultural understandings. (K, STSE, A)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Engage in place-based learning to gain a deeper understanding and appreciation of the environment. (S, STSE)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Analyze how different worldviews (e.g. anthropocentric, biocentric and ecocentric) are expressed through various environmental action plans or environmental policies developed by individuals, industry, government and non- governmental organizations and First Nations, Métis and Inuit groups. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Recognize essential characteristics of First Nations and Métis worldviews regarding the environment, including the importance of the four elements (i.e., earth, water, wind and fire), a sense of interconnectedness with the environment and respect for Mother Earth. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Recognize environmental science as a newly developing field that integrates knowledge, theories, models and processes from other scientific disciplines such as ecology, atmospheric science, biology, chemistry, physics, oceanography, geology and human geography to investigate human impacts on the environment. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Differentiate between environmental science and environmental studies, including the types of questions asked, methods used to address those questions and the types of data collected. (STSE)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Outline key events, including the industrial revolution, medical revolution, green revolution (agriculture) and the environmental revolution (stewardship), of the environmental movement and their interrelationships with environmental science. (K, STSE, S)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Examine how principles of sustainability (i.e., environmental, economic and social justice) are integral to environmental science. (STSE)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Investigate how data produced through environmental science can be used in environmental impact assessments, such as those outlined in the Canadian Environmental Assessment Act, 2012, to guide projects or policies. (STSE)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of systems thinking (e.g., boundaries, initial conditions, inputs and outputs, feedback loops, energy flows and matter transfers) to understanding environmental issues. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Assess how the assumptions and approximations that are incorporated into a model of a particular environmental system influence the reliability and precision of the model. (STSE)

outcomes.statement: Assess the impact of human activities on indoor and outdoor air quality and the need for regulations and mitigating technologies to minimize risks to human health.
outcomes.printedWith: SI, DM

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Pose questions regarding how human activities and technologies have influenced air quality. (S)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate the role of stratospheric ozone layer depletion as a contributor towards human health issues such as cancers and cataracts. (STSE, K, A)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe the sources of indoor and outdoor air pollutants such as particulate matter, sulphur dioxide, nitrogen dioxide, volatile organic chemicals (VOCs), carbon monoxide, lead, tropospheric ozone, sulphuric acid, radon, mold and allergens and their potential effects on human health. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze the role of various government regulations (e.g., Air Quality Health Index (AQHI) and the National Ambient Air Quality Objectives (NAAQOs)), and legislation (e.g., Canadian Environmental Protection Act, 1999 and The Clean Air Act in Saskatchewan) in minimizing risks to human health. (S, K, STSE)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate the sources and production of industrial and photochemical smog and identify measures that can be undertaken to mitigate their effects to human health. (K, STSE, A)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Design and carry out a process to assess indoor or outdoor air quality, using appropriate technologies to collect and analyze data. (S, A)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explain the scientific principles underlying technologies and processes such as air scrubbers, baghouse filters, electrostatic precipitators and catalytic converters that were developed to reduce contaminants in motor vehicle and industrial emissions or to improve indoor air quality. (K, STSE, S)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Investigate whether a personal protective device or substance (e.g., sunscreen, mosquito repellent or protective clothing) is effective in protecting a person from an environmental factor that affects human health. (STSE, S)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Develop a generalization about the relationship between human population density and human health. (S, STSE)

outcomes.statement: Analyze the production, reliability and uses of geoscience data to investigate the effects of a changing climate on society and the environment.
outcomes.printedWith: CP, DM, SI

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine the types of questions that scientists attempt to answer with respect to Earth's climate and past, present and potential future climate changes. (STSE, A)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine how different techniques (e.g., satellite imagery, ice core samples and dendrology) provide scientists with a variety of data regarding climate change. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate the Arctic as an indicator region of climate change, including the impact on traditional lifestyles of northern peoples, given the general vulnerability to climate change effects at northern versus equatorial latitudes. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine how and why organizations such as the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), Canadian Centre for Climate Modeling and Analysis and Prairie Adaptation Research Collaborative (PARC) work to provide scientific research related to climate change and its potential environmental and societal implications. (STSE)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify the contributions of Indigenous knowledge in policy decisions related to climate change. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine the degree to which the scientific community has achieved consensus regarding the reality of anthropogenic climate change. (STSE)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Investigate potential environmental, economic and societal impacts of climate change in Saskatchewan on human health, population distribution and access to water and other resources. (STSE)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Interpret climate data (e.g., tables, maps, graphs, visualizations and other representations) to determine climate patterns and trends over specific periods. (S, STSE)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Investigate how climate models simulate important aspects of past and present climate and climate changes, and provide projections about future effects of climate changes with varying degrees of complexity and reliability. (K, STSE, S)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Recognize how phenomena such as El Niño, La Niña and ocean acidification provide evidence of how the effects of climate change on one earth system (i.e., geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere and biosphere) can produce effects across other earth systems. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Investigate the adaptation and mitigation strategies developed to minimize the potential impacts of climate change on the agriculture, energy, forestry, transportation and/or tourism sectors in Saskatchewan. (K, STSE, S)

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Hypothesize how life on earth might respond to a changing global climate given different scenarios change such as sea level rise, extreme weather events, water shortages, increased spread of disease, flooding and acidification of the oceans. (K, STSE, S, A)

outcomes.statement: Investigate technologies and processes used for mitigating and managing resource use, waste generation and pollution associated with a growing human population.
outcomes.printedWith: CP, DM, SI

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify factors that have contributed to historical and contemporary trends in human population growth and that may influence future growth. (K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate the environmental impact of human population changes over the last century on a specific region or area with respect to resource use, waste generation and pollution. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research First Nations and Métis beliefs and practices that demonstrate a sustainable perspective on using resources wisely and minimizing waste. (K, STSE, S)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the strengths and limitations of models (e.g., I=PAT) that scientists use to quantify the impact of population, consumption, technology and stewardship on the environment. (STSE, A)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Assess the impact of factors such as advances in food security and access to medicine that support a growing human population. (K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Analyze benefits and challenges associated with the use and production of fertilizer for food crops necessary to sustain a growing human population. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe technologies and processes that have been developed to minimize the impacts of mining, forestry and/or agricultural operations on air, water and soil quality and quantity. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Investigate the waste generated throughout the life cycle of a product. (STSE, S)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Design and carry out a waste audit, and propose a plan of action for waste reduction and/or diversion based on the findings. (S, A, K)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Investigate advances in technologies and processes (e.g., sewage treatment plants, incineration, composting, engineered landfills and curbside recycling) used for storing, handling and disposing of human and/or livestock waste. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Debate the benefits and consequences of public policies (e.g., municipal, provincial or federal) regarding the handling, storage, transportation, treatment and disposal of hazardous waste. (STSE)

outcomes.statement: Analyze the function and condition of freshwater aquatic systems such as rivers, streams, lakes, wetlands and watersheds.
outcomes.printedWith: CP, DM, SI

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain how to measure the condition of an aquatic ecosystem using chemical factors, physical factors and biological indicators including indicator species, keystone species and invasive species. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify how the presence or absence of traditional medicines can serve as indicators of water body health. (STSE, K, A)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Measure abiotic factors (e.g., turbidity, temperature, dissolved oxygen and particulates) of an ecosystem using a variety of techniques and technologies (e.g., probe ware, pH paper, Secchi disk, Imhoff settling cone and chemical water quality test kit) effectively and safely. (S, STSE, A)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine the diversity of life in a specific aquatic ecosystem through water sampling, classifying aquatic biota, assessing biodiversity and calculating a water quality index and/or algal productivity. (K, S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Assess the interdependencies between abiotic (e.g., pH, dissolved oxygen, turbidity, temperature, total dissolved solids, phosphorous, nitrogen, stream flow and biochemical oxygen demand [BOD]) and biotic factors in a functioning aquatic ecosystem. (K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate bacterial content in surface water and compare the presence of coliform bacteria to surface water quality standards following appropriate safety procedures. (A, S, STSE)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Assess how an integrated watershed management approach can address issues (e.g., water supply, drainage, storm water runoff, habitat protection and water rights) that affect water quality and the health of all living things within a watershed. (S)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Describe the benefits of the ecological goods and services provided by riparian zones and wetlands (e.g., marshes, swamps, bogs and fens) in protecting water resources. (K)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Recognize different characteristics of lakes from naturally oligotrophic to eutrophic as well as possible causes (e.g., clearing of land, excessive fertilizer runoff and treatment plants) and consequences of cultural eutrophication. (K)

outcomes.statement: Assess the importance of maintaining healthy water for humans and the environment.
outcomes.printedWith: SI, DM

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Analyze emerging health challenges such as the spread of disease, mercury in fish, blue-green algae and E. coli in drinking water that result from changes to the condition of aquatic systems. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Analyze the rationale for developing and enforcing water quality standards such as the Saskatchewan Surface Water Quality Objectives and the Canadian Water Quality Index and legislation such as the Canada Water Act and the International River Improvements Act. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine how individuals, organizations (e.g., watershed associations), First Nations and government agencies (e.g. Saskatchewan Water Security Agency) work to ensure clean and abundant water through producing water regulations and allocation policies. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Assess how irrigation projects affect food production, water availability, soil salinization and groundwater. (STSE)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe the operation and effectiveness of technologies and processes developed to protect drinking water sources locally and globally. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Analyze the impacts of point source and non-point source pollution on humans and aquatic systems. (STSE, K, A)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Research the sources, effects, and management and mitigation strategies of contaminants such as pathogens, organic matter, heavy metals, sediment, heat, petrochemicals and inorganic chemicals such as pesticides in aquatic and/or marine ecosystems. (STSE, A)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Investigate how human activities (e.g., overfishing, photo- degradation of plastic waste, shipping, coastal development and offshore extraction of oil and minerals) impact marine ecosystems (e.g., coral reef degradation, introduction of invasive species and reduced fish populations). (STSE, A)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Investigate the role of muskeg and moss in water filtration and food preservation for First Nations and Métis and other communities. (K, STSE, A)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Research advances in technologies such as desalinization plants, water treatment plants and home water filtrations systems, which are designed to maintain and improve water quality. (K, STSE, A)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Design a system of source water protection for a community`s drinking water recognizing the precautionary principle (STSE, A, S)

outcomes.statement: Analyze the importance of soils as an integral component of terrestrial ecosystems.
outcomes.printedWith: SI, DM, CP

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss how First Nations and Métis people value soil as an integral component of Mother Earth, including traditional ways of looking after soil. (STSE, A)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Recognize how the breakdown of parent material through various processes (e.g., weathering, erosion, deposition and decomposition of organisms) results in soil with varying properties (e.g., colour, texture, structure and pH). (K)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Understand the interconnectedness between soil characteristics, ecozones and natural vegetation in Saskatchewan. (K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Experiment with different soil mixtures, using black earth, compost, sand, top soil, manure, peat moss, vermiculite, loam and/or sand, to determine their suitability for growing different plant species. (S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain common methods scientists use to sample and monitor soil quality over time. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Collect and analyze soil data (e.g., pH, nitrate, phosphate, potassium, porosity and moisture) using technologies such as sensors and soil test kits safely and effectively. (A, S, STSE)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Research causes and consequences of soil degradation (e.g., wind and water erosion, salinity and desertification) and mitigation strategies (e.g., conservation tillage, contour farming, grassed waterways and shelterbelts) used to reduce the loss of topsoil. (A, K)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Recognize the role and diversity of organisms (e.g., nitrogen fixing bacteria, fungi, mycorrhizae, insects, plants and protists) found within soil environments. (K)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Discuss the role of soil in biogeochemical cycling, including carbon storage and nitrogen fixation, nitrification and denitrification. (STSE)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Examine how phenomena such as erosion, desertification and soil pollution, whether natural or human-caused, affect soil productivity and food production. (STSE)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Investigate how various small- and large-scale composting systems such as composting toilets, trench composting, vermicomposting, windrow composting, anaerobic digestion and mechanical biological treatment work to maintain and improve soil quality. (S, STSE)

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Collaborate with a group of peers to propose a landscaping investigation or action plan concerning an aspect of an urban ecosystem (e.g., rooftop gardens, green walls and green spaces) while ensuring conditions affecting local soil are represented. (A, STSE)

outcomes.statement: Examine the role plants play in an ecosystem, including the ways in which humans use plants.
outcomes.printedWith: SI, CP, DM

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the many roles of plants including their roles as providers of ecological goods and services as well as natural capital. (K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine the significance (e.g., medicinal, spiritual, nutritional and shelter) of plants, including tobacco, in First Nations and Métis cultures. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain how plant morphology and physiology determines the role of plants in an ecosystem (e.g., anchoring soil, filtering air and water, providing shelter for other organisms and providing organic matter to the ecosystem). (K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Interpret the relationship between photosynthesis, respiration and net primary productivity. (K)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify factors that influence plant pollination and reproduction, including the role of integrated pest management. (K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Analyze the relationship between plants and climate change, including plants' roles in reducing greenhouse gases, as well as potential impacts of climate change on plant growth and distribution. (STSE)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine advances in crop science that have influenced the types and yields of agricultural and/or horticultural crops grown in various areas of Saskatchewan. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Assess the economic, environmental and societal impacts of various agriculture practices (e.g., industrial, traditional, subsistence, sustainable agriculture, organic farming, urban agriculture, local food and community supported agriculture). (STSE)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Analyse forestry practices (e.g., selective cutting, clear cutting, shelterwood system and integrated resource management) in terms of productivity, profitability and environmental stewardship. (STSE)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Assess the impact of agriculture or forestry on a natural ecosystem. (S)

outcomes.statement: Recognize the need for intact habitat to support animal populations and biodiversity.
outcomes.printedWith: SI, CP, DM

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Justify the need for habitat protection and restoration in terms of biodiversity (e.g., genetic diversity, species diversity and habitat diversity) and resilience within ecosystems both locally and globally. (K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe examples of First Nations and Métis people's contributions in recognizing the effects of natural and human- caused changes to habitat on historical migration patterns of animals in Saskatchewan. (STSE, A)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine how habitat management and protection decisions are influenced by the extent to which Indigenous land rights (e.g., custodians of the land versus individual land ownership) are reflected through the spirit and intent of various treaties. (K, STSE, A)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain the roles of individuals, governmental and non- governmental organizations such as the Saskatchewan Prairie Conservation Action Plan, Ducks Unlimited and the Committee on the Status of Endangered Wildlife in Canada (COSEWIC), and legislation such as the Species at Risk Act (SARA) in protecting and maintaining habitats and biodiversity. (A)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Relate an organism's specific adaptations and behaviour to its niche in an ecosystem. (K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Correlate the range and habitat of various animals with Saskatchewan's ecozones and ecoregions and identify changes to an animal's range and habitat due to human activities such as agriculture, mining, oil and gas development, forestry, urbanization and recreation. (K)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss the implications of the competitive exclusion principle with respect to animals and plants in an ecosystem, including the introduction of invasive species and the potential for shifting ecozones due to climate change. (K)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Evaluate the importance of a keystone species in a specific terrestrial ecosystem. (S)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Assess current or potential impacts of a changing climate on a specific representative animal and its habitat. (S)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Provide examples of projects undertaken to restore damaged or destroyed habitats. (STSE)

outcomes.statement: Explore how value systems, social factors, personal experiences and cultural backgrounds can influence financial decision-making.

indicators.text: Explore the impact value systems developed in childhood can have on attitudes towards finances.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate how culture, religion and family belief systems can influence trust in, and value of, financial institutions.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore how social influences and personal experiences shape one’s attitudes toward financial decision-making.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine various cultural perspectives on income, budgeting, saving, sharing and accessing credit.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research various approaches to financial decision-making based on different perspectives or traditions (e.g., halal banking, Indigenous beliefs on sharing).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss how community and societal norms (e.g., expectations regarding gender roles) influence the financial well-being of self, family and community.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore ways to gather, interpret and utilize information to make responsible financial decisions.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore how financial security can have a positive influence on personal mental health and well-being.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore how accessing high-risk financial loans (e.g., payday loans, cash advances) can impact mental health.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe the financial pressures that may be created by accessing credit cards, credit lines and loans.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore the potentially addictive nature of spending and its connection to financial and mental wellness.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate resources, services and programs (e.g., debt consolidation, financial advice, credit counselling, addictions counselling) to support and address financial challenges.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Compare various types of financial institutions (e.g., virtual banks, traditional banks, credit unions, alternative lenders).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify Indigenous financial institutions and others responsive to various cultures in Canada.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Compare youth, student and adult bank accounts.

e
f

indicators.text: Explain how to obtain direct deposit information from your financial institution.

outcomes.statement: Explore various ways of earning an income.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the importance of a Social Insurance Number (SIN) and how it is obtained.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research payment methods for employees (e.g., wages, salary, commission, tips) and frequency of pay (e.g., biweekly, monthly, bonuses).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore how entrepreneurs earn an income from various methods of self-employment, such as a traditional store, an online store, and services.

indicators.text: Analyze the advantages and disadvantages of different employment situations (e.g., employee, self-employment, contract, passive income, side hustle).

indicators.text: Examine the information provided on sample pay stubs including gross income, net income and mandatory and optional deductions.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explain the impact of overtime on gross and net income.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Investigate income associated with treaties (e.g., treaty education outcome TR10 - Examine contemporary economic implications of Treaties for all the people of Saskatchewan and other Canadian jurisdictions).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Discuss how to manage a substantial financial gain (e.g., generational income, gift, prize, bursary, settlement).

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify services funded by tax revenue (e.g., healthcare, education, infrastructure).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Differentiate between types of taxes (e.g., income tax, sales tax, property tax).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine how sales taxes (e.g., Provincial Sales Tax [PST], Goods and Services Tax [GST]) are applied to new and used purchases.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore how taxation applies to Indigenous Peoples in Saskatchewan, including the eligibility criteria for exemptions related to income tax and sales tax.

outcomes.statement: Explore the purposes of money.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 1: Why Money Matters (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-4 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Explore common responses to questions such as:
- Why do people and communities need money?
- How much money does one really need?
- What are common financial decisions people and communities face?
- How do personal and community financial decisions affect self and others?
- Why is it important to manage personal and community finances?
- What influences one’s perception of, and value of, money?

indicators.label: d

indicators.text: Describe types of employment and self-employment typically available to students.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Reflect on personal interests and opportunities for earning an income in one’s community.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Differentiate among methods of earning an income such as contract, salary, wages, piecework, gig employment, commission and self-employment.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss ways (e.g., direct deposit, cheque, cash, e-transfer and bartering) in which earnings can be paid to workers.

outcomes.statement: Assess the financial, ethical and legal implications associated with different methods of paying for work.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 15B: Payment for Work (Core) · Suggested Time: 6-10 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 15A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Compare the advantages and disadvantages of being self-employed to being an employee.

indicators.label: b

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Differentiate between gross pay and net pay or “take home pay.”

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore the impact of different pay periods (e.g., project completion, weekly, bi-monthly and monthly) on managing one’s finances.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Examine the ethics, legality, financial implications and human impact associated with various ways of paying for work (e.g., bartering and under the table payments).

outcomes.statement: Examine the components of a pay stub.

indicators.text: Identify the common components of a pay stub including pay period, gross pay, deductions, net pay, employer contributions, hours worked or projects completed.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the purpose of each component of a pay stub.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Differentiate between required and voluntary deductions on a pay stub.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss ways to deal with discrepancies in calculations on a pay stub which result in an inaccurate net pay.

outcomes.statement: Analyze how transactions for goods and services occur.
