indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the differences between goods and services.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Analyze options (e.g., e-commerce, retail, private exchange, text messaging and social media) for buying and selling goods and services.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate requirements for collecting and remitting Provincial Sales Tax (PST) and Goods and Services Tax (GST) as a seller of goods and services including the responsibilities associated with conducting business on a First Nations reserve.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the advantages, disadvantages and security measures associated with various methods of payment (e.g., cash, cheque, money order, bank draft, debit card, e-transfer, credit card, virtual debit and worldwide online payments) for goods and services.

indicators.text: Investigate ways that payments are made in other areas of the world (e.g., WeChat or Alipay in China and CashU in the Middle East) and security measures (e.g., facial recognition) that are used.

indicators.text: Speculate on future methods of payment and associated technologies (e.g., CryptoCurrency, biometrics and blockchain) and the move towards cashless societies.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss potential risks associated with future methods of payment and associated technologies.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Calculate total costs for a variety of transactions, taking into consideration taxes and fees such as transaction fees, shipping and handling, GST, PST, Harmonized Sales Tax (HST), duties and brokerage fees.

outcomes.statement: Explore career options to support one’s desired lifestyle goals.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define the term, lifestyle.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Reflect on one’s current lifestyle including needs and wants.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore how various perspectives (e.g., cultural, religious and community) affect one’s lifestyle.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe one’s desired lifestyle goals for after high school.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research costs (e.g., housing, transportation, entertainment and education) associated with one’s desired lifestyle goals.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate the earning potential of several career options of personal interest.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Compare the costs of one’s desired lifestyle with the anticipated earning potential of several career options.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss ways (e.g., increase income and reduce expenses) to align the earning potential of one’s chosen career with the costs associated with one’s desired future lifestyle.

outcomes.statement: Evaluate the viability of one’s chosen career to support one’s desired future lifestyle.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Compare the earning potential of one’s chosen career to the costs associated with one’s desired future lifestyle.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss ways (e.g., increase income and reduce expenses) to align the earning potential of one’s chosen career with the costs associated with one’s desired future lifestyle.

indicators.label: c

indicators.label: d

indicators.text: Investigate advantages and disadvantages (e.g., flexibility of hours, worker benefits and sick days) associated with one’s chosen career.

indicators.label: f

indicators.text: Analyze the advantages and disadvantages associated with each type of leave.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate how one applies for a variety of leaves.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the impact of each type of leave on one’s finances.

indicators.label: e

indicators.text: Discuss the risks and rewards associated with various types of pension plans.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research approaches for investing in pension funds commonly used at different life stages (i.e., adolescence, early adulthood, middle adulthood and later adulthood).

indicators.label: d

indicators.text: Discuss the role of a Registered Retirement Savings Plan (RRSP) in contributing to one’s retirement income.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss the role of a Tax-Free Savings Account (TFSA) in retirement planning.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Explore how various perspectives (e.g., cultural, religious and community) affect one’s retirement planning.

indicators.label: m

indicators.text: Discuss the role of interest in borrowing and saving/investing.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the variables of simple and compound interest, including time, interest rate and principal.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Compare the effect of compound and simple interest on short- and long-term savings.

indicators.text: Solve contextual problems that involve simple and compound interest.

indicators.text: Perform credit calculations (e.g., monthly payments, total interest andtime to pay balance in full) using various technologies including online tools.

indicators.label: d

indicators.text: Identify the costs ofowning and operating a vehicle.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of buying versus leasing a vehicle.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Calculate the costs of buying versus leasing using lease calculation and owner’s calculation formulas.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Determine an individual’s ability to afford a vehicle using strategies or guidelines such as the 20-10 rule and total loan cost.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the consequences of relying primarily on the monthly payment amount to determine affordability of a vehicle loan.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explore finance options for vehicle loans and leasing vehicles from a variety of providers (e.g., car dealership and bank).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Compare the advantage and disadvantages of buying or leasing a new andused vehicle.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Investigate where and how (e.g., through dealerships, privately and online) vehicles might be purchased.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Discuss the role of a down payment in financing a vehicle purchase or lease.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Investigate the process of trading in a vehicle to purchase another.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Research how vehicles depreciate and ways to help a vehicle hold value.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Define the concept of negative equity and discuss situations (e.g., accident and length of ownership) that may result in negative equity on a vehicle loan.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Explore the consequences of trading in a vehicle with negative equity to purchase another, and doing so too frequently.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Research and compare insurance and warranty options for vehicles.

indicators.label: o
indicators.text: Discuss the repercussions of financing a vehicle on access to credit for future purchases.

indicators.label: p
indicators.text: Apply decision-making strategies or approaches to a variety of scenarios that include the option to purchase or lease a new or used vehicle.

indicators.label: l

outcomes.statement: Explore economic factors that impact personal or community financial decisions.

outcomes.statement: Prepare for the work placement.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent, teacher or other school staff, employer) involved in the work placement.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the business/organization to become familiar with its operations.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: In collaboration with all partners, develop personal and learning goals for the work placement.

indicators.label: d
e
indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents needed for the work placement (e.g., personal career documentation such as a resume or portfolio, permission forms, logs, self- and employer evaluation forms).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Develop a list of questions that could potentially be asked by the employer/work placement in an interview situation as well as answers to the questions.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Participate in an interview with the employer prior to beginning the work placement.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Reflect upon one’s performance during the interview.

outcomes.statement: Integrate safety practices into food preparation.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 1: Kitchen Safety (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of focusing on personal tasks while maintaining an awareness of others working in proximity.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Demonstrate safety procedures (e.g., knife safety, proper use of equipment) as they apply to food preparation.

indicators.label: c
d
indicators.text: Identify hazards and safety practices outlined in manufacturer’s operator’s manual for large and small appliances (e.g., mixers, food processors, stoves) used during food preparation.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Demonstrate safe and hygienic food and cooking preparation techniques using current and advanced technologies to produce a quality product.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Apply relevant food safety standards when preparing, cooking and serving food.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explore fire prevention and control strategies for kitchen areas.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss the principles of basic first aid (e.g., treatment of burns and scalds, bleeding, poisoning, eye injuries and choking).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Demonstrate safe work practices in the kitchen to prevent accidents (e.g., cuts, slips, falls and burns).

outcomes.statement: Explore the importance of safe food handling, preparation and storage.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 2A: Safe Food Handling (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 1

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine the importance of personal hygiene and using personal protective equipment (e.g., gloves) for food safety.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss causes of food borne illnesses.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate common symptoms (e.g., vomiting, diarrhea, cramps, bloating) of food poisoning.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain the importance of proper food storage (e.g., dried, frozen, refrigerated, food-safe containers) in safe food handling.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of safe thawing practices using various methods (i.e., cool running water, microwave, refrigerator).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research best practices (e.g., proper food storage, wearing and changing gloves, using separate equipment) involved in mitigating the risk of cross-contamination for individuals with severe food allergies.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explore aspects of food contamination such as how it occurs and how to identify spoiled food.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Determine safe food temperature zones for various foods (e.g., poultry, egg dishes, pork, beef).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Discuss the two types of contamination (i.e., direct and indirect/cross contamination).

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Analyze the conditions (e.g., temperature, time, acidity [pH], moisture, a food source, poor personal hygiene and poor sanitation) necessary for a food borne illness to survive.

indicators.label: k
l
indicators.text:
Research and compare the three categories of contamination:
- biological (e.g., bacteria or viruses);
- physical (e.g., objects that enter any stage of food preparation); and,
- chemical (e.g., cleaning products and naturally occurring).

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Demonstrate how to safely dispose of used oils.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Examine safe and responsible recycling and disposal of kitchen waste.

indicators.label: o
indicators.text: Demonstrate how to prepare recipes using proper food safe practices (e.g., frequent hand washing, avoiding food cross-contamination, washing produce, cooking to proper food temperatures).

outcomes.statement: Produce a quality food product by accurately using a recipe.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 4: Recipes (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-10 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 2A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Evaluate recipes from a variety of sources to select recipes according to set criteria.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss food preparation vocabulary and equipment used in a recipe.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify components of recipe development and modification, including ingredients and their functions, proportions, temperatures and preparation methods.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Demonstrate the ability to follow a recipe accurately (e.g., proper measuring techniques, following step by step, using equipment properly).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Distinguish between ingredients that are required in a recipe from those that are optional.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Adapt recipes for adjustments, corrections and substitutions in ingredients, equipment and methods in order to achieve similar results.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explore reasons (e.g., cost, ingredient availability, nutrition) to modify or adapt recipes.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Demonstrate correct dry and liquid measuring techniques with metric and imperial measurement units.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Convert measurements (e.g., weight versus volume, changing the yield of a recipe) accurately in food preparation tasks.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Complete recipes according to specified criteria, including timelines, to produce a quality product.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Examine the information (e.g., ingredients, quantities, cooking time) provided in a recipe.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Plan, prepare and serve food items using a recipe.

outcomes.statement: Explore the use of common kitchen tools and equipment.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify common kitchen tools and equipment.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine criteria and standards (e.g., heat conductivity, sturdy handles, heavy-gauge materials) of quality cookware and kitchen tools.

indicators.label: c
d
indicators.text: Investigate the effect of increasing and decreasing measurements in recipes.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine safe and proper use and storage of various cutting and chopping (e.g., cutting boards, scissors, peelers) tools.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explore staples (e.g., seeds, spices, oils) needed to build a well-stocked pantry.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Investigate best storage methods for various kitchen staples (e.g., herbs, flours, nuts).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop a list of must-have basic tools and supplies (e.g., dishes, bakeware, measuring utensils) for one’s kitchen.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text:
Design an efficient kitchen layout including:
- creating optimized flow for work;
- establishing zones for prep work, cooking, clean up and storage; and,
- determining utensils and small appliances to keep in each zone.

outcomes.statement: Investigate Canada’s Food Guide.

indicators.label: a
b

indicators.text: Compare food guides from other countries to Canada’s Food Guide.

indicators.label: d

indicators.label: e

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Prepare or describe how to prepare a meal based on Canada’s Food Guide.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Consider how food marketing can influence daily eating patterns as indicated in Canada’s Food Guide.

outcomes.statement: Investigate elements of meal preparation, serving and dining.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore table settings (e.g., formal, basic, casual) for various occasions.

indicators.label: c

indicators.label: d

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explore various food presentation and plating techniques (e.g., landscape, free form, alternative receptacles).

outcomes.statement: Explore the essential components of basic baked products.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Determine the role of ingredients for successful baking.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe the function of the seven major ingredients (i.e., flour, fats, sugars, eggs, liquids, leavening agents and flavouring agents) in baking.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Evaluate the four types of flour mixtures (i.e., pour batter, drop batter, soft dough, stiff dough).

indicators.label: d
e
indicators.text: Discuss different types of cookies (i.e., bar, rolled, drop, pressed, sliced or icebox and molded).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Compare the components (e.g., cost, nutrition, flavour) of homemade and convenience baked goods.

indicators.label: g

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Describe the three basic mixing methods for quick breads (i.e., blending [muffin], cutting [biscuit], creaming [cake]).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Prepare or explain how to prepare a variety of baked goods that use different types of flour.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Characterize baked goods from around the world.

outcomes.statement: Investigate ingredients and processes used to create baked goods.

indicators.label: a

indicators.label: b

indicators.label: d

indicators.label: e

indicators.label: f

indicators.label: g

outcomes.statement: Examine the importance and preparation of eggs.

indicators.label: a

indicators.label: b
c
indicators.text: Investigate egg production and processing in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Research ingredients and products made from Canadian eggs.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Inquire into the ways a hen’s diet can affect the quality (e.g., nutrition, yolk colour, taste, size, shell) of an egg.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Analyze information found on an egg carton.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explore kinds of eggs (e.g., quail, ostrich) used in cooking.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Examine factors such as salmonella and pasteurization involved in buying and storing eggs.

indicators.label: i

indicators.label: j
k
indicators.text: Investigate alternatives for eggs in recipes.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Explore the various methods of egg preparation (e.g., poaching, frying, boiling, baking).

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Compare aspects (e.g., cost per serving, time to prepare, nutritive value, taste) of convenience egg products to those of fresh eggs.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Prepare or describe the preparation of recipes that showcase eggs as an ingredient.

indicators.label: o
indicators.text: Identify key nutrients (e.g., fats, minerals and protein) of eggs and the health benefits gained by including eggs as part of a healthy eating pattern.

outcomes.statement: Examine a variety of milk products and plant-based alternative products.

indicators.text: Identify a variety of milk and plant-based (e.g., nut, seed and grain beverage) products.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore key nutrients in milk and plant-based beverage products and the health benefits gained by including milk and plant-based beverage products as part of a healthy eating pattern.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Define curdling, scald, casein, boil over, skim and scorching.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore ways to use types of milk (e.g., fresh, dried, evaporated, condensed) in food preparation.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Compare types of milk (e.g., non-fat, 2%, whole, fat reduced, buttermilk).

indicators.label: f

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Compare aspects (e.g., taste, cost, nutrition, health benefits) of milk and plant-based beverages.

indicators.label: h

indicators.label: i

indicators.text: Prepare or describe the preparation of recipes made with milk and plantbased beverages.

indicators.label: k

indicators.label: g

indicators.label: o

outcomes.printedWith: Module 80A: Work Study Preparation (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III – Occupational Health and Safety in The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019:
- the right to know – the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate – in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,
- the right to refuse – work that you believe is unusually dangerous.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent, teacher or other school staff, employer) involved in the work placement.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the business/organization to become familiar with its operations.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: In collaboration with all partners, develop personal and learning goals for the work placement.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents needed for the work placement (e.g., personal career documentation such as a resume or portfolio, permission forms, logs, self- and employer evaluation forms).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop a list of questions that could potentially be asked by the employer/work placement in an interview situation as well as answers to the questions.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Participate in an interview with the employer prior to beginning the work placement.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Reflect upon one’s performance during the interview.

indicators.text: Analyze the impact of fires on Saskatchewan forests over time (e.g., regeneration, how specific tree and plant species respond after a fire).

outcomes.statement: Investigate forest fire management.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 14B: Forest Fire Management (Optional) · Suggested Time: 7-9 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 14A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify language used within forest fire management (e.g., fire status, contained, values protection, monitored and cultural values of the landscape).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss the role of a controlled burn in forest fire management (e.g., impact on plant diseases and prevention of wildfires).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain the impact forest fires have on wildlife.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify agencies that collaborate and share resources to assist with forest fire management in Canada.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Evaluate different forest fire management strategies and factors used to prioritize fires (e.g., location of fire, communities, infrastructure, timber and industry).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe the six levels used to rank forest fires and how they impact response strategies.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Research how First Nations and Métis communities have used natural fire management in the past and present day.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explore the knowledge of Elders and Knowledge Keepers on natural forest fire management used in First Nations and Métis communities in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Reflect on forest fire management techniques (e.g., controlled burn, natural forest fire management) and how these techniques may differ based on worldviews (e.g., First Nations and Métis).

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Analyze how public perception or media portrayal of forest fire management has changed over time (e.g., Smoky the Bear campaign).

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Investigate the existence of old and very old forests in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Explain the impact of fire prevention in provincial and national parks.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Discuss how fire history maps from 1945 to the present in Saskatchewan and Canada help inform forest fire management today.

outcomes.statement: Explore methods, planning and processes of harvesting.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 15: Harvesting (Optional) · Suggested Time: 5-7 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify the components of harvesting a forest including natural forest patterns, clear cutting, shelter wood, logging, regeneration and environmental protection.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe the stages in the harvesting process (i.e., falling, delimbing, skidding, loading and hauling).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore applications of different methods of forest harvest (e.g., clear cutting, selective cutting and shelter wood cutting) and regeneration (e.g., natural, artificial and intensive).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Compare harvesting methods and the different worldviews that are reflected within them.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research the evolution of harvesting methods including techniques and equipment.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Recognize factors that influence harvesting methods such as timber characteristics and condition, growth, and utilization.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explore the impact of wildfires on the planned area for harvesting trees.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Examine environmental concerns when planning and conducting harvest.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Examine harvesting plans for pertinent information such as timber species, quality, allowed cut, volume, age, layout, cutting area, roads and landing sites.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the role of silviculture within the forestry industry.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 16: Silviculture (Optional) · Suggested Time: 10-12 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 11, 12, 13

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define silviculture and describe how it differs from forestry.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Summarize different natural and artificial silviculture techniques.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Practise growing techniques including bare-root, container seedlings or broadcasting seeds.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Conduct an experiment to determine what factors (e.g., soil pH, moisture, sunlight and carbon dioxide) impact growing conditions.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research silviculture practices such as natural regeneration, fire, thinning and rotation ages, by different companies in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify reasons for reforestation and afforestation practices used in Saskatchewan (e.g., shelterbelts, wildlife habitat protection, decreasing erosion and increasing biodiversity).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explain ecological requirements (e.g., soil and moisture) and management implications (e.g., growth rates, yield, wildlife impact, height and diameter) for a chosen tree species (e.g., spruce, aspen and pine).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss how emulating natural disturbances (e.g., wind, fire, insects and disease) is accomplished in silviculture.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Research how harvesting practices have changed over the years (e.g., move from geometric shapes of clear cuts, leaving intact islands or retention structures to maintain diversity, clear cut to maintain even aged and pure stands) because of silviculture.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into how the Indigenous worldview (i.e., humans are keepers of the land and all living creatures are connected) relates to current silviculture practices.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the impact of ecosystem-based management on forestry.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 17: Ecosystem-based Management (Optional) · Suggested Time: 10-12 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 16

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define ecosystem-based management.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Recognize factors (e.g., human impact, fire, insects, disease and climate change) considered in ecosystem-based management.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify the benefits of using ecosystem-based management on forests, the Earth, communities, businesses and economies.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Research how ecosystem-based management is used within the forestry industry (e.g., woodland caribou habitat connectivity to forestry).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain how ecosystem-based management contributes to sustainable development and biodiversity protection.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate how ecosystem-based management is used within provincial and national parks in Saskatchewan.

outcomes.statement: Explore the use of heavy equipment in the forestry industry.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 18: Heavy Equipment (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify heavy equipment (e.g., buncher, skidder, bulldozer, scraper and rolling equipment) used in various areas of the forestry industry (e.g., harvesting, reforestation, milling and pulping operations).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Compare levels of training, certification and specialized skills required to operate heavy equipment used in the forestry industry.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe safety requirements for heavy forestry equipment.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the importance and role of routine inspections and maintenance of heavy equipment in the safety of employees and life of the equipment.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate the historical evolution of heavy equipment used in the forestry industry.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Analyze the impact of heavy equipment on the forestry industry.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Research innovations in heavy forestry equipment.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry on a heavy equipment operator in the forestry industry.

outcomes.statement: Explore the use of light equipment in the forestry industry.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 19: Light Equipment (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 18

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Recognize the difference between light and heavy equipment in the forestry industry.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate the types and application of light forestry equipment (e.g., axes, hatchets, winches and water pumps).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Compare levels of training, certification and specialized skills required to operate light equipment in the forestry industry.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe safety requirements (e.g., safety boots, eye and ear protection) of various light forestry equipment.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate storage, transportation and shipping regulations for forestry light equipment.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the importance and role of maintenance and routine inspections of light equipment in the safety of employees and life of equipment.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explain how light equipment is used in the forestry industry.

outcomes.statement: Explore how mapping and remote sensing are used for forest protection and sustainability.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 20: Mapping and Remote Sensing (Optional) · Suggested Time: 8-12 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain how different types of maps (e.g., base, topographic or contour, soil type, geologic, forest stand or type and road) benefit the forestry industry.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Distinguish between mapping and remote sensing.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Analyze the importance of using current remote sensing techniques (e.g., GPS, aerial laser 3D mapping and real-time satellite imaging) in forest exploration.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain how mapping is part of the planning process in sustainably harvesting forest products.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research the benefits of Geographic Information System (GIS) mapping and how it can provide information to the forestry industry.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe how mapping can support the evaluation of forest structure and age.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Investigate how mapping can be beneficial in fire management and prevention.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Analyze how forest mapping can show the relationship between common biogeochemical cycles (i.e., carbon, water, phosphorus and nitrogen).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Describe the three main ways remote sensing and mapping can be applied to the forestry industry (i.e., reconnaissance mapping, commercial forestry and environmental monitoring).

outcomes.statement: Investigate the processes and applications of measuring a forest.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 21: Measuring a Forest (Optional) · Suggested Time: 8-10 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 3A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate the conducting of a forest survey, the type of information gathered and the purpose for collecting data.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Distinguish between forest samples and forest populations.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the goals and techniques for conducting a forestry survey.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss what technology and equipment are used to measure a forest and conduct a forestry survey.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Collect boreal forest measurements (e.g., diameter, circumference and height of trees and distribution of species) accurately and reliably.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Apply appropriate safety procedures and use of equipment when taking forest measurements.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Select appropriate and efficient ways to organize data collection (e.g., chart, table and technology) for analysis.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Analyze collected data to determine the condition and distribution of tree or wildlife species in the forest.

outcomes.statement: Investigate how forest ecosystems and climate are linked.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 22: Climate Change (Optional) · Suggested Time: 9-11 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Analyze how climate and weather influence Saskatchewan forests.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the history of forests and how glaciation and climate have shaped them to what they are today.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discover how the increase in human population and resources directly impact forests.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe how a forest can be a carbon source or a carbon sink and how that can affect climate change.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate how forests store carbon and are an important part of the carbon cycle to balance greenhouse gases in the atmosphere.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain the importance of the earth maintaining a carbon balance.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe the National Forest Carbon Monitoring, Accounting and Reporting System (NFCMARS) and its significance in providing information on climate change.

outcomes.statement: Explore the impact forestry has on the Saskatchewan economy.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 23: Forestry Economy (Optional) · Suggested Time: 7-9 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify forestry industry products (e.g., pulp and construction material) that are manufactured in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Define gross domestic product (GDP) as it relates to the forestry industry in Saskatchewan.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine the contribution of forestry on the GDP over the past 50 years.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the role of marketing in the forestry industry.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Compare the marketing of forest products over the past 50 years.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research how technology has impacted marketing, products and production practices within the forestry industry.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine how different worldviews influence marketing, production and profit sharing.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Conduct an inquiry into how First Nations forestry partnerships share profits within their communities.

outcomes.statement: Execute a project connected to the forestry industry that includes a trip into the boreal forest.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 24: Forestry Exploration (Optional) · Suggested Time: 10-15 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Plan an excursion into an area of the boreal forest in Saskatchewan, considering terrain, conditions, wildlife and habitat.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the excursion area by consulting maps, local experts, guidebooks, photographs and weather patterns.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Collect information about a topic within forestry (e.g., treaty education, reforestation, harvesting, wildlife, mapping and forest fires) as it applies to the location being visited or studied.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Complete a planned excursion to compare collected information on a topic in forestry.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Reflect on a personal experience in an area within forestry studies (e.g., harvesting, reforestation, climate change, sustainability, treaty education and land-based education).

outcomes.statement: Complete a project to compare the portrayal of the forestry industry in society with information obtained from a trip to a company, community or organization.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 25: Forestry Excursion (Optional) · Suggested Time: 10-15 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 24

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Plan an excursion with a company, First Nations community, tribal agency or government organization that is connected to the forestry industry.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the portrayal of a topic within the forestry industry that will be compared during the excursion.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Collect information about a topic within forestry (e.g., treaty education, reforestation, harvesting, wildlife, mapping, remote sensing, forest fires and conservation) as it applies to the location, community, company or government organization visited or studied.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Compare how the forestry industry was portrayed with the in-person information gathered.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Reflect on a personal experience in an area within forestry studies (e.g., treaty education, land-based education, harvesting, reforestation, climate change and sustainability).

outcomes.statement: Prepare for the work placement.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 80A: Work Study Preparation (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate, Advanced · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III - Occupational Health and Safety in The Saskatchewan Employment Act:
- the right to know - the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate - in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,
- the right to refuse - work that you believe is unusually dangerous.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent, teacher or other school staff, employer) involved in the work placement.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the business/organization to become familiar with its operations.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: In collaboration with all partners, develop personal and learning goals for the work placement.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents needed for the work placement (e.g., personal career documentation such as a resume or portfolio, permission forms, logs, self- and employer evaluation forms).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop a list of questions that could potentially be asked by the employer/work placement in an interview situation as well as answers to the questions.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Participate in an interview with the employer prior to beginning the work placement.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Reflect upon one's performance during the interview.
