outcomes.statement: Reflect and report on the work experience including but not limited to hours of work, personal relationships, employer expectations, evaluation criteria, and overall personal performance.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 23B: Work Study Follow-up (Optional) · Suggested Time: 2-4 hours · Level: Intermediate, Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 22A and B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Design and participate in an exit interview with the workplace.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Prepare and present a report on the work study experience including aspects such as:
- Expected hours of work
- Dress code
- Job description
- Employer expectations
- employer evaluation process
- Absence and late policies
- Problem solving
- Communication.

outcomes.statement: Service Learning – Explore how participation in activity-based service learning benefits self and community.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss how participating in service learning develops positive citizenship and community involvement, including relationship building to support reconciliation.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate a variety of fitness-related opportunities (e.g., coaching/officiating minor sports, helping seniors who are housebound, senior centre fitness class, Special Olympics and walking school bus) that can benefit the well-being of self and/or community.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Assess personal interests and skills to determine the most appropriate role (e.g., coach, instructor, manager, official, volunteer) in a specific activity-based service learning opportunity.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explore requirements (e.g., safe contact standards in football, concussion protocol and criminal record check) for individuals seeking a role in activity-based service learning.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Participate in activity-based service learning such as local, provincial and national cultural (e.g., pow wow, children's festival and multicultural celebrations) and sporting (e.g., rodeo, track and field and national championships) events.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Document participation in activity-based service learning.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Reflect on perceived benefits for self and community from participation in activity-based service learning.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explore careers in your community related to physical activity, health and wellness.

outcomes.statement: Health- and Skill-Related Fitness – Explore components of health- and skill-related fitness through physical activity.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Reflect on questions such as:
- How might participation in physical activity affect my lifestyle?
- What factors might influence how I pursue personal fitness goals?
- How might my physical activity interests change based on my fitness goals?
- What organizations and events exist to support my fitness?

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify how to measure components of health- (e.g., cardiovascular endurance, flexibility, muscular strength and endurance) and skill-related (e.g., agility, balance, coordination, power, reaction time and speed) fitness.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research how to use fitness appraisal tools (e.g., fitness apps, sit and reach board and stop watch) to collect data on specific components of health- and skill-related fitness.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss how to apply principles of training such as FITT (Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type), overload, progression, reversibility and specificity to improve health- and skill-related fitness.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Assess, through participation, how different training styles and approaches (e.g., cross fit, pilates, plyometrics, weight training and yoga) improve components of health- and skill-related fitness.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the drawbacks of overemphasizing specific components of fitness when engaging in physical activity.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify personal aerobic thresholds, such as maximum and target heart rates, while participating in physical activity.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Collect and analyze health -and skill-related data, using fitness appraisal tools and available equipment (e.g., free weights, medicine balls, stability balls and wobble boards), to identify personal strengths and weaknesses.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Develop a personal fitness plan with a focus on improving components of health- and skill-related fitness.

outcomes.statement: Body Management – Explore and participate in body management activities as pathways towards personal well-being.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Participate in body management activities (e.g., aquatics, dance, gymnastics, karate, pilates, weight training and yoga) to enhance personal well-being.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Analyze how fundamental movement skills transfer between different body management activities.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss physical, emotional, mental and spiritual benefits that can result from participating in body management activities.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Propose solutions to potential challenges (e.g., cultural, financial, safety, motivation and time) that might restrict an individual's participation in body management activities.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Apply knowledge of a body management activity from another culture by teaching it to peers or other members of the community.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine the physical, emotional, mental and spiritual benefits of participation in First Nations and Métis body management activities (e.g., jigging, hoop dance, pow wow and hand games).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Evaluate the influence of current societal trends (e.g., CrossFit and yoga) on individuals' participation in body management activities.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Examine the benefits of technology (e.g., apps, fitness watches and heart rate monitors) when engaging in body management activities.

outcomes.statement: Complex Skills – Demonstrate improvement in performance of complex skills.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Demonstrate complex skills within various activities and/or games in multiple environments (e.g., air, land, snow/ice and water).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate First Nations and Métis perspectives on holistically developing complex skills (e.g., throwing a ball using either hand).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify the components of a specific complex skill.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Determine, through feedback, which components of a complex skill to target in order to improve performance.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Apply principles of practice (e.g., part-whole and whole-part-whole) to improve performance of complex skills.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify how improved performance in a complex skill can influence proficiency in other complex skills.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Document progress (e.g., blog, journal, photos and video) of improved performance of one or more complex skills.

outcomes.statement: Physical Activity within Multiple Environments – Investigate how physical activity within multiple environments contributes to the well-being of self and others.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify the benefits for well-being of self and others that can result from participating in physical activities within multiple environments (e.g., air, land, snow/ice and water).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify opportunities to participate in outdoor physical activities within your community.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Participate in fitness, leisure and/or competitive activities in multiple environments.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Design and/or participate in an outdoor experience (e.g., biking, canoeing, geocaching, hiking, ice-fishing, skiing and trapping) that promotes personal well-being.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Demonstrate respect for the environment when participating in physical activities.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate, and follow when appropriate, First Nations and Métis protocols, traditional knowledge and practices when interacting with the environment.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Use technology (e.g., backpack, compass, fitness and activity apps, global positioning satellite, hiking boots, maps and satellite phone) appropriately and responsibly when participating in physical activities.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Propose potential solutions for challenges (e.g., cultural, financial and geographical location) that might limit individual's participation in physical activities.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Document and reflect on how participation in physical activities within multiple environments contributes to the well-being of self and others.

outcomes.statement: Games, Tactics and Strategies – Compare how effective tactics and strategies enhance performance and enjoyment in physically active games.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Recognize how prior knowledge of tactics and strategies can transfer to different games.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify tactics and strategies used in traditional First Nation and Métis games (e.g., double ball, knuckle hop, lacrosse, leg wrestling and snow snake).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Incorporate effective tactics and strategies in target, invasion/territorial, net/wall, striking/fielding, low organization and inventive games to enhance performance and enjoyment.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Differentiate between individual and team tactics and strategies used in individual/partner and group/team games.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Demonstrate an understanding of effective tactical and strategic decisions used in a variety of game situations while participating in individual/partner and group/team games.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Assess personal use of effective tactics and strategies incorporated in game situations.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Modify tactics and strategies to enhance participation in games for all students.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss and apply different models (e.g., teaching games for understanding, sport-model and Long-Term Athlete Development) for teaching games, tactics and strategies.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Present a game from another culture, including its tactics and strategies, to peers or members of the community.

outcomes.statement: First Nations and Métis – Examine First Nations and Métis worldviews regarding learning through physical activities.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine how First Nations and Métis ways of knowing inform people's interactions with self, others and the environment through physical activity.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss how First Nations and Métis people use story-telling to convey knowledge about learning through physical activity.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain how the benefits of physical activity (e.g., endurance, flexibility and social skills) serve a purpose to meet the demands of activities such as hunting, observation skills or learning social values.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify, and follow when appropriate, First Nations and Métis protocols, traditional knowledge and practices when engaging in physical activities.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Incorporate local, traditional First Nations and Métis ways of relating to and using the environment when participating in activities (e.g., orienteering and navigation, setting fishing nets and traps, and snowshoeing).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Participate in traditional First Nations and Métis games (e.g., snowsnake, double ball, lacrosse, leg wrestling and knuckle hop), dance (e.g., jigging, hoop and pow wow) and activities (e.g., snowshoeing and archery).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explore how skills developed in traditional games, dance and activities could be transferable to other contexts.

outcomes.statement: Nutrition – Examine how healthy nutritional choices support a physically active lifestyle.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Compare personal nutritional practices to the recommendations in Canada's Food Guide.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify how an individual's nutritional choices may be influenced by factors such as cultural eating practices, finances, advertising and marketing and/or geographical location.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Analyze personal daily caloric intake to determine if it meets energy requirements (e.g., basal metabolic rate calculation) of a physically active lifestyle.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate the limitations of calorie counting as a method of determining how much food to eat to support a physically active lifestyle.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the role of macro and micronutrients and hydration in supporting a physically active lifestyle, before, during and after activity.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine how nutrition-related illnesses (e.g., cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes) may be impacted by participation in physical activity.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine how nutritional trends (e.g., ketogenic, gluten free and high protein diets) compare with the recommendations in Canada's Food Guide.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify how a specific nutritional trend can influence personal nutrition practices.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Create or evaluate a nutrition plan that supports a physically active lifestyle considering food availability, cost, likes and dislikes.

outcomes.statement: Skeletal and Muscular Systems – Investigate the effect of physical activity on the skeletal and muscular systems of the human body.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify the major bones, joints and muscles that are affected by participation in a specific physical activity.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Demonstrate the three types (i.e., concentric, eccentric and isometric) of muscle contractions.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore the impact of the three types of muscle contractions on muscle development.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate and perform isolated and compound movements that target major muscles.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify and perform different exercises that increase the efficiency of slow and fast twitch muscle fibres.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain how various types of exercise incorporate specific joint actions (e.g., abduction, adduction, circumduction, eversion, inversion, pronation and supination).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Research common injuries (e.g., fracture, sprain and tear) to bones, joints and muscles that result from physical activity.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explore the cause and treatment of injuries (e.g., stress fracture, tendonitis and muscle strain) that result from over-use of a bone, joint and/or muscle during physical activity.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Analyze the impact of a sedentary lifestyle on skeletal and/or muscular systems in the short and long-term.

outcomes.statement: Personal Mental Health – Investigate the benefits of physical activity on mental health.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine the short- and long-term effects of physical activity on factors that can affect mental health such as anxiety, body image, depression, self-esteem and stress.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the interrelationship between physical activity, hormone levels (e.g., dopamine, cortisol, endorphin and serotonin) and physical, emotional, mental and spiritual health.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss First Nations and Métis understandings of the interrelationships between physical, emotional, mental and spiritual health.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Incorporate physical activity as a strategy to enhance personal positive mental health.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Document personal perceptions of how physical activity affects mental health over an extended period of time.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Reflect on how participation in individual (e.g., jogging, meditation and yoga) and group (e.g., cooperative games, fitness classes and team sports) activities may provide mental health benefits.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Communicate (e.g., brochure, display, oral, presentation software, video and website) research findings on community resources (e.g., Kids Help Phone and Sask Health) designed to support individuals and raise mental health awareness.

outcomes.statement: Student-Directed Study – Create and implement a plan to explore one or more topics of personal interest relevant to Physical Education 20.

indicators.label: a
b
indicators.text: Assemble and reflect on a portfolio that demonstrates understanding of a Physical Education 20 topic of interest to the student.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Share the results of student-directed study through a display, presentation, performance, demonstration, song, game, commercial, fine art representation or research paper.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Construct a tool (e.g., rubric, checklist, self-evaluation form or peer-evaluation form) to assess the process and products involved in a student-directed study.

outcomes.statement: Leadership through Service Learning – Assess, through participation, how leadership in activity-based service learning benefits self and community.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Recognize the contributions that young adults have made to their community and province through activity-based service learning.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss what is known about leadership within physical activity (e.g., what leadership means; why it is important to give back to the community and province; what it means to be a mentor or an advocate in the community/province).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Assess personal strengths and weaknesses in communication and building relationships with others.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine how First Nations and Métis ways of knowing guide the development of relationships with others and the environment through activity-based service learning.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate leadership roles in a variety of activity-based service learning opportunities in the community.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explore the requirements (e.g., safe contact in football, concussion protocol and criminal record check) for individuals seeking certification in a specific leadership role (e.g., coaching, officiating and volunteering).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Participate, in a leadership role, in activity-based service learning.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Document personal leadership in activity-based service learning.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Reflect on how participation in activity-based service learning has enhanced personal leadership skills.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Reflect on perceived benefits for self and community from leadership in activity-based service learning.

outcomes.statement: Lifelong Fitness – Explore methods and opportunities for sustaining lifelong fitness.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Reflect on questions such as:
- How might my lifestyle change after graduation?
- What factors after graduation might influence how I pursue personal fitness goals?
- How might my physical activity interests change as I age?
- What organizations and events exist to support my lifelong fitness?

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Implement various principles of training (e.g., specificity, progression and reversibility, overload and FITT: Frequency, Intensity, Time and Type) and reflect on how they address health- and skill-related components of fitness.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Demonstrate how to incorporate suitable technologies (e.g., heart rate monitor, fitness and activity tracker, pedometer and video) to enhance physical activity goals.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Recommend physical activities that maximize an individual's ability to improve aerobic thresholds (e.g., target and maximum heart rate).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify events (e.g., annual winter games, fun run, yoga in the park, cycling, Spartan race and pow wow) in the community that support lifelong fitness.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify organizations in the community (e.g., fitness facilities, recreational sport leagues and community-based leisure services) that promote lifelong fitness.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Create a plan to identify events and organizations in a community that promote lifelong fitness.

outcomes.statement: Body Management – Explore how participation in body management activities affects the wellbeing of self and community.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Participate in body management activities (e.g., dance, pilates, yoga, aquatics, karate, walking, spinning/cycling, Zumba, Tai Chi and aerobics classes) that are available in the community.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore potential use of community space (e.g., rink, golf course, community green space, parks, walking/bike path, recreation center and public/private gyms) for body management activities.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Propose body management activities that address a community need.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine the physical, emotional, mental and spiritual benefits of participation in First Nations and Métis body management activities (e.g., jigging, hoop dance, pow wow and hand games).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Demonstrate leadership through organization and participation in a chosen community-based body management activity.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Document your leadership role in a community-based body management activity.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Reflect on how participation in community-based body management activities has enhanced personal leadership skills.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Compile the participants' perceptions of the impact of a community-based body management activity on their well-being.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Discuss how self and community may benefit physically, emotionally, mentally and spiritually from participation in body management activities.

outcomes.statement: Movement in Multiple Environments – Investigate how movement in multiple environments promotes lifelong physical activity for self and others.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine the potential lifelong benefits, for self and others, from participating in physical activities within multiple environments (e.g., in the air; on the land; on snow and ice; and in and on water).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Participate in physical activities (e.g., fitness, leisure and/or competitive) in multiple environments.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Construct first aid and safety plans that support physical activity in multiple environments.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze the advantages and disadvantages of technology (e.g., global positioning satellite, adjustable dumbbells, fitness and activity tracker, exercise ball and clothing/footwear) used during physical activities.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate, and follow when appropriate, First Nations and Métis protocols, traditional knowledge and practices when engaging in experiences within the outdoor environment.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Demonstrate respect for the natural environment through stewardship.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Document and reflect on how participation in physical activities within multiple environments contributes to the lifelong well-being of self.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Research and design a group physical activity outside of the community while considering logistical and financial details (e.g., destination, budget, equipment, nutrition and transportation).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Propose potential solutions for challenges (e.g., certifications, resources and geographical location) that may limit participation in physical activities outside of the community.

outcomes.statement: Complex Skills, Tactics and Strategies – Assess, through participation, the proficiency of skills, tactics and strategies in target, invasion/territorial, net/wall, striking/fielding and low organization and inventive activities.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Compare at least two complex skills (e.g., swinging a baseball bat and swinging a golf club) that have similar transferrable, basic movement patterns, strategies and performance cues.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Demonstrate a complex skill in a specific activity and compare execution to that of a proficient performance.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: View the execution of complex skills, performed by self or others, and provide feedback to increase proficiency.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Receive and incorporate feedback to improve skill proficiency in a variety of activities.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Apply modifications to complex skills, tactics and strategies in activities and games, considering age and developmental stage, to enhance the confidence and competence of participants.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Develop strategic plans and tactics for individual and multi-player activities and games, including First Nations and Métis games and activities.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Design and implement a plan to teach skills, tactics and strategies required to participate in an individual or multi-player activities and games.

outcomes.statement: First Nations and Métis – Examine how First Nations and Métis perspectives and ways of knowing support lifelong learning through physical activity.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine how First Nations and Métis ways of knowing inform people's interactions with self, others and the environment through physical activity.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain how the benefits of physical activity (e.g., endurance, flexibility and social skills) serve a purpose to meet the demands of lifelong activity such as hunting, observation skills or learning social values.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate, and follow when appropriate, First Nations and Métis protocols, traditional knowledge and practices when engaging in physical activities.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Incorporate local, traditional First Nations and Métis ways of relating to and using the environment when leading physical activities (e.g., setting traps and fishing nets, snowshoeing, orienteering and navigation).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Plan and facilitate traditional First Nations and Métis games (e.g., snowsnake, double ball, lacrosse, leg wrestling and knuckle hop), dance (e.g., jigging, hoop and pow wow) and/or activities (e.g., snowshoeing and archery).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explore how leadership skills developed by planning and facilitating traditional games, dance and activities could be transferable to other contexts.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss the long-term physical, emotional, mental, and spiritual benefits of participation in First Nations and Métis games, dance and activities.

outcomes.statement: Nutrition – Analyze the role of nutritional choices to support participation in self-selected physical activities.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Assess how nutritional choices (e.g., vegetarianism, carbohydrate loading, intermittent fasting and high protein meal) might impact participation in a physical activity.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify how an individual's nutritional choices for a self-selected physical activity may be influenced by factors such as type of activity, cost and geographical location.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Apply a basal metabolic rate formula with an activity factor to determine the daily caloric requirements when participating in an activity.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Assess whether an individual's daily caloric intake meets the daily energy requirements for participating in an activity.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate the limitations of calorie counting as a method of determining how much food to eat to support participation in a physical activity.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe how nutrient timing (e.g., what and when to eat and drink) impacts participation and performance in an activity.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Research the positive and negative effects of supplements (e.g., protein powder, creatine, branched-chain amino acids and steroids) and nutritional products (e.g., meal replacement drink, sports drink, energy gel and protein bar) on physical performance.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Critique how current nutritional trends (e.g., ketogenic, gluten free and high protein diets) might influence nutritional choices when participating in physical activity.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Design a nutrition plan using informed nutritional choices and nutrient timing, to enhance performance in a self-selected physical activity.

outcomes.statement: Physiology and Biomechanics – Analyze physiological and biomechanical principles of movement.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Analyze the physiological benefits of short- and long-term training programs.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify, through participation, how to execute self-selected movement patterns and complex skills.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Critique, for self and others, various movement patterns and complex skills for proper biomechanical (e.g., rotation of a wrist, flexion of a joint and body position) execution.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify, through participation, the movement patterns required to execute self-selected weight training exercises (e.g., proper form for bench press) and fitness activities (e.g., proper foot plant for long distance running).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Critique, for self and others, various weight training exercises and fitness activities for proper biomechanical execution.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the potential long-term effects of using improper movement patterns in a specific activity.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Investigate the importance of rest and active recovery as part of a fitness or training plan.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss the possible short- and long-term effects (e.g., lack of muscle growth and degeneration of joints) of over-training on an individual's physiology.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Explore the importance of participating in multiple activities to support physical development.

outcomes.statement: Exercise Psychology – Investigate psychological factors that impact participation in physical activities.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate personal motivations for participating in physical activity.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the interrelationship between physical activity and physical, emotional, mental and spiritual health.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss First Nations and Métis understandings of the interrelationships between physical, emotional, mental and spiritual health.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine psychological factors (e.g., self-talk, imagery/visualization, regulation of arousal, anxiety and relaxation, motivation, goal setting and concentration) that impact enjoyment, participation and performance in physical activities.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine the role of external (e.g., audience, weather and teammate expectations) and internal (e.g., fatigue, mental toughness and making a mistake) factors on an individual's enjoyment, participation and performance in physical activity.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Incorporate a psychological factor to improve participation, enjoyment and/or performance in a self-selected physical activity.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Reflect on the effectiveness of psychological factors in supporting and maintaining participation in physical activities.

outcomes.statement: Student-Directed Study – Create and implement a plan to explore one or more topics of personal interest relevant to Physical Education 30.

indicators.label: a
b
indicators.text: Assemble and reflect on a portfolio that demonstrates understanding of a Physical Education 30 topic of interest to the student.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Share the results of student-directed study through a display, presentation, performance, demonstration, song, game, commercial, fine art representation or research paper.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Construct a tool (e.g., rubric, checklist, self-evaluation form and peer-evaluation form) to assess the process and products involved in a student-directed study.

outcomes.statement: Analyze and explore physical science related occupations in Saskatchewan, Canada and the world.
outcomes.printedWith: CP, DM

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Generate a list of occupations that require a background in physical science through research and/or participation in events such as a career fair or job shadow. (K, S)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore connection between topics in Physical Science 20 and occupations of personal interest. (S, A, STSE)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify which physical science related occupations are facing shortages and which are oversubscribed locally, regionally and/or nationally. (STSE, S, K, A)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine the roles, responsibilities, educational qualifications and personal and professional qualities common to people involved in physical-science related jobs. (S, A)

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Interview or connect with others to discuss physical science related occupations. (K, S, A)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Communicate research findings related to physical science occupations through a display, brochure, video, presentation software, website or orally. (K, S, A, STSE)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop a plan to attain your dream job in the physical science field. (S, A)

outcomes.statement: Create and carry out a plan to explore one or more topics of personal interest relevant to Physical Science 20 in depth.
outcomes.printedWith: DM, SI, TPS

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Design a scientific investigation related to a topic of study in Physical Science 20 that includes a testable question, a hypothesis, an experimental design that will test the hypothesis and detailed procedures for collecting and analyzing data. (STSE, S).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Carry out an experiment following established scientific protocols to investigate a question of interest related to one or more of the topics of Physical Science 20. (S, A, K, STSE)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Assemble and reflect on a portfolio that demonstrates an understanding of a physical science topic of interest to the student. (S, A)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Design, construct and evaluate the effectiveness of a device, model or technique that demonstrates the scientific principles underlying a concept related to Physical Science 20. (STSE, S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Debate an issued related to physical science, including developing materials to support the arguments for and against a position. (A, K, S)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Share the results of student-directed research through a display, presentation, performance, demonstration, song, game, commercial, fine art representation, video or research paper. (S)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Construct a tool (e.g., rubric, checklist, self-evaluation form or peer-evaluation form) to assess the process and products involved in a student-directed study. (S, A)

outcomes.statement: Analyze, qualitatively and quantitatively, the effect of heat on matter during temperature changes and changes of state using kinetic molecular theory.
outcomes.printedWith: CP, DM, SI

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Distinguish between heat and temperature using the kinetic molecular theory of matter. (K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore the importance of heat and fire for First Nations and Métis peoples, and how they use their understanding of heat transfer to solve practical problems related to cooking and shelter. (STSE, K, A)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss how the concept of a closed system and the law of conservation of energy underlie the study of heat and heat transfer. (STSE)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Measure the specific heat capacity of various metals using a calorimeter. (S, K)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Determine the latent heat of fusion and/or latent heat of vaporization of various substances using a calorimeter. (S, K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Measure some physical properties of water, such as density at various temperatures, specific heat capacity and latent heat of fusion and latent heat of vaporization. (S, K)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Compare, in quantitative terms, the heat capacities of some common materials, including water, and explain how heat capacity can influence choices of materials used in the development of technologies related to clothing, food and shelter. (STSE, S, K)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Construct a heating or cooling curve for water, or other substances, using personally collected data and appropriate graphing techniques or software. (S, K)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Use appropriate technologies such as temperature probes and calorimeters safely when collecting data. (S, A)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Calculate the quantity of heat ($Q = mcT$), specific heat capacity, latent heat of fusion ($Q = mH_f$) and latent heat of vaporization ($Q = mH_v$) during changes of state, using the correct number of significant figures. (S, K)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Calculate and experimentally verify the amount of heat exchanged and final temperature reached when mixing two known quantities of known substances, and suggest sources of experimental error and improvements to experimental design. (S, K, STSE, A)

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Examine traditional and contemporary applications of heat transfer such as heating a drum skin, using heat to make copper tools, energy control in buildings, heat pumps and insulated and moisture wicking clothing. (STSE, S, K)

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Explore, qualitatively and/or quantitatively, the expansion and contraction of matter during heat transfer or temperature change. (S, K)

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Investigate effects of the thermal expansion and contraction of matter in technological applications such as road, bridge and building design, plumbing, power line construction and industrial engineering. (STSE, A)

indicators.label: o
indicators.text: Discuss how the anomalous properties (e.g., density, phase and thermodynamic properties) of water, as compared with other liquids, affect the environment and Earth’s climate. (STSE, K)

outcomes.statement: Determine the quantities of heat involved in chemical reactions through experimentation and calculation.
outcomes.printedWith: SI, TPS

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Distinguish between endothermic and exothermic chemical reactions, including those that occur in solutions. (K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research the historical development of thermodynamics, including significant discoveries and inventions, and the contributions of engineers and scientists such as Carnot, Maxwell, Boltzmann, Lord Kelvin and Gibbs. (STSE)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Measure, using a thermometer or temperature probe, and record the temperature change in an exothermic and/or endothermic chemical reaction. (S, K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Calculate the theoretical quantity of heat absorbed or released in specific exothermic and/or endothermic reactions, including combustion reactions, using various quantities of reactants given the heat of reaction. (S, K)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain why the actual heat of reaction differs from the theoretical heat of reaction, with reference to sources of error and percent error calculations. (S, K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of analyzing the quantities of heat involved in chemical reactions. (STSE)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Calculate the molar heat of reaction associated with dissolving ionic compounds in a solution. (S, K)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Compare the quantity of heat involved in the use of various commercially available cold and/or heat packs. (STSE, S, K)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Design, create and evaluate the effectiveness of a cold pack and/or heat pack given the goal of having no excess reactants remaining at reaction completion. (STSE, S, K)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Compare the fuel consumed and heat energy output of various combustion reactions involving common fuels (e.g., methane, propane, octane and ethanol). (STSE, S)

outcomes.statement: Predict products of the five basic types of chemical reactions and evaluate the impact of these reactions on society and the environment.
outcomes.printedWith: DM, SI

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Observe and analyze synthesis, decomposition, combustion, single-replacement and double-replacement (including acid base neutralization) reactions. (S, K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Represent synthesis, decomposition, combustion, single- replacement and double-replacement (including acid base neutralization) reactions using atomic models, other manipulatives, skeleton equations, balanced chemical equations and International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) nomenclature. (S)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain the importance of skeleton equations, balanced equations and IUPAC nomenclature in communicating understanding of chemical reactions. (S, K, A)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Predict products of synthesis and decomposition reactions given the reactants. (S, K)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Determine the feasibility of single-replacement reactions based on the activity series of metals and/or non-metals. (S, K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Predict products of double-replacement reactions, including acid-base neutralization reactions, and precipitate formation using solubility rules. (S, K)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Distinguish between the products of complete and incomplete combustion reactions and potential consequences of the latter for living things and the environment. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Design, and carry out if practical, an investigation to demonstrate the difference between a complete and incomplete combustion reaction. (S)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Select and apply proper techniques for handling and disposing of lab materials, as outlined in Workplace Hazardous Materials Information System (WHMIS 2015) standards, and interpret Safety Data Sheets (SDSs). (K, STSE, A)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Analyze and compare the fuel consumed and carbon output of various combustion reactions (e.g., methane, propane, octane and ethanol). (STSE, S)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Describe how the outcomes of various chemical reactions may benefit or harm living organisms and affect the environment. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Research how industrial, mining and/or agricultural processes involve chemical reactions. (STSE, S, K, A)

outcomes.statement: Construct an understanding of the mole as a unit for measuring the amount of substance.
outcomes.printedWith: DM, SI

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Pose questions about how to measure quantities of substances that are not readily countable. (S)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Relate counting by weighing to the sale of a granular product such as grain or gravel, the purchase of bulk foods, rolled coin deposits at the bank and purchasing propane for a barbeque. (K)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Provide examples to demonstrate the size of the Avogadro constant ($6.02 x 10^23$) in relation to common items such as coins, water drops, sand grains and marbles. (K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain why chemists use the mole to represent the amount of a substance. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Outline how individuals such as Avogadro, Berzelius, Davy, Proust and Dalton have contributed to modern understanding of the composition of compounds. (STSE, A)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Celebrate mole day on 10/23 or 6/02 by bringing a multiple of a mole of substance to school, consuming a mole of a substance and creating and/or sharing cartoons, articles, pictures or songs relevant to the mole. (A)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Calculate the molar mass of various molecular and ionic compounds. (S)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Perform molar conversions, including mass to mole, number of particles to mole, volume to mole, concentration of a solution to mole and their inverse operations, using the correct number of significant figures. (S)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Prepare solutions of known concentration using molarity and dilution calculations. (S, K)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Research the use of solutions in industrial, mining and agricultural processes. (STSE, S, K)

outcomes.statement: Use stoichiometry to determine the relative amounts of substances consumed and produced in chemical reactions.
outcomes.printedWith: SI

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Pose questions about how to determine the amount of material required to produce a finished product. (S)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Determine the relative numbers of moles of each substance in a variety of chemical reactions using balanced chemical equations. (K, S)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Relate the use of the mole to the coefficients in a balanced chemical equation, and compare this to mass and volume as measurable quantities. (K, A, STSE)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Perform stoichiometric calculations to predict the outcomes (e.g., concentration, mass, volume, number of particles and energy transferred) of chemical reactions, using the correct units and correct number of significant figures. (S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Design and carry out experiments to support stoichiometric hypotheses using appropriate instruments to collect data accurately and precisely. (S, A)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Communicate results of experiments using narrative and formal lab reports. (S, A)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Determine the limiting and excess reagents in a variety of chemical reactions through stoichiometric calculations and experimentation. (S, K)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Compare the theoretical and actual yield for a variety of chemical reactions by calculating the percent yield. (S, K)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Explain how actual yield differs from theoretical yield using the concept of sources of error. (STSE, S)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Predict how to maximize the yield of a particular chemical process. (STSE, S)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Discuss the economic impact of the yield of chemical reactions with respect to maximizing product and profit and minimizing waste production. (STSE, A)

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Research how the reactants used and products formed through chemical reactions in industrial, mining and/or agricultural processes can affect human health and/or the health of the environment. (STSE, A)

outcomes.statement: Investigate the properties and characteristics of one-, two- and three- dimensional waves in at least three different media (e.g., springs, ropes, air and water).
outcomes.printedWith: SI

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Pose questions about the nature and prevalence of waves in the world around us (e.g., What are waves? Where do we find waves in the world around us? Do all waves exhibit the same properties and behaviours? Why are waves important to study?). (S, STSE, A)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine First Nations and Metis perspectives on waves, including waves as carriers of energy. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Recognize that scientists understand waves as the transmission of energy originating from a vibrating source that determines the frequency and amplitude of the wave. (K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Communicate information about the properties and characteristics of waves using appropriate terminology, including medium, pulse, vibration, cycle, periodic motion, frequency, period, amplitude, phase and wavelength. (S, K)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Rephrase questions about waves (e.g., What controls the frequency of a wave? What controls the speed of a wave? What happens when two or more waves meet?) into experimentally testable formats. (S, A)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify characteristics of transverse and longitudinal waves including crests (positive pulse), troughs (negative pulse), compressions, rarefactions and the relationship between direction of vibration and energy transfer. (K)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe the characteristics of the transmission of waves, including rectilinear propagation and the nature of the medium and its relationship to the speed of the wave. (S, K)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Trace the historical developments of technologies used to measure the speed of light and/or sound. (STSE)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Solve problems related to speed, period, frequency and wavelength using the universal wave equation ($v = λf$), the period-frequency relationship ($T = 1/f$) and the correct number of significant figures. (S, K)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Illustrate constructive and destructive interference in one-, two- and three- dimensional waves, including the principle of superposition and standing waves, using point-source and straight-source waves. (S, K)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Observe and describe diffraction of waves through single and double slits and diffraction gratings. (S, K)

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Provide examples of applications of the properties and characteristics of waves or electromagnetic radiation in various technologies (e.g., ultrasound, sonar, Doppler Effect, sonic booms, satellite dishes, microwaves, mobile phones, wireless routers, Bluetooth, radio waves, X-rays, radar and remote controls). (STSE, K)

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Explore wave-related phenomena such as natural vibrations, forced vibrations, resonance and harmonics in the context of musical instruments and human hearing. (STSE, S, K)

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Examine data or experimental results that provide evidence for the scientific theory of wave-particle duality of light. (STSE, S)

outcomes.statement: Examine, using physical materials, ray diagrams and mathematical equations, how waves reflect from a variety of barriers.
outcomes.printedWith: CP, DM, SI

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate the behavior of waves as they strike parallel, oblique, and curved barriers. (S, K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Compare the characteristics of specular (regular) and diffuse reflection of waves. (S, K)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Demonstrate the application of the law of reflection when a wave strikes a straight barrier and when a wave encounters the boundary between two different media. (S, K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Provide examples of wave and particle reflection in everyday situations such as echoes, reverberation, room acoustics, radar, sonar, parabolic microphones, ultrasound, water waves, satellite dishes, billiard balls and ball-based sports. (STSE, K, A)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate image formation in plane, concave and convex mirrors, including constructing ray diagrams. (S, K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify the properties, including type (real or virtual), attitude/orientation (upright or inverted), magnification (smaller, larger or same size) and position (relative to the mirror surface or vertex), of images formed in plane, concave and convex mirrors. (K)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Apply the laws of reflection, the magnification equation ($M = h_i/h_o = -d_i/d_o$) and the curved mirror equation ($1/f = 1/d_o + 1/d_i$) to solve problems related to the reflection of waves. (S, K)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Describe the implications of wave-based technologies in furthering scientific understanding of phenomena such as Earth’s internal structure, the topography of the ocean floor and the rock cycle. (STSE, K)

outcomes.statement: Analyze, using physical materials, ray diagrams and mathematical equations, how waves refract at boundaries between different media.
outcomes.printedWith: DM, SI

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Pose scientific questions about how waves behave when they travel from one medium to another. (S)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine the behavior of waves, including partial reflection and refraction, the critical angle and total internal reflection, at a boundary between different media. (S, K)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Relate refraction, and the refractive index of a medium, to the change in the speed and direction of waves at a boundary between different media. (S, K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate image formation in converging and diverging lenses, including constructing ray diagrams. (S, K)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify the properties, including type (real or virtual), attitude/orientation (upright or inverted), magnification (smaller, larger, or same size) and position (relative to the optical center) of images formed in converging and diverging lenses. (K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Apply Snell's Law ($n_1\sinθ_1= n_2\sinθ_2$), the magnification equation ($M = h_i/h_o = -d_i/d_o$) and the lens equation ($1/f = 1/d_o + 1/d_i$) to solve problems related to the refraction of waves. (S, K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore applications related to fiber optics, lenses and human vision including polarization, the lens makers equation and total internal reflection. (STSE, S, K)

notes: Indicator label (b) printed more than once on the official page.

courses.name: Physics 20, 30
courses.problem: No outcomes are published on the site for this curriculum.

outcomes.statement: Create and carry out a plan to explore one or more topics of personal interest relevant to Physics 30 in depth.
outcomes.printedWith: DM, SI TPS

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Design a scientific investigation related to a topic of study in Physics 30 that includes a testable question, a hypothesis, an experimental design that will test the hypothesis and detailed procedures for collecting and analyzing data. (STSE, S)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Carry out an experiment following established scientific protocols to investigate a question of interest related to one or more of the topics of Physics 30. (S, A, K, STSE)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Assemble and reflect on a portfolio that demonstrates an understanding of a topic of interest related to physics. (S, A)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Design, construct and evaluate the effectiveness of a device, model or technique that demonstrates the scientific principles underlying concept related to a Physics 30 topic. (STSE, S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Debate an issue related to physics, including developing materials to support the arguments for and arguments against a position. (A, K, S)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Share the results of student-directed research through a display, presentation, performance, demonstration, song, game, commercial, fine art representation, video or research paper. (S)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Construct a tool (e.g., rubric, checklist, self-evaluation form or peer-evaluation form) to assess the process and products involved in a student-directed study. (S, A)

outcomes.statement: Analyze the importance of relativistic principles and quantum mechanics in our world.
outcomes.printedWith: SI, DM

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research the development of quantum mechanics and relativity, including perspectives of key scientists such as Albert Einstein, Maxwell Planck, Erwin Schrödinger, Werner Heisenberg, Thomas Young and Stephen Hawking. (STSE)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Differentiate how Newtonian mechanics, quantum mechanics, relativity and emerging theories describe the universe on different scales. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Distinguish between the theories of general and special relativity with respect to space and time (e.g., curvature of space-time, time dilation, length contraction and relativistic mass). (K, STSE)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Consider the implications of inconsistent time with respect to a frame of reference (e.g., time travel and the twin paradox). (S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore the impact of scientific understanding of relativity on the development of technologies such as the Global Positioning System, atomic clocks and communication systems. (K, S, STSE)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain the importance of phenomena such as the photoelectric effect, Young's double slit experiment, black body radiation and Compton scattering to understanding the quantum nature of light. (S, K)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss the implications of conducting observations while investigating wave-particle phenomena and objects at a quantum-scale. (K)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Determine Planck's constant experimentally or using simulations and discuss its implications for quantum mechanics. (S, K)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Explore the photoelectric effect including the influence of various frequencies and energies of electromagnetic radiation. (S, K)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Discuss the ongoing debates within physics regarding contradictory and differentiated interpretations (e.g., Collapse, Pilot Wave, Many Worlds and Copenhagen) of quantum mechanics. (STSE)

outcomes.statement: Assess the effects of radioactivity and applications of nuclear technology on society and the environment.
outcomes.printedWith: CP, DM, SI

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research the contributions of women (e.g., Harriet Brooks, Marie Curie, Lise Meitner, Chien-Shiung Wu, Mileva Maric and Ida Noddack) from various cultures to the development of scientific understanding of radioactivity. (STSE)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify natural and artificial sources of radiation on Earth and throughout the universe. (K)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Compare the characteristics (e.g., composition, penetrating power, speed and potential danger) of alpha, beta and gamma radiation. (K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Represent nuclear reactions involving alpha, beta and gamma decay using words, diagrams and equations. (S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain that some isotopes undergo natural radioactive decay, and that half-life is a measure of the rate of radioactive decay. (K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Assess the short- and long-term implications of radiation on living things, including the effects on different types of tissues and cells. (A, K, STSE)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss how the difficulties in detecting effects of radiation on living things lead to lack of agreement among scientists and others about those effects. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Describe the characteristics of the weak nuclear force and its role in beta decay. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Model the process of nuclear fission, including conditions necessary for a chain reaction. (K, S)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Compare the amount and rate of energy released in various man-made fission reactions (e.g., nuclear energy production, nuclear weapons, nuclear propulsion and satellites). (K)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Examine the process of nuclear fusion and the difficulties in harnessing nuclear fusion as an energy source. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Explain the characteristics of the strong nuclear force and its role in maintaining atomic stability. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of mass defect and $e=mc^2$ and why this particular equation has gained such prominence in society. (STSE, A)

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Analyze societal and environmental impacts of applications of nuclear technologies such as medical isotopes, food irradiation, smoke detectors, industrial radiography, pesticide tracers, nuclear weapons, nuclear reactors and nuclear waste disposal. (A, STSE)

outcomes.statement: Analyze motion in one- and two-dimensions, including uniform motion, uniformly accelerated motion, circular motion and projectile motion.
outcomes.printedWith: SI

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Provide examples of situations in which everyday objects undergo uniform motion, uniformly accelerated motion, circular motion and projectile motion. (STSE)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Critique examples of realistic and non-realistic motion in popular culture such as movies, TV shows and comics. (STSE)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Solve problems involving different types of motion in one- and two-dimensions, including relative motion, using graphical methods, vector analysis and kinematics equations. E.g. $v ↖ {→} = {\Δd}/t$, $v ↖ {→}_f = v ↖ {→}_i+a ↖ {→}\Δt$, $v ↖ {→2}_f = v ↖ {→2}_i+2a ↖ {→}\Δd ↖ {→}$, $\Δd ↖ {→} = v ↖ {→}_i \Δt + 1/2a ↖ {→} \Δt^2$, and $\Δd ↖ {→} = 1/2(v ↖ {→}_i+v ↖ {→}_f)\Δt$. (S)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Experimentally determine the value of the acceleration due to gravity near Earth's surface. (K, S)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Analyze the horizontal and vertical components of a projectile's motion using tools such as video analysis and/or online simulations. (K, S)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Solve problems involving projectile motion and objects in free fall using graphical (e.g., scale diagrams) and/or mathematical (e.g., vector components, sine law and cosine law) methods. (S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Design and perform an experiment that includes collecting, analyzing and interpreting data from objects that undergo projectile motion or uniform circular motion. (STSE)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Determine the characteristics (e.g., speed, velocity, period, distance travelled and acceleration) of uniform circular motion. (K, S)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe the orbits (e.g., geosynchronous, elliptical and/or circular) of satellites and celestial bodies using uniform circular motion concepts. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Predict the path an object (e.g., shot put, discus, hammer throw, bolo, particles in a synchrotron and rocket undergoing gravity assisted space travel) will follow once released from uniform circular motion. (K, S, STSE)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Discuss the challenges in representing real world motion using models of ideal motion, which normally treat objects as a single center of mass and which disregard frictional forces. (STSE)

notes: Indicator labels (b), (c) printed more than once on the official page.

outcomes.statement: Analyze the effects of forces on objects undergoing uniform motion, uniformly accelerated motion and circular motion.
outcomes.printedWith: SI

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Pose questions related to practical examples of the effects of forces on objects. (STSE)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Provide examples of how Newton's three laws of motion can describe the movement of objects in the real world. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of the concepts of inertia and inertial mass with respect to the development of Newton's laws of motion. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate the effect of changing the mass of an object and/or force applied to an object on the acceleration of that object. (STSE, S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Solve problems involving force, mass and acceleration, using free-body diagrams and Newton's second law of motion $F = ma ↖ {→}$. (K, S)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe the effect of friction and air resistance, including terminal velocity, on objects in motion (e.g., rollercoasters, skydiving, snowboards, meteors entering Earth's atmosphere, inclined plane situations, rolling balls, spacecraft and satellite re-entry, aircraft, race cars and artillery). (K, STSE)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Predict and investigate the effect of balanced or unbalanced forces, including the effect of friction, on an object that is at rest, undergoing uniform motion or undergoing uniformly accelerated motion. (K, S)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Solve problems involving forces acting in one- and two-dimensions using graphical (e.g., scale diagrams) and mathematical (e.g., vector components, sine law and cosine law) methods. (K, S)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Explore the limitations of Newton's laws of motion in relativistic and quantum situations (e.g., objects moving at or near the speed of light and subatomic particles). (K, STSE)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Examine the vertical and horizontal forces involved in various types of circular motion (e.g., roller coaster, Ferris wheel, merry-go-round and figure skater) with reference to the concepts of centripetal and centrifugal. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Examine the horizontal and vertical forces that act on a projectile throughout its trajectory. (K)

outcomes.statement: Investigate the nature of mechanical energy and efficiency in mechanical systems in relation to the law of conservation of energy.
outcomes.printedWith: SI

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Recognize work as the transfer of energy that takes place when a force acts over a displacement. (K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify the conditions required for positive, negative and zero mechanical work and their relation to the angle between the applied force and displacement. (K)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss how common usage of the terms work, energy and power differ from their operational definitions in physics. (K)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify the properties (e.g., boundaries, inputs and outputs) of a system with respect to total mechanical energy. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explain the law of conservation of energy in terms of isolated and non-isolated systems and conservation of mechanical energy. (STSE, K)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Solve problems related to kinetic, potential and total mechanical energy using relevant equations. E.g. $W=Fd \cosθ$,$W=\ΔE$,$E_k={mv ↖ {→2}}/2$,$E_p=mg ↖ {→}h$, and $TME=E_k+E_p$. (K, S)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Design and perform experiments and/or simulations, including collecting, analyzing and interpreting data, to determine the kinetic energy involved in elastic and inelastic interactions (e.g., curling stones, billiard balls, bouncing ball, seatbelts and automobile collisions). (STSE, S)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss the challenges in modeling conservation of energy in real-life situations. (STSE)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate the efficiency of energy transformations in various technologies with reference to useful work, friction and the production heat, sound and light. (K, STSE)

notes: Indicator labels (b), (c), (d) printed more than once on the official page.

outcomes.statement: Analyze the motion of objects and interactions between objects using momentum concepts, including the law of conservation of momentum.
outcomes.printedWith: SI

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore how impulse and momentum concepts apply to motion-related technologies in fields such as sports science, transportation and space science. (STSE)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Derive the formula for impulse from Newton's second law of motion. (S)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate how changing the net force applied to an object or the amount of time the force is applied affect the momentum of an object, with reference to the formula $F\Δt=m\Δv ↖ {→}$. (S)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Provide examples that show how momentum is or is not conserved in everyday situations. (K)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Conduct an experiment or simulation, including collecting, analyzing and interpreting data, to determine the extent to which momentum is conserved in elastic and inelastic collisions. (STSE, S)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Solve problems using the law of conservation of momentum in one- and two-dimensional interactions (e.g., head-on collisions, glancing collisions, rocket launches and explosions). (K, S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze applications (e.g., neutrino detection, Large Hadron Collider, crash test dummies and personal safety devices) of the law of conservation of momentum. (STSE)

notes: Indicator labels (b), (c) printed more than once on the official page.

outcomes.statement: Investigate gravitational fields and their interactions with matter.
outcomes.printedWith: SI, DM

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the value of the concept of fields and field theory and the meaning of field strength in understanding the effects of non-contact forces (i.e., action at a distance). (STSE)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe the characteristics of the gravitational force and its effect on large-scale phenomena throughout the universe. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore phenomena such as gravitational lensing, dark matter, universal expansion and contraction and time dilation as they relate to gravitational fields within the universe. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Relate gravitational field strength near Earth's surface, and variations in that field strength, to the accepted value of acceleration due to gravity near Earth's surface. (K, S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Distinguish, qualitatively and quantitatively, between weight and mass. (K, S)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain variations in gravitational field strength as a function of inverse-square dependence. (K)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Discuss the relation between common misconceptions about perceptions of weightlessness in microgravity environments and people's understanding of gravitational field strength. (A, STSE)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Research how scientists use an understanding of microgravity environments to further scientific understanding in fields such as biotechnology, fluid physics, materials science, combustion science and fundamental physics. (STSE, A)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Solve problems involving gravitational field strength using $g={Gm}/r^2$ and Newton's law of universal gravitation $F=G{m_1m_2}/r_^2$. (K, S)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Explore the nature of scientific collaboration and contribution in researching questions related to emerging topics such as gravitational waves and the graviton. (STSE, S)

outcomes.statement: Investigate electric and magnetic fields and their interactions with matter.
outcomes.printedWith: SI, TPS

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Recognize that electric fields act on point charges, including action at a distance and following the inverse-square law to determine strength of field. (S, K)

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Draw and describe electric field lines for like and unlike point charges and plates separated by a distance. (K, S)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine how the electric field strength at a point varies according to the inverse square of the distance between two charges, with reference to the equation $E={kQ}/d^2$. (K, S)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Solve problems related to Coulomb's law $F = k{q_1q_2}/d^2$, including electrostatic equilibrium in one- and two-dimensions. (K, S)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe current scientific thinking regarding the electromagnetic force, one of the four fundamental interactions. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Recognize how our understanding of the interrelationships between magnetic and electric fields has led to the development of technologies such as generators and electromagnets (e.g., moving charged particles create a magnetic field, interaction of electric and magnetic fields). (K, STSE)

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Represent magnetic fields using magnetic field lines. (K, S)

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Represent the direction of the magnetic field around current-induced conductors, including linear wires and wire coils, using the right hand and/or left-hand rules. (K, S)

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Research the characteristics of Earth's magnetic field, including the effects of short- and long-term changes to the field. (STSE, K, A)

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Analyze the direction of positive, negative and neutral charges moving in natural (e.g., solar flares and aurorae) and man-made (e.g., particle accelerators and MRI's) magnetic fields. (K, STSE)

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Design, construct and evaluate a prototype of a technology (e.g., electric motor, generator or electromagnet) to demonstrate principles of electromagnetism. (K, S)

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Analyze ways in which natural and technological sources of electric and magnetic fields can influence society and the environment (e.g., changes in animal migration, health concerns and increased communication). (K, STSE, A)
