outcomes.statement: Conduct an in-depth inquiry investigating a consistent theme or idea within a body of work demonstrating insight into ways that artists create in order to learn.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Set inquiry goals and parameters with teacher guidance that foster strengths and allow the investigation to shift or extend.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Initiate research by using art strategies, such as thumbnail sketches, annotated or illustrated text and maquettes, to explore, reveal and develop the inquiry.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Establish and apply safe studio practices that respect the health and well-being of everyone sharing the space.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Pursue varied responses to the inquiry, including storytelling through art, to demonstrate artistic competencies with concept, composition, execution and analysis.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Extend the investigation through independent study that explores related and/or unexpected questions inspired by other disciplines.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Reflect regularly on own portfolio and continue personal practice to develop artistic competencies, including pushing the boundaries of selected media.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Critique work for a focused, emotive message, skillful use of select media and varied visual arrangements relating to a strong underlying visual idea.

outcomes.statement: Invent and adapt style variations in new works influenced by selected artists.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate a wide range of artworks, including those from other disciplines, for the maker’s influences and present findings about artistic integrity for class discussion.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss artworks, along with possible controversy, that make use of appropriated imagery in the service of the artist’s intent.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine emerging trends, alternative media and current technologies in art and reflect on how information from the past and present may be integrated in own exploration of recurring themes.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Evaluate and apply methods to establish authenticity and avoid imitation such as making use of own photographs as source material, rendering imagery directly from life and using symbols or visual words to convey personal meaning.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss legal and ethical issues associated with art making and marketing (e.g., authorship, copyright, ownership, censorship, appropriation, use of responsible practices, respecting cultural/religious symbols or iconography).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research plagiarism policies of universities, colleges, art schools and art programs.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Consult Indigenous Knowledge Keepers and artists to understand and develop respect for sacred imagery and practices of gifting learning.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Play with styles and approaches, while building skills and investigating own ideas.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Evaluate own portfolio for possible copyright infringement or the unethical use of the work of others, including using another medium to copy work, and refine or alter works as needed.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Explain how portfolio pieces show own ideas and evidence of significant development in work inspired by the creative property of other artists maintaining reference citations or visual bibliography.

outcomes.statement: Regularly document and develop own creative process (e.g., inspiration, research, sketches, production, media skills, evaluation, refinement) up to and including completed works.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe stages of own creative process and compare them to those used by practicing artists from a variety of fields.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Compile and photograph own creative products including methods for initiating new work through practice and research.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe and record own distinctive way of approaching a creative task to develop understanding of strengths and weaknesses of that approach.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Maintain a sketchbook or art journal containing initial sketches and drafts, research and reference work demonstrating persistence in skill development.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text:
Explore and experiment with additional methods to foster a broader creative process, including for example:
- flexibility with new media and technologies
- fluency in observational work including life drawing
- on-site art making during experiential field trips
- responses to visual culture and personal environment.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Compose own library of inspirational references, notations, artifacts, own photographs, media exploration, visual notes and other source materials inspired by surroundings, other artists and other disciplines.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Research and co-create criteria for the selection, storage and display of portfolio items (e.g., documentation in digital and other formats of one’s creative process and products, depth and breadth of ideas, media and techniques represented).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text:
Track own progress (e.g., new ideas, skills) and regularly record the development of work up to completion through well-composed photographs, including for example:
- selecting and photographing completed works for submission to external agency or post-secondary institution meeting their criteria for submission
- optimizing images for print, digital sharing, and/or display.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Evaluate effectiveness of creative process in developing works that demonstrate active risk-taking and thoughtful revision.

outcomes.statement: Produce works that purposefully and creatively manipulate compositional and design strategies to express a point of view or communicate an idea.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research varied methods of visual organization and stylistic approaches and their cultural influences including those used by Indigenous artists.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Engage in a series of quick skill-building challenges to explore the effects of focusing on selected elements of art, principles of design and/or image development strategies.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Use one or more of these preliminary works as starting points for a more extensive piece.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Play with visual organization beyond implied boundaries of compositional rules (e.g., rule of thirds, rule of odds, rule of space, orientation, vantage point, geometry, focal point, rest areas) through directed studio practices.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Build a collection of work demonstrating increasing technical skill and consistent trial and error in manipulating the elements of art, principles of design and image development strategies.

outcomes.statement: Prepare and present own work in a professional manner to share ideas with wider audience.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Research the range of ways artists can promote and present their work for different audiences and different purposes.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research exhibition opportunities for students initiated by local, global or online communities (e.g., performance piece, community project/show, website, social media, art competitions, etc.).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Co-construct and rank criteria for exhibition, including health and safety considerations, and apply to overall design within selected space.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Select works to exhibit that highlight own strengths.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Design exhibitions utilizing multimedia, lighting, sound, video and/or digital spaces.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Consider inclusive curatorial practices including purpose of show, selection process, exhibition space, matting work, producing advertising and show cards, when viewing a collection of art in a gallery or other exhibition space.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Articulate intentions of works and choices for overall show through exhibition text and curatorial rationale.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Document process and reflect on the impact of sharing work on self and the community.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Predict the future of visual art exhibitions considering factors such as diversity, inclusion and technological developments.

outcomes.statement: Examine and critically respond, orally and in writing, to the work of professional artists utilizing a range of art criticism models.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: View and evaluate professional art, including Indigenous art, by interacting with guest artists and by visiting galleries.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe initial reactions and responses and determine what the artist did to initiate that reaction in the viewer.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Compare and contrast selected artworks through analysis of formal concerns, societal perspectives and artist intentions.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Use a critical process to convey an informed opinion within a formal critique/research paper including properly cited sources.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Use the language of art and appropriate terminology when writing or discussing artworks.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify how design principles, image development strategies and elements and principles of design affect the overall impact of works selected for study.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Describe the visual language and conventions of the time period in which work was created.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Analyze connections between self and selected art works.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Inquire how different people respond to the same work in different ways and how that reflects life experiences, cultural context and world view.

outcomes.statement: Evaluate, for the purpose of improvement, own works in progress and completed works during regular critiques with peers.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Set norms for respectful understanding of diverse cultures and personal histories prior to beginning analytical discussion of student works.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Evaluate artwork against co-constructed criteria using art terminology.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe own decision making and problem-solving processes and reflect on the effectiveness of choices made.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Demonstrate an understanding of the complexity of communicating through art.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Use descriptive and constructive feedback making suggestions for improvements or extensions.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Determine which aspects of the work are most important to alter or revise and what makes an artwork most successful.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Suggest solutions to artistic problems and set goals during regular progress checks.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Articulate and assess own role in the creative process leading to the work under review.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Conduct a critical inquiry into own practice by reviewing creative process and portfolio development and share learning with peers.

outcomes.statement: Assess how knowledge is produced and shared in various ways through a range of art forms including those produced by First Nations and Métis artists.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine and interpret the work of First Nations and Métis artists to learn how knowledge is shared and culture is sustained across generations.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Differentiate between knowledge that is spiritual or sacred and knowledge that is secular and how these are represented in art (e.g., architecture, painting, craft).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe the significance of specific art works in shaping content or challenging assumptions in history, society or culture.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Research an artist whose work is personally meaningful and reflects aesthetic, cultural, historical or spiritual knowledge.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Describe how visual culture and personal history contribute to own practice and knowledge formation.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explore the interconnected relationship between the artist, the art and the viewer.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Make interdisciplinary links between art, science, technology, design and mathematics.

outcomes.statement: Research and discuss the business of art including supports offered by arts organizations.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Deepen understanding of gallery culture and community by visiting galleries and arts organizations and presenting career information to peers.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research artist associations and supporters of the arts (e.g., Sask Arts, SaskCulture, Canadian Artists’ Representation/Le front des artistes canadiens, Organization of Saskatchewan Arts Council, Canada Council), artists’ guilds, artist-run centres and arts education organizations (e.g., Canadian Society for Education through Art, National Art Education Association).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the mandate of a gallery and investigate the roles of gallery personnel (e.g., curators, educators, conservators, director, communications office).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Co-construct health and safety procedures for using shared studio spaces.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Make community connections by meeting with local artists and/or business people to explore mentorship possibilities.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Document and present learning and outline plans for continuing connections as a practicing artist.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Reflect on experiences that will inform engagement and set the foundation for life-long learning in the arts.

outcomes.statement: Research, plan, produce, analyze and resolve a series of works exploring, through independent inquiry, big ideas of personal significance.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Brainstorm big ideas for sustained investigation drawing on experiences, interests, visual culture and/or contemporary issues.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Generate inquiry questions to guide own investigations.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Plan and create works demonstrating personal artistic voice from direct observation, dreams, fantasies, inspirations, combinations of found references and own photographic compositions and designs.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Strive for increasingly sophisticated and/or sensitive works that build on existing strengths while challenging current level of technical proficiency.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Connect with artists, including Indigenous, to learn how they speculate, hypothesize, research, test, discover and experiment throughout their career.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Articulate a clear planning, research, production and reflection process to develop a portfolio of work shaped through inquiry and the possibility of real-world applications.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Exercise creative voice and critical decision making to convey an informed perspective and real-world application of selected inquiry.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Evaluate and critique own art works, with input from peers and teacher, at various stages for technical success and relationship to selected inquiry.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Research interdisciplinary connections along with cultural and historical examples, including Indigenous, that expand on selected investigation to determine how other disciplines or cultures might respond to same inquiry.

outcomes.statement: Create original works inspired by artists of personal interest while maintaining own intentions and artistic vision.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine works of various personal, social, cultural and historical contexts recording inspirational aspects, visually or in writing, and define intentions for responding artistically to this work.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Experiment with mashups, collages or mixed media works that demonstrate appropriately placing own work ‘in conversation’ with another artist or style.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Evaluate own portfolio for instances of copying and revise derivative works by interpreting, stylizing, layering or abstracting to communicate own ideas in new ways.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Alter significantly several aspects of own work when referencing photographic, illustrative or other work that belongs to another artist using methods such as:
- improvising a mashup of three works while exploring an idea of personal significance
- referring to an inspiration file and sketchbook to alter and combine ideas in new ways.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research legal and ethical concerns in the context of intellectual, virtual and physical property influencing own work particularly when similarities to the work of others is intended.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the concepts of ethics, authenticity and originality along with community norms and values related to art production and marketing, including online, in the context of contemporary art practices.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Provide rationale for historical, cultural and stylistic references in own work and describe how personal experiences, interests and intentions are depicted in portfolio.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Research plagiarism policies of universities, colleges, art schools and art programs.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Create through multiple lenses, design strategies and perspectives to apply new ways of communicating own views.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Respond knowledgeably and sensitively to the work of others with inventive interpretations to merge and mold to own style and message.

outcomes.statement: Refine and document full range of own creative process (e.g., idea generation, sketches, drafts, maquettes, reference work, source material, research, production, media exploration, critique, refinement) including completed works, providing evidence of critical inquiry.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Connect with artists who create work for a variety of purposes to inquire about creative process.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Critically analyze and compare own creative process to methods used by practicing artists in order to incorporate relevant aspects to own practice.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe and experiment with the fluid, cyclical nature of the creative process.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Actively record own practice, experimentation and revision of works up to and including final versions demonstrating, for example:
- preliminary rough drafts, written reflections, artist study
- reasoning and motivations during process
- risk-taking with mixed media, layering and current techniques for creating visual interest and nuanced meaning
- critical responses to contemporary conceptual approaches in art making
- analysis of strengths and weaknesses of own creative process
- how feedback has been applied to elevate works included in presentation portfolio
- documentation of selected aspects of own process through photographs.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Demonstrate evidence of regular exploration and independent thinking through ongoing studio work.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Evaluate current portfolio and/or sketchbook to assess strengths that can be built on and incorporated into future works.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Prepare for portfolio submission by creating high quality, well composed, high resolution photographs of completed works.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Edit, during post-production, digital images of own work to aid in presenting the clearest, most accurate representation of the work and ensure that images meet the requirements of selected digital submission web application.

outcomes.statement: Cultivate proficiency in manipulating visual, stylistic and conceptual conventions to solve a range of challenging art making investigations.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Use compositional and design strategies in a variety of ways to convey meaning and create visual interest.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Accentuate personal style and voice when applying image development strategies.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Take risks with elements of art, principles of design, and composition/design rules to work beyond the confines of those theories and increase visual impact.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Use synectics as a tool to develop creative thinking strategies.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Evaluate and make revisions to existing works to employ innovative or imaginative visual arrangements.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Demonstrate a unique, personal voice while extending art works beyond common artistic clichés or exercises.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Apply critical and creative thinking to define ways to work within and push the boundaries of artistic conventions.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Research the philosophy of aesthetics and assess own work for the application of these principles.

outcomes.statement: Prepare and curate an exhibition of own work in a professional and collaborative manner.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Collaboratively research the changing role of the curator in diverse and inclusive institutions and communities.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss how contemporary curatorial work has evolved to include historically-excluded worldviews such as Indigenous, feminist and minorities.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe a range of methods of, and purposes for, presenting art to the public.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: View various visual art exhibits in locations such as galleries, land-based environments, pop-ups and community centres, to analyze and discuss how the curated show tells a story.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Consider how the public is involved in the exhibition and ways that artists engage viewers to reflect and respond to work.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify the elements of a marketing strategy that are likely to generate interest in a student art exhibition.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Engage in critical decision making to select and prepare own works for public display.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Plan and develop one or more projects that showcase artwork with the local, school or online community.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Identify and apply gallery conventions of mounting an exhibition such as signing works, matting works, framing works, selecting lighting, designing invitations and catalogues, writing an artist statement, handling and display of art pieces, use of signage, traffic flow patterns, promotion, disassembly and follow-up.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Document exhibition with camera and ensure that digital images accurately represent the original works on display and format of the overall design of show.

outcomes.statement: Utilize creative and systematic investigations to critically analyze, interpret and respond to professional art, orally and in writing, across formats, styles, cultures and time periods.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Compare/contrast the function and social impact of selected works that explore similar topics.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Utilize recognized critical analysis processes in addition to informal and personal approaches to examine how art reflects on and contributes to culture and society.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate how perspectives of diverse cultural groups, including Black, First Nations, Métis, and people of colour, are represented in their art forms.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Reflect on the role of audience, critic and consumer by researching initial reactions of critics at the time selected work was produced and the response of the audience of the day in contrast to today’s audience.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Deconstruct visual content within a range of works, created for a variety of purposes, to acquire lessons that can be applied to own work.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Identify cultural, political, historical or spiritual factors affecting the work of several artists across disciplines or time periods.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Assess the effect of viewing and deconstructing art on own perspectives, perceptions and biases.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Study works to determine how artists conceptualize and communicate ideas and apply to own work.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Select works to investigate from applied and commercial disciplines including traditional and emerging technologies and practices.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Make connections to work studied and own creations.

outcomes.statement: Critique works in progress and portfolio development with peers and other experienced reviewers to inform the development of that work and/or lead future work.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Collectively choose criteria for reviewing student art including how to determine if work is complete rather than abandoned.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Use a variety of formal and informal art appreciation approaches to guide feedback.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain how inquiry and research inform inception of own work.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Refer to documentation of initial ideas and explain how intentions may have evolved through creative process.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify own influences, intentions and processes in the creation of non-derivative works and development of personal aesthetic vision.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Conduct portfolio review identifying areas of strength and areas for growth that guide goals for improvement.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Assess and apply select feedback from trusted sources to improve or fully resolve own work.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explain how own work is situated in current culture and reflects own views.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Compose a presentation portfolio (e.g., select items from one’s working portfolio) to best showcase one’s strengths and development as an artist.

outcomes.statement: Appraise current trends and emerging practices to determine how artists produce and embed knowledge within work.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore inventive contemporary art (e.g., maker and hacker cultures, game design, video culture, interactive art, land art) to formulate personal definition of art and understand its purposes.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Study cultural and historical themes in art (e.g., equality, politics, family, poverty, gender) to learn how artists contextualize or re-contextualize content.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine how art uses non-verbal visual language to embed knowledge (e.g., traditional First and Métis ways of knowing, world cultures, historical artifacts) and apply to own work.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate how art that persuades and/or protests is used to affect beliefs (e.g., propaganda, advertising, film, folk art).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze methodologies used by artists as researchers and apply to own inquiry.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate examples of interdisciplinary work involving arts and non-arts fields.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine art as a social critique and means of promoting global understanding.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Reflect and identify how the production and consumption of artistic knowledge can positively impact health and well-being.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Discuss aesthetic knowledge in art and principles of universal beauty (e.g., golden ratio).

outcomes.statement: Activate self-advocacy and agency as an emerging artist by connecting with arts professionals, including First Nations and Métis.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Expand entrepreneurship skills by studying art as a business (e.g., copyright, insurance, income tax, art contracts, art dealers, and art suppliers).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore and develop skills for pursuing a career in the arts within a work study, apprenticeship or mentorship experience (e.g., local artists, First Nations and Métis artists).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Demonstrate awareness of post-secondary study in the arts and local and global career opportunities.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine criteria used to determine the sale value of art and estimate the sale value of own artwork.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Demonstrate agency and independence as an emerging artist by maintaining physical studio spaces that are safe and utilizing resources appropriately considering practices that respect the environment and minimize impact.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Evaluate the financial and other supports (e.g., grants, exhibition space, marketing, community members) available to practicing artists.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Create materials to market one’s skills (e.g., compose a résumé and artist statement).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Create artist social media presence or website including posts of process, progress and final products.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Investigate ways to apply visual art skills to careers that are seemingly unrelated to the arts.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the roles and responsibilities of theatre production team members.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 1A: Introduction to Theatre Production (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-6 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the functions of theatre such as theatre that entertains, informs, documents, challenges and inspires.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Generate and examine inquiry questions regarding the perceived value of theatre, such as:
- What makes theatre unique?
- Why do audiences continue to attend theatre after many hundreds of years?
- What do theatre production teams contribute to an audience’s experience?

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss the functions of theatre production teams (e.g., to bring artistic vision to life, to ensure production tasks are carried out in an aesthetically satisfying, safe, timely and cost-effective manner).

indicators.label: d
e
indicators.text: Identify and categorize team member responsibilities, discuss the collaborative nature of theatre production and co-develop school-based ‘company’ rules and procedures.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Create a visual representation (e.g., flowchart, map) to demonstrate relationships and interdependence among various theatre jobs.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Organize and maintain a learning log (i.e., theatre log) including items such as tasks, schedules, experiences and understandings, to support planning, self-reflection, documentation and evaluation of learning.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify and explore the responsibilities of production department heads.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Describe the relationships among department heads and theatre crews.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Investigate how theatres are funded (e.g., commercial, not-for-profit) and discuss the roles of producers and management teams in moving productions from inception to performance (e.g., licensing, budgeting, assembling creative and technical teams).

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Discuss similarities and differences between large and small theatre companies, considering the impact of the availability of resources (e.g., human and financial) on production.

outcomes.statement: Investigate how designers create and collaborate to bring a theatrical vision to life.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 1B: Collaborative Processes of Theatrical Design and Production (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-6 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 1A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine the collaborative nature of theatre.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate ways that designers (e.g., set, costume, lighting, sound) get their ideas (e.g., identifying play requirements, researching, discussing with director).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine the roles of individuals and teams in production design.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss functions of design areas (e.g., lighting to establish time, sound to reveal mood, set to establish place, costume to reveal character).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate the purposes and content of various theatrical toolboxes or toolkits (e.g., lighting designer’s, costume designer’s).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explore and apply components of a designer’s toolbox (e.g., visual skills, use of maquettes, representation of mood, use of symbol/metaphor, light, colour, sound) for aesthetic purposes.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Analyze scenes to generate design ideas and determine technical requirements.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Use communication tools (e.g., language, maquettes, pictures, visual storyboard) to convey design ideas (e.g., mood, environment, symbolism).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Discuss purposes of a paper tech wherein designers meet with the stage manager to discuss and notate costume changes, light and sound transitions and other technical elements.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Interpret a scene through innovative use of various theatrical toolboxes (e.g., director’s, lighting designer’s, scenic designer’s, costume designer’s).

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Use a technical design component (e.g., light, costume, sound, digital technologies) for symbolic purposes as a mode for communicating ideas.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Change the point of view of a scene or dramatic work by amplifying a technical or artistic component (e.g., incorporate audience interaction, replace an actor with an object or technical feature, project digital images on moving actors, use social media conventions in performance).

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Create a production plan, budget and timeline, and identify roles for a real or imagined (e.g., paper or digital project) production.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Use the language of theatre purposefully.

indicators.label: o
indicators.text: Demonstrate willingness to take creative risks, understand that not all ideas will be realized and recognize the value of learning through failure.

indicators.label: p
indicators.text: Reflect on the impact of design decisions on an audience.

indicators.label: q
indicators.text: Examine and experiment with selected traditional world theatre conventions (e.g., design a piece related to a specific theatre arts context).

outcomes.statement: Investigate the history and evolution of technical theatre design practices.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 2: Roots of Theatrical Design (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-6 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 1A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss purposes of technical theatre design (e.g., set, properties, lighting, sound, costume, hair and makeup) including creative functions and practical considerations.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Conduct an inquiry into the history and evolution of technical theatre design, exploring questions such as:
- How do theatre artists and companies create other worlds on stage?
- What lighting was used in spaces and theatres before the advent of electricity?

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research early technical theatre including conventions (e.g., historic play formats, cultural traditions) and evolution of stage machinery (e.g., engineers such as Adolphe Appia, moveable scenery, flying machines, hydraulic stages, traps).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine technical theatre practices from the 1800s (e.g., early special effects, wind machines, waves, elevator stages).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Experiment with elements of technical theatre (e.g., world theatre, Western) using design practices such as thumbnail sketches, renderings and/or models.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Apply ideas, inspired by the history of technical theatre, to own work (e.g., surrealist set, 1940s costumes and hair, Greek or Italian masks, live sound effects).

indicators.label: g
h
indicators.text: Examine the effects of theatrical or playing space locations, architectures and stage configurations (e.g., outdoor, in the round, site- specific, thrust stages, arena stages, black-box, platform, shoebox) on audiences and consider how these diverse contexts impact technical theatre practices.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Explore the role of technical teams when working with collaboratively-devised theatrical performances.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Discuss challenges of early theatrical performances that didn’t have access to technology.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Examine how artistic desires have created technological innovations (e.g., Cirque du Soleil using aerospace engineers to solve artistic problems).

outcomes.statement: Assess performance spaces including those in the school and community.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 3: Performance Spaces (Core) · Suggested Time: 4-6 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate and compare the advantages and disadvantages of various indoor and outdoor performance spaces (e.g., arena/in the round, thrust, proscenium, black box, environmental).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify common areas (e.g., booth, fly gallery, catwalk) and aspects (e.g., curtaining system, grid and lighting system) of a traditional Western theatre performance space.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss Western theatre stage terms (e.g., front of house, apron, arena, backstage, down stage, flexible theatre, in the round, onstage, off stage, proscenium, stage left, stage right, thrust stage, upstage, wings) in the context of a variety of performance spaces.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Differentiate between working parts of a stage and scenery.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research and examine examples of Canadian Indigenous theatre staging considering performance spaces and technical theatre examples (e.g., use of symbolism and imagery, masks, wardrobe, lighting, sound, music, dance, properties, scenic design).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research performance spaces of a variety of traditions (e.g., forum theatre, environmental theatre, theatre that moves from venue to venue, First Nations longhouse).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Investigate technical theatre practices of selected world cultures (e.g., Japanese Kabuki makeup, Greek masks, Indonesian gamelan music sound design and shadow puppet theatre).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Identify features of the stage, house and backstage areas of a school, community or professional theatre facility.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Discuss how theatre professionals plan for adaptability to adjust for performance limitations (e.g., space, time parameters).

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Explore opportunities and challenges for a production team related to a selected performance space (e.g., potential interior and exterior performance areas and stages in the school or community) and discuss innovative options.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Recognize the effect the theatre location such as outdoor, theatre in the round, site-specific or historical theatre has on the audience.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Examine how digital technologies could be used in selected performance spaces.

outcomes.statement: Examine and apply basic safety standards in theatre arts work and performance spaces.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 4A: Safety in the Theatre – Rights and Responsibilities (Core) · Suggested Time: 1-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss employers’ and employees’ rights and responsibilities pertaining to workplace hazards and how they can work together to prevent workplace hazards in the theatre.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify risks, potential safety hazards and procedures used to ensure safety in theatre environments.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe basic safety procedures used in performance spaces and theatre environments for a variety of tasks such as working with rigging or lighting and working in darkness or at heights.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine how safety standards are specific to each area of technical theatre (e.g., electrics, set construction, chemicals, overhead rigging, paints and glues, pyrotechnics, power tools, stage machinery).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research Occupational Health and Safety regulations that apply to school, community and professional theatre facilities as they pertain to the use of items/features such as steps, risers, ladders, handrails on risers, rigging and traps in stage floor).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the purpose, scope and application of Safety Data Sheets in the theatre environment.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Research various safety codes (e.g., Canadian Electrical Code) and guidelines used in theatre including their purposes and related procedures.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Investigate safety protocols and guidelines from theatre spaces similar to the school or community playing space.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Co-construct a list of safety rules for general stage use (e.g., wearing close- toed shoes, no drinks on stage, procedures for using machines and stage devices).

outcomes.statement: Examine potential hazards in theatre production and apply injury prevention practices.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 4B: Safety in the Theatre: Hazards and Injury Prevention (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 4A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore risk assessment as it relates to the work area and how it can prevent injuries.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss how an injury might affect an injured worker and others such as the employer, supervisor, work colleagues, family and friends.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Analyze the importance of proper orientation, training, appropriate supervision, theatre inspections and following safe work practices.

indicators.label: d
e
indicators.text: Generate and discuss examples, within the context of theatre arts, of potential workplace hazards and injuries in the four major categories.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Compare a variety of industry safety guidelines and requirements for different areas of the theatre.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify potential safety hazards in the school theatre or performance spaces.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Demonstrate consistent and proper use of personal protection equipment or PPE (e.g., dust or ventilation masks, gloves, closed-toe shoes, clothing) and safety procedures (e.g., correct lifting of heavy objects, organization of storage areas, proper use of tools and equipment) in personal theatre arts experiences.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Discuss and use standard verbal warnings such as “Heads up!” or “Clear!”.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Explain health and safety regulations that apply to technical theatre occupations and identify employer and employee responsibilities.

outcomes.statement: Examine ways to maintain psychological health and safety in the theatre workplace.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 4C: Safety in the Theatre: Psychological Health and Safety (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-5 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 4B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the inclusion of psychological health as a safety concern in the theatre.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe potential challenges in achieving life/work balance in theatre arts careers and discuss ways of maintaining personal wellness.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss how self-employment and project-based contract work may impact one’s mental and physical health both positively (e.g., pursuing one’s passions, opportunities to be creative, a sense of accomplishment, pride in one’s work) and negatively (e.g., periodic financial stress, rejection of project proposals, long hours leading up to and during show runs followed by periods of less work).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe practical ways that theatre employees and employers can contribute to a psychologically healthy and safe workplace.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Research accommodations (e.g., modification of work duties, flexible hours, modifications to the work environment) that employees experiencing mental health problems or issues can request.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research sources of support (e.g., Professional Association of Canadian Theatres [PACT], Associated Designers of Canada [ADC], performing arts unions, Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety, Canadian Actors’ Equity Association, Theatre Saskatchewan) for psychological health and safety in the theatre.

outcomes.statement: Investigate artistic and technical approaches used in set design.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 5A: Set Design A (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-8 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 1B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine the function of a set designer.

indicators.label: b
c
indicators.text: Explain and reflect on how sets can create environments for dramatic work (e.g., realistic versus suggested set).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Research and examine the creation of illusions (e.g., projections, transformational set pieces, revolves).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore ways that a set design can be rendered using hand skills and digital technologies.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of researching and honouring the cultural significance of items (e.g., art, furniture, symbols) before incorporating them into set design.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine strategies for identifying protocols and processes concerning the representation or use of culturally-sacred items in set design.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Examine the stage and/or set requirements of a selected play or scene and propose ways to create the environment.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Render a simple stage design considering factors such as the design scheme and scale for that space.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Create a basic floor plan using relative scale.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Investigate the purpose (e.g., artistic, functional) of a set model.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Design and create a model (e.g., shoebox), in relative scale, of a real or imagined performance space for one style of set (e.g., realistic, suggested, period, abstract, digitally created).

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Reflect on personal successes and challenges experienced during design and creation of a real or imagined performance space.

outcomes.statement: Apply artistic and technical components in set design.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 5B: Set Design B (Optional) · Suggested Time: 10-12 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 5A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Review and explore techniques (e.g., inspirational image bank, thumbnail sketches, ground plans, models) and aesthetic approaches (e.g., minimalism, selective realism, abstraction) used by set designers.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss purpose and processes for drafting ground plans.

indicators.label: c
d
indicators.text: Investigate how set design decisions are informed by the thematic interpretation of the play or traditional practice.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine the purpose of renderings and explore colour theory, techniques and media (i.e., traditional and digital).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Create set design renderings for the same play or scene located in two different performance spaces and build a maquette for one of them, considering physical performance space and aesthetic interpretation.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Present set design renderings and maquettes and explain key parts of the decision-making process.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss how a rendering informs own design decisions and identify how it impacts decisions of other production team members.

outcomes.statement: Plan and create a set design for a real or imagined multi-set play, musical or devised drama/theatre production.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 5C: Set Design C (Optional) · Suggested Time: 10-12 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 5B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate how physical performance space and artistic interpretation can shape a set design (e.g., sightlines, elevations, symbolism, style).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss advantages and disadvantages of manual, mechanized and automated set pieces.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine the purposes, effects and mechanics of various types of stage machinery (e.g., revolves, scrims, drops, cycloramas, flying set pieces).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Prepare ground plans for selected scenes or full production using hand or digitally-created scaled drawings including elevations, top view and side view.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Incorporate design factors such as doorway dimensions, weight, portability, transporting, load in and load out to inform creation of a set design.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Create a coloured scaled model and/or maquette based on ground plans for selected scenes from a multi-set play, musical or devised drama or theatre piece, real or imagined (e.g., paper or digital project).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Research and examine modeling software for digitally-created renderings for set and scenery construction (e.g., creating ground plans, adding furniture and properties, drawing scenic elements).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text:
Discuss advantages that digital media have over traditional rendering methods, such as:
- speed - rendering digitally can be faster than traditional techniques when considering time spent to redo a traditional rendering;
- ease - detailed or photographic looking elements can easily be reworked without having to start over; and,
- duplication - a digitally rendered master image can save different looks as separate images for multiple sets.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Examine the practice of re-purposing materials for theatre sets and discuss benefits of sustainable practices.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Conduct a cost analysis and ensure that design plans work within a prescribed budget.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Present design including rationale and explanations for design decisions reached in collaboration with production team.

outcomes.statement: Apply methods of categorizing and creating stage properties.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 6A: Stage Properties A (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-10 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Modules 1A and 4A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define ‘stage properties’ and discuss their purpose in a production.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Brainstorm ways (e.g., hand/action, background, breakaway, consumable/perishable, dress, dummy, rehearsal, set, static, stunt) of categorizing stage properties.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Categorize a variety of stage properties such as food, magazines, weapons, signs, puppets, money, campfires, imaginary creatures and masks.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Create an image bank (e.g., digital, print) to use as inspiration for different categories of properties.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Design and create a three-dimensional property based on inspiration materials (e.g., photos, drawings, renderings) for a real or imagined production.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Brainstorm and propose solutions to potential problems and situations that might occur in regard to properties.

indicators.label: h
i
indicators.text: Identify reasons why properties must be organized backstage.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Collaborate on a plan to organize the properties for one or more acts of a play that is real or imagined.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Practise safety precautions and procedures when working with stage properties in theatre.

outcomes.statement: Create stage properties for a real or imagined production.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 6B: Stage Properties B (Optional) · Suggested Time: 10-12 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Modules 6A and 4B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine the relationship between the set designer and a properties builder.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss the role of a properties/set designer in relation to the director.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Participate in production design meetings and demonstrate collaboration with the director and design team (e.g., set, lighting and costume designers).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Review methods for categorizing, acquiring and managing properties.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research and design properties (e.g., food, weapon, appliance, decorative pieces, masks) representing specific places and times.

outcomes.statement: Prepare for the work placement.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 80A: Work Study Preparation (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Modules 1B and 4C plus one or more of the following: 5B, 6B, 7B, 8B, 9B, 10B, 11B, 12B, 15B, 17, 18B, 19

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III – Occupational Health and Safety in The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019:
- the right to know – the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate – in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,
- the right to refuse – work that you believe is unusually dangerous.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explain the roles and responsibilities of each partner (e.g., student, parent, teacher or other school staff, employer) involved in the work placement.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the business/organization to become familiar with its operations.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: In collaboration with all partners, develop personal and learning goals for the work placement.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Compile an employer information package that includes documents needed for the work placement (e.g., personal career documentation such as a resume or portfolio, permission forms, logs, self- and employer evaluation forms).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text:
Brainstorm a list of questions to ask the employer before beginning the work placement; these may include:
- What is my schedule of work hours?
- Who is my supervisor?
- What should I wear?
- When will I be provided with safety training?
- What potential hazards might I encounter in the work placement?
- Where do I find fire extinguishers, first aid kits and emergency assistance?
- What type of safety gear am I expected to wear? Is it provided?
- What should I do if I get injured or have an accident in the workplace?
- How can I contact my health and safety committee or representative?
- Are there any health and safety procedures I should follow?
- Who is the first aid person?
- Where are safety notices posted?
- What should I do in case of a fire or emergency?

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Develop a list of questions that could potentially be asked by the employer/work placement in an interview situation as well as answers to the questions.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Participate in an interview with the employer prior to beginning the work placement.

indicators.label: j

indicators.text: Assess the importance of good communication and interpersonal skills for workers in the travel services industry.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify factors (e.g., excellence in customer service, accessibility and competitive edge) that influence the success of a travel services business.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explore sustainable practices used by the travel services industry.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Research strategies for managing the safety and security of both guests and workers in a variety of travel services related businesses and scenarios.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of a risk mitigation plan including communication strategies to ensure the safety and security of both employees and patrons in response to unforeseen events (e.g., natural disaster or security threat).

outcomes.statement: Examine the importance of professionalism for workers in the tourism sector.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 13: Professionalism (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 2

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe personal qualities and behaviours (e.g., demonstrating a positive attitude; showing responsibility; being adaptable; showing respect for self and others; demonstrating communication skills; and being an ambassador for one’s school, community and province) that demonstrate professionalism as it relates to working in the tourism industry.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Discuss:
- the importance of professional appearance, good personal hygiene and conduct for a career in tourism;
- professional etiquette in using a variety of communication tools such as email, telephone, social media and smart phone applications both on- and off-the-job while employed in the tourism industry; and,
- common ethical standards (e.g., confidentiality and privacy) related to customer service in the tourism industry.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine the contributions of employees and volunteers and how their actions and attitudes can positively or negatively shape the identity of a business, community, province and country.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Assess the importance of acknowledging and respecting customer diversity.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Reflect on the potential impact of personal beliefs and unconscious bias on relationships and interactions with clients and co-workers in the workplace.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss what it means to be a good ambassador for a community.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Reflect on and commit to undertaking personal actions that demonstrate professionalism and being a good ambassador for one’s school and/or community.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the impact of customer service on the visitor experience.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 14A: Customer Service A (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 13

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify fundamental principles (e.g., respect, reliability, accountability, caring and responsiveness) of good customer service.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of a first impression and its impact on the visitor experience.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe ways to provide a good first impression when serving a customer in a tourism job.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Strategize approaches to accommodate and effectively serve customers from diverse backgrounds (e.g., cultural, social and demographic) and with diverse needs (e.g., accessibility, communication and mobility).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze customer rights to service and protection from discrimination as provided by the Human Rights Act of Canada and the Saskatchewan Human Rights Code.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research acceptable reasons (e.g., violent or threatening behaviour, intoxication and theft) for refusing service to a customer.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Suggest ways to effectively deal with a situation when denial of customer service is warranted.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Reflect on positive and negative customer experiences personally observed or encountered.

indicators.label: i

outcomes.statement: Analyze the importance of proactive customer service.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Distinguish between internal (co-workers) and external (guests) customers and provide examples of both within a tourism business.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe common or typical expectations (e.g., to be served in a timely manner, to be treated with kindness and respect and to receive or experience the desired outcome) of both internal and external customers.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Compare expectations (e.g., supports that help co-workers do their jobs effectively) of internal and expectations (e.g., being served with a positive attitude and receiving accurate information) of external customers.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Differentiate between proactive and reactive customer service.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of proactive customer service.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Describe ways to provide proactive customer for a variety of real-life or fictitious scenarios.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Create and present a scenario that demonstrates a proactive approach to customer service when dealing with internal and/or external customers.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss ways to salvage customer loyalty when attempts to provide good customer service seemingly fail.

outcomes.statement: Assess problem- solving skills required for effective customer service recovery.

indicators.text: Examine the concept of service recovery and its importance for business success.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Propose challenges (e.g., having to service multiple customers at the same time, being time-pressed to provide a response while being unsure of the response, facing an irate customer, having no solution to a customer’s problem, not being able to give a bigger discount and dealing with a service outage or crisis situation) that service professionals may face on the job.

indicators.label: c
d
indicators.text: Role-play situations that demonstrate the successful and unsuccessful application of service recovery skills in dealing with situations one has encountered or witnessed as a customer or service provider, or for fictitious scenarios (e.g., hotel guest is unhappy with an unclean room, guest reservation is lost or customer’s credit card is declined).

outcomes.statement: Analyze the purpose and benefits of tourism marketing.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define marketing and describe its purpose.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe potential benefits (e.g., economic, social and cultural) of marketing for the tourism sector.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of each element of the tourism marketing mix known as the 5 Ps and C (i.e., product, place, price, promotion, partnership and packaging, and convenience).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine the value of conducting market research (e.g., helps determine the target audience and viability of product/idea/experience and helps one identify competitors) when considering the tourism marketing mix.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify the 5 Ps and C of the tourism marketing mix applied to various local and provincial examples (e.g., a local summer fair, sports tournament, cultural event or trade show; Tunnels of Moose Jaw; Regina Folk Festival; Canadian Western Agribition; or a Saskatchewan Roughrider home game).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Differentiate between destination marketing organizations (e.g., Tourism Regina and Tourism Saskatoon) and provincial marketing organizations (e.g., Tourism Saskatchewan) and the roles they play in the tourism sector.

b

indicators.label: d

indicators.label: h

indicators.label: a

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify trends in tourism marketing.

indicators.label: f

outcomes.statement: Analyze the importance of branding in the tourism sector.

indicators.text: Describe the concept of branding.

indicators.text: Brainstorm examples of branding in the tourism sector (e.g., Moose Jaw as “Canada’s Most Notorious City,” Paris as the “City of Love,” Walt Disney’s Mickey Mouse ears, Las Vegas as the “Entertainment Capital of the World” and WestJet’s “Love Where You’re Going” platform).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Research the advantages (e.g., building customer recognition and loyalty, enhanced credibility, attracting customers who share the same values and developing an emotional connection with customers) and disadvantages (e.g., costs to develop and the potential difficulty in changing perceptions of the brand in the future) of branding.

indicators.text: Discuss the relationship between branding and marketing and the importance of a strong brand for business success in the tourism sector.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text:
Research answers to questions related to the geography of the community or area, such as:
- location - Where is it (e.g., absolute location, referencing latitude and longitude and relative location, referencing other locations)? Why is it there?
- place – What is it like there, considering both physical and human characteristics?
- human/environment interaction – What is the relationship between humans and the environment? How has the landscape been shaped by humans?
- movement – What examples of movement of people, goods or ideas are present? Has immigration impacted the area? What are the modes of transportation and transportation routes?
- region – In what region is it located, and how is it similar or dissimilar to other regions?

indicators.text:
Describe and reflect on the three basic rights that all workers have under Part III – Occupational Health and Safety in The Saskatchewan Employment Act, 2019:
- the right to know – the hazards at work and how to control them;
- the right to participate – in finding and controlling workplace hazards; and,

outcomes.statement: Use inquiry to create a work of art inspired by the work of national and/or international artists.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Propose topics, identify big ideas, generate questions for inquiry, create a plan to guide the inquiry and document the creative process.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Create an art work based on individual or collaborative inquiry, including for example:

- comparing and contrasting the work of selected artists
- researching and viewing works of recognized national or international artists
- experimenting with techniques and media used by the artists
- documenting the inquiry (e.g., portfolios, sketches, visual journals, notes, digital photos)
- describing own decision-making and problem-solving processes, and reflecting on the effectiveness of choices made.

indicators.label: e

outcomes.statement: Identify and analyse criteria for critiquing and valuing various forms of visual art.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Generate questions and conduct an inquiry into factors that influence judgements about the aesthetic quality or economic value of various forms of art (e.g., What is art? indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify criteria that are most appropriate to a particular form or style of art and apply when critiquing (e.g., architecture, designed object, cultural artifact, contemporary urban street art, comic, controversial public art).

indicators.text: Collaborate with peers to co-construct assessment criteria (e.g., technical skills, compositional qualities, use of images) for reflection on the development and resolution of own work, and identify what will be used as evidence of learning (e.g., journals, sketchbooks, artist’s statements, video documentation, critiques, portfolios).

indicators.label: d

indicators.label: g

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Examine, respect and honour traditional, historical and contemporary connections to the land and the natural world (e.g., treaty education outcome TPP12 - represent personal understanding of the concept, We Are All Treaty People).

outcomes.statement: Examine how visual art expressions have changed over time and/or inspired change in individuals, communities and societies.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine the influence of the evolution of digital media on the creation of art expressions.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Investigate how artists from various cultural backgrounds draw on their historical traditions in different ways as contemporary art practices evolve over time.

indicators.label: d

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine how visual art, and the other arts, contribute to personal and social wellbeing in communities (e.g., fostering connections, sharing stories, creating empathy).

indicators.label: d
