indicators.text: Take personal and musical risks by trying new ways to express oneself in the jazz idiom, using new ideas, new concepts and a variety of styles.

outcomes.statement: Infuse, independently, the understanding of the muscial text into a personal musical performance.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Prepare, rehearse and perform music in jazz style in solo, small group and/or large ensemble settings.

indicators.label: b
c
indicators.text: Create original text to pre-existing melodies and improvisations (vocalese)

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Integrate knowledge of conventions regarding jazz articulation and use those conventions in performance.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Show proficient use jazz vocabulary and use this vocabulary to describe personal musical practise, learning, theory and performance (see Jazz Glossary).

outcomes.statement: Identify the elements of music and apply these to create a musical product.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Individually design, implement and evaluate a plan to improve individual performance and to enhance the knowledge and uderstanding of vocal jazz. As part of this process of improvement, include recording and listening back to performances, practices and/or rehearsals.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Integrate into performance the knowledge of standard notation conventions (e.g., note durations up to eighth notes, repeats, codas, D.S.s and dynamic markings). Identify jazz conventions that differ from traditional classical notation (e.g., falls, glisses, slides, inflection marks and hats).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Sing a variety of vocal jazz styles (e.g., swing, funk, ballad) accompanied and a cappella.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Integrate an understanding of the relationship of form and text in music, particularly blues and ABA, AABA song forms.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify different elements of music such as articulation, rhythm, beat, metre, time placement and tone that help create a jazz style and apply this knowledge while music making.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Integrate an understanding of the different elements of music such as articulation, rhythm, beat, metre, time placement and tone that help create a jazz style, and apply this knowledge while music making.

outcomes.statement: Model individual vocal techniques and apply these to create or show a musical product.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Consistently sing with a tone appropriate to the style and personal development.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Model a consistent connection between the breath and the voice.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Internalize and consistently the key concepts related to singing expressively (e.g., work painting, phrasing, motion and dynamics). Show the knowledge of these concepts through singing.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Individually generate technical inquiry questions and take action on the findings of the inquiry (e.g., "What can I do to get better?" or "How could I improve this performance, paper, or arrangement?").

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Consistently use good microphone techniques in rehearsals and the performance of music.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Sing harmony a cappella maintaining key centre.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Sing a one octave chromatic scale, scending and descending, unaccompanied.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Sing one octave major, harmonic minor, dorian, mixolydian and blues scales, ascending and descending, unaccompanied.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Sing the chord tones of major and minor triads, dominant and major 7ths, major and minor 6ths and 9ths, and scale triads.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Sing a jazz standard (with recorded or live acompaniment) demonstrating scat singin and other appropriate jazz stylings.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Sight-read a simple 2 - 4 part composition

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Compare and contrast vocal jazz style to other vocal styles.

outcomes.statement: Listen and respond as a vocal jazz performer when singing jazz.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Respond to qualities of personal tone such as pitch, dynamics, style, colour, blend, rhythm, time, and consistent vowel use.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Respond to the rest of the ensemble (e.g., its tone, colour, pitch, dynamics, style, rhythm, time, balance, consistent vowel use and blend).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Immediately respond to the ensemble's response (e.g., When singing, does the student match and change vowel sounds and shapes to match the group?).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Respond to the conductor/leader, including gestures, cues, tempo, expressions and body language.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Listen to the acoustic properties of the performing space, including the sound, tone, loudness, and reverb of the room and adjust singing and microphone technique accordingly.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: React to the audience, their presence (or nor), body language, expressions and reaction to the music (e.g., applause, cheering, being asked to sing louder or quieter).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Know the history, culture, style, form and tempo of the music being performed and respond to the music by reading it and/or performing the notes and/or changes appropriately

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Recall previous experiences and knowledge (in music and in life) and integrate these into solo group vocal jazz performances.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Know any special emotional context that may apply to the music, generate the appropriate emotional feeling or energy and/or synchronize the personal emotional state of the performer with the emotional context of the music being performed.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Know, predict and/or anticipate what is next or might bve next in the music and prepare for that while performing in the moment of the music.

outcomes.statement: Listen to jazz as a jazz performer when not personally performing the music.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Listen to jazz music and independently analyze form, tone, style, era, dynamics, articulation, time signature, characteristic rhythms, time, balance, blend, key, monde and/or pitch.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Analyze the development of the jazz music(melody, arrangement, changes, or improvisation) as a whole or in smaller sections.
;

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Analyze the characteristic sounds, licks, tone and other elements of well-known singers and/or groups. Identify these singers and/or groups. Identify these singers and/or groups on recordings aurally, only by listening to the characteristic sounds or ideas presented in the music.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze and reflect on just one voice or instrument from the beginning to the end of a musical selection (e.g., Does the singer or player perform the same way all the way through? How was it different or the same? What did he/she sing or play that the student also might be able to sing or play?)

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Listen to music analyzing and reflecting on the melody, other voices, bass line, drums and percussion, background lines, background vocals, roots and chord progression and sing with the recording.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the history, cultural heritage and effect of current events as these apply to the musical selection.

outcomes.statement: Independently analyze vocal jazz music in real time while making or listening to the music.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Individually identify, experiment with, and purposefully use strategies to solve different challenges related to music making.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine common chord structures including, but not limited to, triads, seventh and ninth chords in music performed and/or listened to.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify the time signatures on first hearing a piece of music, including 6/8, in addition to simpler duple time signatures. Demonstrate the patters of strong and weak beats that are identified with the time signatures

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Use strategies to identify the types of scales being used (pentatonic, blues, major, etc.) in music performed and/or listened to.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Develop strategies for hearing 2 and 4 on first hearing a piece of music in an appropriate time signature.

outcomes.statement: Listen to performances of vocal jazz music and individually or with assistance develop and apply critical criteria to use in critical evaluation of one's own work and other's work.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Listen to the music of the great jazz and vocal jazz performers.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Generate criteria of excellence through listening to the music of the great performers (e.g., What is it that makes the music great? what do the great performers do that the student or student's ensemble does no do?)

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Design and implement a plan for improvement (personal and ensemble) based on the criteria generated from listening to the great performers.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Upon first hearing a musical selection, describe and classify the music using appropriate jazz language (e.g., style, period, compose, culture and performer).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Broaden knowledge of skills and components of listening actively, continue to develop these listening skill and recognize that listening contributes to the authenticity of performances.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Recognize and discuss the value of original thought, technical proficiency, place, era and other concepts in the music of the great jazz performers.

outcomes.statement: Synthesize the knowledge and implementation of the skills, techniques and attitudes necessary for successful ensemble performance.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Know the role of each of the parts within the student's ensemble by demonstrating the ability to perform those specific tasks that are particular to the vocal part or instrument that the student sings or plays in the ensemble (e.g., bass part in the choir, comping for guitar and piano, walking lines for the bass, solo parts in the choir and position in a section).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Individually attend to melodic phrasing, rhythmic accuracy and articulation in perparation and performance of vocal jazz.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Sing in tune with good balance and tone and be aware of the qualities of the student's own voice (e.g., range, where the break in the student's voice is).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Demonstrate leadership as a performer by offering help, ideas and guideance to other performers during rehearsals and sectionals.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Demonstrate a professional attitude towards conduct, focus and communication skills in rehearsal, preparation of materials and presentation of products.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Consolidate the learned characteristics of different styles, eras, etc. to the performance of the student's music.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Demonstrate significant understanding of PA systems including set up, tone and level settings for microphones, and so on.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Show respect for the personal work of self and others through appropriate critique.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Critically examine and assess the student's individual work and personal contributions to group projects/performances, with assistance as necessary.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Be accepting ofappropriate critiques from others, and work towards implementing the solutions to those critiques.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Demonstrate and record technical development, and from that, develop strategies to improve.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Know the value of individual practice, know how to practive, conduct an ongoing evaluation of the student's personal practice skills, and implement a plan for improvement.

outcomes.statement: Aurally distinguish the different eras, genres, styles and feels of vocal jazz through listening to and/or performing the representative music.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Individually listen to recording of vocal jazz, develop a list or understanding of the basic characteristics of different jazz styles, genres, periods and place and implement that knowledge into practice and performance.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: On first hearing, catagorize jazz music into styles, genres, periods and/or place.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine aspects of jazz such as history, performers, styles and eras through a variety of media, with a focus on Canadian or Saskatchewan jazz artists.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Demonstrate awareness of vocal jazz music by suggesting listening and/or performing opportunities for the ensemble.

outcomes.statement: Explore jazz music and its performers and educators and their influence in the world.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Examine roles that vocal jazz artists might have beyond being performers, and identify individuals who fit those particular roles (e.g., Bobby McFerrin, Phil Mattson, and Gene Puerling).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: A number of jazz artists have First Nations or American Indian heritage (e.g., Mildred Bailey, Lena Horne, Joe Williams and Julia Keefe). Discuss possible reasons why this is not widley known and the effect that this heritage may have had on their music and lives.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify influential singers or players of the student's instrument, investigate why these performers are so influential and listen to their music. Give special attention to performers from Saskatchewan and Canada.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss the influence of jazz on contemporary First Nations music.

outcomes.statement: Evaluate the degree of influence that vocal jazz has had on other types of music with an emphasis on the music of Canada and Saskatchewan, and assess possible careers in vocal jazz and music

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate the influence of jazz in pop, rock and other current music (e.g., the use of jazz themes and rhythms in hip-hop, rap, funk), and the influence of these current styles on jazz.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate the relationship between instrumental and vocal jazz, with particular emphasis on on vocalese.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Describe how Canadian and international copyright laws affect the lives of those who work in the jazz field.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Research career pathways in vocal jazz and music in general.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine "crossover" artists and how categorization of music affects the artist and musical product.

outcomes.statement: Apply principles and techniques for unintentional injury prevention to ensure safe work performance in the welding area.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 1: General Shop Safety (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-3 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify the purpose and demonstrate the proper use and fit of personal protective equipment (PPE) including eye protection (lens shades), clothing, hearing protection, and footwear while identifying the hazards from which they protect individuals.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Analyze potential risk situations and solutions that apply specifically to slips and falls, as well as lifting heavy material, and identify safe solutions.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Recognize hazards associated with oxy-acetylene welding equipment (i.e., tanks, hoses, gauges) and take the necessary measures to avoid unintentional injuries, including those caused by flashback and backfire.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Recognize hazards associated with electric welding processes and take necessary measures to avoid unintentional injuries.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Evaluate the fire plan for the shop, including components such as fire alarms, fire extinguishers, exits, and procedures; and make recommendations for improvements.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Demonstrate the proper procedures to follow when reporting an unintentional injury.

outcomes.statement: Work safely with properly maintained safety equipment in an organized environment.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 2: Intermediate Safety (Core) · Suggested Time: 1-2 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 1

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Express knowledge of safe handling of materials according to WHMIS, using materials safety data sheets (MSDS).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research and discuss Occupational Health and Safety regulations which apply to the welding industry.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Recognize and apply safe and fair work practices including freedom from violence and harassment.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Complete an assessment of all safety and welding equipment and, in consultation with the instructor, perform maintenance to repair or replace defective or worn parts.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate and explain the correct procedures for the safe use, care, and handling of the hand tools and power equipment used in a welding shop.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 3: Hand and Power Tools (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-15 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify and define the safe use of hand tools such as hammers, pliers, wire brushes, strikers, anvils, files, tip cleaners, hand shears, hacksaws, clamps, vices, and marking tools.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Demonstrate and articulate the correct procedures for operating power tools such as grinders (stationary and portable), buffers (stationary and portable), power shear, power hacksaw, band saw, and drill press.

outcomes.statement: Assess the condition of and the maintenance of tools used in the welding shop.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 4: Intermediate Hand and Power Tools (Core) · Suggested Time: 1-2 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 3

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Demonstrate the proper method for cleaning weld-spattered tools.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Assess and report any potential faults with electrical cords and receptacles.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Repair or replace welding-distorted surfaces on benches or table tops in consultation with the instructor.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Demonstrate the proper techniques to remove and replace saw blades.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Identify potential maintenance issues with hand and power tools and consult with the instructor to determine a solution.

outcomes.statement: Develop and apply a systematic routine for setting up and putting away oxy-acetylene equipment.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 5: Oxy-acetylene Start-up, Shut-down, and Cutting (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Describe and perform the accepted start-up and shut-down procedures for the oxy-acetylene system which includes valves, regulators, torches, tips, types of flames, and safety precautions.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Understand and describe how to cut 3⁄8” mild steel including the correct flame, flame distance, angle of the tip, direction of travel, speed of travel, and motion of tip.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate safe and effective cutting using an oxy-acetylene torch after determining the proper tip size and gas pressure for the gauge of metal.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 6: Introduction to Oxy-acetylene Cutting (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 5

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify precautionary procedures to limit the danger to others in the shop.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe the relationship between the tip size, metal thickness, and gas pressures.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Demonstrate the specified cuts on the provided material using an oxy-acetylene cutting torch.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate use of an oxyacetylene torch to make specified cuts.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 7A: Oxy-acetylene Cutting Skills (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-7 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 6

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Cut straight lines on 3⁄8” mild steel.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Complete bevel cuts on 3⁄8” mild steel.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Cut holes and circles on 3⁄8” mild steel.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate cuts to fit a given template to increase accuracy to within 1⁄16” tolerance.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 7B: Oxy-acetylene Cutting Skills (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 6 and 7A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Complete round and/or curved cuts specified by the instructor.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Complete square and/or rectangular cuts specified by the instructor.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate cutting with an oxy-acetylene torch on a variety of metal thicknesses to achieve a high quality cut.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 8: Oxy-acetylene Cutting Practice (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-7 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 7B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Demonstrate the correct settings for the oxygen and the acetylene regulators and explain the relationship between the settings and the metal thickness.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Demonstrate and evaluate oxy-acetylene cutting torch work on a variety of thicknesses and types of metal.

outcomes.statement: Use oxy-acetylene equipment to complete the specified welds and analyze the results.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 9: Oxy-acetylene Welding (Core) · Suggested Time: 5-6 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: Module 5

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Run lines of fusion without the use of filler rod in the flat position on gauge mild steel.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Assess the quality of personal work on practical assignments including butt weld, edge weld, and lines of fusion.

outcomes.statement: Effectively use oxy-acetylene equipment to increase the quality of the specified welds.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 10: Intermediate Oxy-acetylene Welding (Core) · Suggested Time: 1-2 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 9

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Perform and analyze a variety of specified welds, including butt weld, edge weld, and lines of fusion.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Compare and chart personal progress to identify increasing skill.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Assess personal technique and document results in consultation with the instructor.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate an increasingly high quality of both welding skill and self-assessment of that skill while using oxy-acetylene equipment.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 11A: Oxy-acetylene Welding Practice (Core) · Suggested Time: 10-12 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 10

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Create examples of basic oxy-acetylene welding practices, including beads with no filler, edge weld, corner weld, beads with filler, butt weld, and lap weld.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Perform an outside corner weld, no filler rod, in the flat position, on gauge mild steel.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Run lines of fusion using filler rod, in the flat position, on gauge mild steel.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Perform a butt weld using filler rod, in the flat position, on gauge mild steel.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Assess personal technique and results in consultation with the instructor.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate increasing proficiency in oxy-acetylene welding skills.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 11B: Oxy-acetylene Welding Practice (Core) · Suggested Time: 20-25 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 10

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Perform a butt weld using filler rod, in the flat position, on gauge mild steel ensuring 100% penetration.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Perform a butt weld using filler rod, in the vertical position, on gauge mild steel.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Perform a lap weld using filler rod, in the flat position, on gauge mild steel; overlap by half.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Assess personal technique and document results in consultation with the instructor.

outcomes.statement: Select, complete, and assess an approved oxy-acetylene welding project to demonstrate welding proficiency.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 12A: Advanced Oxy-acetylene Welding Projects (Optional) · Suggested Time: 5-10 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 11A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Create a drawing and develop a cutting list of materials.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text:
Use organized and practised skills to construct a project using appropriate technical language. Utilize the following guidelines to complete a project:
- Generate different project ideas
- Plan and manage the project including assessment criteria in consultation with the instructor
- Plan and use drawings with appropriate symbols
- Set a procedural sequence
- Prepare a material list and cost estimate
- Create a timeline
- Determine fabrication techniques
- Cut material and set up in the proper sequence
- Complete each part as specified
- Interpret and follow directions
- Adhere to timelines
- Work cooperatively
- Follow all safety requirements
- Follow all handling and storing procedures
- Fulfill cleanup and tool maintenance responsibilities
- Present the completed project and complete a self-assessment based on the criteria for the project.

outcomes.statement: Plan, complete, and assess an oxy-acetylene welding project to demonstrate increasing welding proficiency.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 12B: Advanced Oxy-acetylene Welding Projects (Optional) · Suggested Time: 5-10 hours · Level: Advanced · Prerequisite: Module 11B

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Create a scale drawing of the project using appropriate symbols including a cutting list.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Calculate the cost of material including incidentals.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Demonstrate increasing development of welding skills.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Develop a project plan to include major stages of development and a timeline needed for completion as outlined in module 12A.

outcomes.statement: Effectively use plasma arc cutting equipment to cut metal of various thicknesses and types.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 13: Plasma Arc Cutting (Core) · Suggested Time: 1-2 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify and describe safety considerations for appropriate use of plasma arc cutting equipment.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Correctly use plasma arc cutting equipment to perform various cuts specified by the instructor.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Verify the correct pressure settings and techniques to safely cut ferrous and non-ferrous metals of given thicknesses.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate a knowledge of and expertise with electric arc welding equipment including common types of electrodes, currents, and welding positions while using the correct terminology.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 14: Shielded Metal Arc Welding Procedures and Equipment (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-4 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Define and appropriately use terminology related to electric arc welding including alternating current, ampere, anode, arc, backing or backup, backhand welding, backstep welding, base metal, bead, bevel, brazing, capillary attraction, cathode, chipping, circuit, complete penetration, contraction, constant current, cover glass, crater, direct current, distortion, downhand welding, ductility, duty cycle, elasticity, electrode circuit, expansion, ferrous, finished bead, finished surface, flux, forehand welding, fusion welding, gaseous shield, generator, kerf, non-ferrous, parent metal, peening, penetration, polarity, porosity, rectifier, root opening, slag, solder, spatter, strain, stress, tensile strength, transformer, uphand welding, voltage, warping, yield point, and yield strength.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe the differences in welding electrodes such as 6011, 6013, 7014, and 7018.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Categorize and explain the uses of direct current with straight and reverse polarity.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Categorize and explain the difference between alternating current and direct current with straight and reverse polarity.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Demonstrate start-up and shut-down procedures as well as striking the arc, setting and adjusting amperage, correct electrode angle, and appropriate rate of travel.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Compile a list of specialty electrodes including those used for stainless steel, aluminium, nickel, and hard surfacing.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Identify situations where flat, horizontal, vertical, and overhead positions would be used.

outcomes.statement: Identify, diagnose, and provide remedies for common arc welding faults.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 15: Electric Arc Welding: Welding Faults (Core) · Suggested Time: 1-2 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Identify faults such as crater-cracking, gas pockets, porosity, and undercutting.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Justify and demonstrate corrections for electric arc faults.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate the proper techniques for striking an arc and running a bead using four types of welds in flat and horizontal positions.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 16: Electric Arc Welding (Core) · Suggested Time: 1-2 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Compose a list of uses for common welds including butt, flat, corner, and fillet.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Run continuous weld beads on mild steel.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Demonstrate basic welding practices such as striking the arc, electrode angle, rate of travel, amperage settings, and electrode selection.

outcomes.statement: Describe critical aspects of electric arc welding such as types, uses, and characteristics of electrodes, types of current, polarity, joints, and welding positions.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 17: Electric Arc Welding Electrodes (Core) · Suggested Time: 1-2 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the significance of each position in the classification number for welding electrodes.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Categorize the following electrodes according to uses and weld characteristics such as penetration, slag, spatter, and application: 6010, 6011, 6013, 7014, 7018, and 7024.

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate increasing skill in running a continuous bead using arc welding equipment.

indicators.text: Investigate the multitude of factors that exert influences on life balance (e.g., relationships, gender, culture, stress, sense of belonging, leisure, traditions, socio-economic factors, physical and mental fitness, technology use).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Critique community and societal norms (e.g., expectations regarding gender roles, norms regarding alcohol consumption) that influence the well-being of self, family, and community.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Assess one's motivations (e.g., appearance) and limitations (e.g., time management) that improve and/or impede one's personal wellness.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Analyze individual and civic responsibility in nurturing well-being and examine the social factors (including expectations of self and others) that influence personal wellness.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Examine available supports (both formal and informal) for attaining and maintaining optimal wellness and establish strategies to effectively access these supports.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Analyze one's current level of wellness (e.g., wellness inventory).

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Initiate an ongoing multi-dimensional (i.e., physical, psychological, social, spiritual, environmental) Personal Plan for Wellness based on a comprehensive analysis of personal well-being.

outcomes.statement: Assess, through participation in service learning opportunities and other means (e.g., interviews, discussions, observations), how service learning enhances the well-being of the volunteer and to the individual or organization/community.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Reflect on and discuss what is known about service learning (e.g., what volunteers do, where volunteering occurs, why people volunteer/ do not volunteer).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate historical, contemporary, and evolving needs and opportunities (e.g., time, situations, programs, technology, and/or environments) in the community which might benefit from acts of service.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Determine a variety of community service opportunities that would benefit the well-being of one's community (e.g., meals on wheels, senior centres, canvasser, walking school bus, Special Olympics, coaching/officiating minor sports, Save the Planet, ditch picks, helping seniors who are housebound).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate the impact of volunteering on the overall well-being of self and community (e.g., motivation and sense of accomplishment, sense of belonging, enhanced personal skills, career opportunities, advocacy, cleaner natural environment).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze the contributions that young adults can make through service to their community.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Assess personal skills and aptitudes to find the most effective community service opportunities for self.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Set personal goals, that are documented in one's Personal Plan for Wellness, of what one wants to accomplish from service learning.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Evaluate, revise, and continue to implement Personal Plan for Wellness to be actively engaged in at least 12 hours of participation in service learning in the community (i.e., local community, global community).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Document, monitor, and communicate, using a variety of technologies (e.g., photos, video), one's involvement in, and understanding of, service learning.

outcomes.statement:
Plan for and engage in movement activity to increase confidence, competence, and sustainability in self-selected individual and/or partner movement activities from each of the following categories:
- Body Management Activities (e.g., dance, yoga, pilates, martial arts, aerobics)
- Alternate Environment Activities (e.g., cycling, snowshoeing, cross-country skiing, swimming, hiking, skating, canoeing, trapping, weight lifting/going to a fitness centre)
- Target games (e.g., bowling, golf, archery, bocce ball)
- Net/Wall games (e.g., tennis, table tennis, racquetball, squash)
Reminder: Health-related fitness includes cardiovascular endurance, flexibility, muscular endurance, muscular strength, and body composition.
Skill-related fitness, includes power, agility, speed, reaction time, balance, and coordination.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Reflect on and make conclusions about one's own personal preference for participation in movement activities as based on the dimensions of wellness (i.e., physical, psychological, social, spiritual, environmental).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Assess own level of confidence and competence in participating, in each of the four basic physical environments (i.e., on the ground, in the water, on snow and ice, in the air).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Evaluate perceived and actual personal levels of confidence and competence when utilizing the required complex skills needed to participate in self-selected movement activities.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze the impact that current personal strengths and weaknesses in health-related fitness have on personal performance of complex skills used in self-selected movement activities (e.g., I have good upper body strength so I am successful at swimming lengths in the pool).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze a complex skill required in each self-selected movement activity to determine which Basic Movement Patterns/Skills require practice for enhancing sustainable performance of the skills.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Assess personal understanding of tactics (e.g., response to a specific moment in time such as what to do in the case of unexpected fatigue during long-distance running) and strategies (e.g., predetermined plan such as choosing a golf course based on your ability) in self-selected movement activities.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Apply relevant biomechanical principles (e.g., laws of motion, friction) to enhance complex skills required for competent participation in self-selected movement activities.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Analyze influences (e.g., fluid intake, commitment to practice, available technology, audience, nutrition) that affect optimal personal performance during participation in movement activities.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Locate, evaluate, and use resources (e.g., websites, people in the community, agencies in the province) to help support and build one's understanding of effective skill performance, tactics, and strategies to be used in individual/partner movement activities.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Analyze personal utilization of movement skills, tactics, and strategies utilizing technology (e.g., video motion analysis of self and others, pedometers, technological applications) and other means (e.g., checklists, rubrics).

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Analyze transferable skills, tactics, and strategies to be used in the performance of various other self-selected individual and/or partner movement activities.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Utilize visualization and other mental preparation strategies to enhance performance in self-selected movement activities.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Critique, after participation in self-selected movement activities, decisions made regarding the utilization of skills, tactics, and strategies.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Evaluate, revise, and continue to implement a Personal Plan for Wellness to increase competency in complex skills and enhance participation in individual and/or partner movement activities that support sustainable wellness.

outcomes.statement: Assess the impact of mental health on overall well-being of self, family, and community.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Reflect on and discuss personal and community beliefs and biases about mental health.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine common misconceptions and negative stigmas/ connotations related to both the area of and the language of mental illness (e.g., misconception that an individual with a mental illness has a weak character or is inevitably dangerous).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Consider ways to reduce stigma, address discrimination, and eliminate structural barriers related to mental illness.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe, with information from a variety of mental health experts, the factors that contribute to positive mental health (e.g., involvement in extracurricular activities, belonging to a team/group).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss prior understandings of how thoughts, actions, and behaviours are all connected to brain function.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Recognize that there is no single cause of any mental health problem or illness and no one is immune regardless of where they live, how young or old they are, or their social standing.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine evolving theories about the complex causes of mental illnesses (i.e., social, economic, psychological, biological, and genetic factors).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Assess the influence of mental well-being on each of the dimensions of wellness (i.e., psychological, physical, social and environmental).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Investigate various personal, environmental, biological, and social influences (e.g., sports competitions, use of cannabis, support networks) on mental health and determine one's relationship to these influences.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Determine why particular mental illnesses (e.g., anxiety disorders, depression, bipolar mood disorder, eating disorders, schizophrenia) are common in adolescence.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Investigate the relationships between personal mental health and personal wellness (e.g., feeling well, functioning well and being resilient, making positive changes, being physically fit).

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Examine the relationships among defense mechanisms, feelings, behaviours, and mental health (i.e., ways we protect ourselves from things we do not want to think about or deal with).

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Examine the interconnectedness and interdependence of mental health and a variety of activities (e.g., leisure activities, competitive sports, physical activities, helping someone or some cause).

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Analyze mental fitness factors (e.g., placing things in perspective, using stress management strategies, cultivating and maintaining a strong sense of humour) as they relate to personal well-being.

indicators.label: o
indicators.text: Evaluate, revise, and continue to implement a Personal Plan for Wellness based on new understandings about mental health.

outcomes.statement: Assess one's self-awareness (i.e., one's ability to perceive own emotions and tendencies) and self-management (i.e., ability to stay flexible and positively direct personal behaviour) for the purpose of enhancing well- being of self and others.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss personal standards, interests, abilities, and privileges, and how these influence one's well-being.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Complete a variety of personal inventories to analyze learnings about self.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Assess one's emotional intelligence (i.e., the ability to perceive, control, and evaluate emotions) using a variety of measurement tools.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Analyze how overall well-being is affected by biases and stereotyping (e.g., gender, physical abilities, culture, body composition).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze own ability to manage physical fitness for a lifetime versus relying on others (e.g., a coach and a team).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Reflect on one's ability to recognize and manage emotions in self and in personal relationships.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine emotional and behavioural patterns of self and others and determine related impact on optimal wellness.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Practise and reflect on variety of self-awareness strategies (e.g., treat feelings as good or bad, identify triggers, seek feedback, keep a journal of emotions, observe others' reactions to your emotions).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Reflect on and explain the 'what' and 'why' of one's own preference (e.g., alone, with a partner, in a group, on a team, competitive, recreational) for engagement in particular movement activity.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Examine internal (e.g., thinking patterns) and external (e.g., triggers) influences on one's emotional intelligence.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Analyze and practise effective identification and communication of feelings.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Justify one's overall placement on the listening continuum (i.e., ignoring, pretending, selecting, attending, empathizing) and recognize opportunities for improvement.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Determine the benefits of proactive decision making in managing personal well-being.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Analyze one's preferred decision-making style in terms of its impact on well-being of self and others.

indicators.label: o
indicators.text: Evaluate, revise, and continue to implement a Personal Plan for Wellness based on new understandings about self.

outcomes.statement: Model and promote a local culture/norm of safety and injury prevention (i.e., physical safety, social safety, psychological safety, spiritual safety, environmental safety) to optimize well-being of self, family, community, and the environment.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Evaluate the norm/culture of safety in one's peer groups, family, and community.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate (e.g., communicate with safety experts in the community) factors that influence safety norms.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Ask and investigate compelling questions about the local culture of safety (e.g., What can be the long-term impact of continuing to be physically active while injured? Are all injuries predictable and preventable? Are there occasions when an injured player should still be 'in the game'? How do you know if a risk is worth the potential consequences? What are personal responsibilities regarding safety in each dimension?).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine how the local culture of safety (i.e., physical safety, social safety, psychological safety, spiritual safety, environmental safety) has been established and nurtured while reflecting on its related impact on community and environmental well-being.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Evaluate risks and safety factors (i.e., physical safety, social safety, psychological safety, spiritual safety, environmental safety) that may affect activity choices (e.g., What are some physical activity options that are safe to participate in when one has a broken leg?) and preferences.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate common safety risks (e.g., driving a motorized vehicle, participating in high-contact sports) for youth in local community and determine injury prevention opportunities.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Analyze common unintentional injuries (e.g., head injury from high jumping, death due to motor vehicle accidents, injury to hand while using a power tool) for youth in local community and discuss related impact on the overall well-being of self and others.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Demonstrate respect, responsibility, and caring for own wellness by applying understandings related to the identification, prevention (e.g., investigate facts, prepare basic first-aid kit, take time outs), and management of common safety risks (e.g., wearing personal protective equipment, following recommended guidelines and instruction for use of equipment).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Analyze moral and ethical conduct in movement activities and sport (e.g., cheating, intentional fouls, performance-enhancing drugs) and their impact on the safety and well-being of self and others.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Evaluate, revise, and continue to implement Personal Plan for Wellness to address the local culture/norm of safety and injury prevention to enhance personal and/or community well-being.

outcomes.statement: Promote sustainable well-being by planning for and engaging in movement activities, alone and with others, that enhance the health-related (i.e., cardiovascular endurance, flexibility, muscular endurance, muscular strength, and body composition) and skill-related (i.e., power, agility, speed, reaction time, balance, and co-ordination) components of fitness.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Engage in, document, and analyze fitness benefits and sustainability potential of participation in 30 minutes of daily moderate to vigorous physical activity outside of class time over a four-week period.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate opportunities (e.g. walking/running groups, recreation centres, green spaces, on-line opportunities) for engagement in movement activities for sustainable well-being at school, at home, and in the community.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Examine how technology (e.g., heart rate monitor, pedometer, fitness software, technological applications) may enhance and support one's health-related and skill-related components of fitness.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Create and justify the importance of the health-related and skill- related components of fitness (e.g., Is balance more important than muscular strength?).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Create and participate in a two-week cost-free FITT (i.e., Frequency, Intensity, Type of Activity, Time) plan that enhances all of the components of both health-related and skill-related fitness.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate and evaluate, through participation in, a student selected pre-made fitness work-out.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Analyze the potential for preferred movement activities and achieved engagement level in those activities that may promote sustainable well-being and lifelong involvement.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explain the direct correlation between committed engagement in cardiovascular endurance activities and calorie-burning potential.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Create and engage others in a fitness workout using items (e.g., towels, books, cans, rocks) and chores (e.g., sweeping, vacuuming, shoveling) and responsibilities (e.g., babysitting, walking pets) commonly found in and around the home and/community.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Examine factors (e.g., determinants of health, body composition, mental wellness, social wellness) that have an impact on one's commitment to achieving and maintaining recommended standards for health-related and skill-related components of fitness.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Evaluate fitness and activity guidelines and/or standards set by different agencies, organizations, or governments (including other countries) to determine suitability for self and community (e.g., Public Health Agency of Canada, ParticipACTION, Saskatchewan in motion, US Department of Health and Human Services, World Health Organization).

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Discuss why scientifically-based measures (e.g., skin-fold tests, BMI) used to determine body composition are not always accurate, effective, or complete indicators of physical fitness and level of well-being.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Examine the pressure and social implications placed on gender related to body composition and participation in movement activities.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Utilize the FITT (i.e., Frequency, Intensity, Type of activity, Time) principle and principles of training (i.e., overload, progressive resistance, specificity, use/disuse) in a plan for health-related and skill-related fitness.

indicators.label: o
indicators.text: Evaluate, revise, and continue to implement a Personal Plan for Wellness to include setting and achieving personal goals for health-related and skill-related fitness.

outcomes.statement:
Assess how relationships (e.g., with self, peers, family, teachers, teammates, opponents, coaches, employers) influence all dimensions of wellness.
Confrontation Model: Select a specific example that illustrates the behaviour/situation you want to change, describe your emotions re: behaviour/issue, clarify why this is important- what is at stake to gain/lose, identify your contribution to this problem, indicate your wish to resolve the issue, invite other(s) to respond. (Scott, 2002)

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Recognize that relationships are dynamic (i.e., variable) and change over time.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Ask and respond to important questions about relationships, such as: What matters most in relationships? Why is it important to step in or speak out in someone's defense? When is it important to keep silent? How do we maintain optimal wellness through our relationships with others? What is most effective for managing/ nurturing/embracing change in relationships?

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Analyze how relationships are developed and enhanced through an awareness of self, others, and by one's overall well-being.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Discuss and examine common challenges in relationships.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Determine own challenges in personal relationships.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate ways in which relationships are initiated, maintained, and terminated and the related consequences to overall well- being.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Analyze negative interactions that may result during competitive participation in movement activities (e.g., a parent/adult yelling at an official, a coach who does not give equal playing time).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Reflect on personal approaches to conflict and how these approaches enhance and/or impede wellness.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Discuss skills and behaviours that are effective in nurturing relationships and those that escalate conflict.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Evaluate and practise different ways to resolve a conflict including the "confrontation model".

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Examine the benefits (e.g., staying connected to a friend who has moved, enhanced opportunity to engage in social justice or political issues) and the harm (e.g., online bullying, inadequate sleep, scams) that may result from the use of social networking, online shopping, internet gambling, etc.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Examine legal rights and responsibilities concerning relationships and how these rights and responsibilities are established to support overall well-being.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Demonstrate and evaluate personal commitment to responsible social behaviour (Hellison, 2011) while participating in and analyzing movement activities.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Reflect on and respond to relationship questions (e.g., Why would someone establish a positive relationship with an opponent in the context of participation in a competitive movement activity? How do I safely end or get out of relationships that are unsafe? How do relationships impact/influence one's wellness?).

indicators.label: o
indicators.text: Evaluate, revise, and continue to implement a Personal Plan for Wellness to demonstrate decision making that enhances relationships and overall well-being.

outcomes.statement: Assess challenges related to community well-being and take action to address these challenges.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Reflect on past, present, and evolving wellness challenges (e.g., physical inactivity, sexual health issues, bullying, drinking and driving, gambling, transportation, unemployment, suicide) in the local community.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine local community norms and practices that affect the well- being of self, family, community, and the environment.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Develop and ask critical questions of particular local wellness challenges while respecting facts, knowledge, and social and cultural contexts.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Critique various points of view concerning community wellness to better understand the influence of underlying values or assumptions.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the complexities of wellness issues within one's community and investigate possible opportunities to address these issues.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Access resources (e.g., community, provincial, national) and agencies (e.g., Saskatchewan in motion, Public Health Agency of Canada) to support and address community wellness challenges.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Conclude that real-life challenges to well-being often have more than one solution.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Describe personal challenges concerning community well-being.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Investigate legislation (i.e., local, provincial, and national) that relates to particular community wellness issues.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Determine the intent of legislation (see indictor i) and question if the intention is realized in the local community.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Initiate, in a variety of ways, community awareness and opportunities to address wellness issues.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Evaluate, revise, and continue to implement a Personal Plan for Wellness to address self-selected community wellness challenges.

outcomes.statement:
Analyze, explain, and apply understandings, skills, tactics, and strategies that enhance confidence and competence in participating in recreational group/team movement activities through participation in various class-selected games from the following categories:
- Target games (e.g., curling)
- Net/Wall games (e.g., volleyball)
- Invasion/Territorial games (e.g., basketball, soccer, touch football, ultimate frisbee, lacrosse, double ball, street hockey)
- Striking/Fielding games (e.g., softball, slo-pitch, cricket).

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Co-construct and apply, as group/team, a list of criteria that exemplifies a recreational experience in a group/team movement activity and supports a positive experience for all participants.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Assess the sustainable wellness potential, for self and others, of participating in particular recreational group/team movement activities.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Reflect on and express personal thoughts on the potential positive and negative impacts of participation in recreational group/team movement activities on overall wellness.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Assess and explain personal level of confidence and competence in utilizing the required complex skills needed to participate in various recreational group/team movement activities.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Analyze group/team members' performance of complex skills, utilizing technology (e.g., video motion analysis of self and others, pedometers, technological applications) and other means (e.g., checklists, rubrics).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Develop and participate in practice opportunities that support all group/team members in enhanced utilization of complex skills.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Assess and explain/demonstrate personal understanding of tactics (e.g., what fake to use prior to shooting or passing) and strategies (e.g., using a zone or one-on-one defence) required for confident and competent participation in selected recreational group/team movement activities.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Locate, evaluate, and use resources (e.g., websites, people in the community, agencies in the province) to help support and build one's understanding of effective tactics and strategies to be used in selected team/group movement activities.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Support others in understanding and applying the tactics and strategies that enhance potential for positive participation in selected recreational group/team movement activities.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Co-develop and apply, group/team tactics and strategies to be used within the context of non-competitive participation in recreational group/team movement activities.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Analyze and discuss the transferable skills, tactics, and strategies to be used while participating in all selected recreational group/team movement activities.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Evaluate, revise, and continue to implement a Personal Plan for Wellness to include participation in recreational group/team movement activities that support sustainable wellness.

outcomes.statement: Make informed decisions regarding personal healthy eating practices based on connections to wellness.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Compare eating practices (e.g., number of meals, snacking habits, time of day/night, fluid consumption, kinds of foods) of the past to those of the present.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Predict and justify what healthy eating might mean in the future.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore some of the controversy that surrounds healthy eating practices and beliefs (e.g., nutrition supplements, digestive cleansing, mega vitamins, carbohydrate loading, vegetarianism, organic foods).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate what is known about healthy eating practices (i.e., for children, teens, adults, athletes, pregnant mothers) from a variety of evaluated sources.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine the various nutrients (e.g., protein, fibre, calcium, omega-3 fat, vitamins) that should be considered for optimal well-being.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Examine cultural eating practices and determine their cultural significance and contribution to optimal wellness.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine what is known about sustainable eating practices (e.g., growing your own food, supporting local, using leftovers) and determine possible changes to personal eating practices.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss food security and its impact on one's ability to make decisions about food practices.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Examine whether members of the community all have the same access to nutritious food, and determine how access influences wellness.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Examine and evaluate several different food guides or healthy eating recommendations related to personal eating practices.

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Design a one-week plan for weight maintenance that balances physical output (i.e., calories burned through metabolism and activity) and food intake (i.e., calories consumed through food and drink).

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Predict the long-term impact, on overall wellness, of consuming more/less calories than one burns over a long period of time.

indicators.label: m
indicators.text: Analyze nutritional factors (e.g., hydration, pre-activity meal, sustainable eating habits) that affect optimal performance for selected movement activities.

indicators.label: n
indicators.text: Evaluate, revise, and continue to implement a Personal Plan for Wellness to incorporate healthy eating practices that enhance personal wellness.

outcomes.statement: Investigate the connection to and importance of spirituality on wellness.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate various meanings of the concepts of spirit, soul, spiritual dimension, and spiritual development.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Examine diverse spiritual beliefs and traditions of individuals and cultures (including First Nations and Métis), past and present.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Analyze the relationships of vision, joy, struggle, and perseverance with regard to spiritual beliefs and practices.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine personal experience in relation to the larger questions of meaning (e.g., Who am I? What is human nature? Why do innocent people suffer?).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine how people have explored the larger questions of human existence (e.g., oral histories, literature, current events, celebrations, artwork) and represented own perspectives.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate the value of silence, stillness, solitude, and an inward focus on one's overall wellness.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Examine the role individual activities (e.g., cooking, travelling, dancing, running) may have in one's spirituality and wellness.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Reflect on the concept of "sacred" (e.g., family, body) and its role in wellness.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Determine how one is influenced by norms, trends, images, and values in various cultures, communities, and groups.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Evaluate, revise, and continue to implement a Personal Plan for Wellness to purposefully enhance the spiritual dimension of one's wellness.

outcomes.statement: Explore the cultural, physical, mental, emotional and spiritual benefits of land-based learning.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 1: Benefits of Land-based Learning (Core) · Suggested Time: 6-10 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the meaning of land-based learning and its effect on human interactions with the environment (e.g., respecting animals and taking only what is needed).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Explore the Indigenous cultural learning opportunities (e.g., petroglyphs, pictographs, rubbing stones, tipi rings and traditional hunting grounds) in land-based learning.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain the physical benefits of outdoor activities (e.g., improves overall well-being, increases vitamin D, lowers blood pressure and boosts immunity).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Investigate the mental benefits of being outside (e.g., helps prevent depression and reduces stress and anxiety).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Examine how time spent in nature contributes to managing emotions (e.g., reduces anger and promotes pleasure).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Discuss the spiritual benefits of spending time outdoors (e.g., connection to the land and sense of belonging).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Research the historical significance of the land upon which classroom excursions take place.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Maintain a journal (e.g., written, digital, photo journal or social media) to reflect on the cultural, physical, mental, emotional and spiritual benefits of outdoor experiences.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Explore outdoor pursuits that lead to personal growth and satisfaction.

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Identify how benefits of nature are expressed through art (e.g., drama, literature, photography and paintings).

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Reflect on the cultural, physical, mental, emotional and spiritual benefits of land-based learning through outdoor solitude practices (e.g., sit-spot, sense of solitude and solo-time).

outcomes.statement: Investigate the connection between “Leave No Trace” principles and traditional ways of sustainably living on the land.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 2A: Leave No Trace - Fundamentals (Core) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
b
indicators.text:
Discuss how the “Leave No Trace” principles align with traditional Indigenous practices, including the ethics of:
- conservation (i.e., not to take more than is needed); and,
- reciprocity (i.e., offer acts of thankfulness).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explain how pre-excursion planning minimizes resource damage.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe how to leave the environment cleaner than found, such as picking up own and others' litter, including biodegradable material (e.g., sunflower seeds).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Explore opportunities for certification in “Leave No Trace” training.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Investigate how “Leave No Trace” guidelines may be applied in different geographical locations depending on population.

outcomes.statement: Practise the “Leave No Trace” principles on outdoor excursions.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 2B: Leave No Trace - Application (Optional) · Suggested Time: 3-5 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 2A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the importance of planning and preparing in advance of excursions, including to ensure safety and minimize resource damage.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Compare the effects on the land of camping and traveling on and off durable surfaces.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text:
Demonstrate respect for the natural setting by:
- minimizing campsite alterations;
- avoiding damage to trees and plants; and,
- leaving natural objects where they are found.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text:
Explore options for proper disposal of human waste outdoors, such as:
- digging catholes;
- portable toilets; and,
- packing out waste (e.g., toilet paper and feminine hygiene products).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate minimal impact alternatives to cooking over a fire (e.g., envirostove, fire box and gas stove).

indicators.label: f
g
indicators.text: Demonstrate respect for wildlife by keeping distance and storing food securely.

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Discuss options for dealing with food waste (e.g., completely burning and packing out).

outcomes.statement: Explore general safety practices when engaging in wilderness activities.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 3A: Wilderness Safety - General (Core) · Suggested Time: 2-5 hours · Level: Introductory · Prerequisite: None

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the importance of establishing a trip plan and leaving it with someone before participating in a wilderness excursion.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Identify potential hazards unique to wilderness excursions.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Demonstrate safe practices (e.g., flagging, setting boundaries and carrying a whistle) when engaging in outdoor solitude.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Describe ways to reduce risk of personal injury (e.g., proper training, adhering to safety precautions and maintaining equipment) when participating in wilderness activities.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate provincial and federal health and safety rules and guidelines for specific wilderness activities (e.g., hunting, fishing, trapping and camping).

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Research opportunities for outdoor skill certification (e.g., Paddle Canada).

outcomes.statement: Explore basic first aid skills used to treat minor to severe injuries.
outcomes.printedWith: Module 3B: Wilderness Safety - First Aid (Optional) · Suggested Time: 4-20 hours · Level: Intermediate · Prerequisite: Module 3A

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the terms “first aid,” “first aider” and “Good Samaritan law.”

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Describe how to ensure the safety of the person providing first aid (e.g., gloves and scan the area).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify injuries common to an activity (e.g., head injuries while cycling) and steps taken to prevent them (e.g., wearing a helmet).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Define primary and secondary surveys in first aid.

indicators.label: e
f
indicators.text: Explain the additional risks of emergency situations that occur in the wilderness, such as lack of proximity to treatment and lack of sterilization.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Compare the items appropriate to include in a personal first aid kit (e.g., band-aids, personal medications and sunscreen) and a group first aid kit (e.g., medical gloves, gauze and bandages).

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Explore opportunities for, and benefits of, being certified in first aid.

outcomes.statement: Participate in a variety of outdoor activities.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the role of physical conditioning in safe and comfortable outdoor experiences.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Compare nutritional and hydration requirements when participating in light to heavy exercise.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Display basic swimming skills such as floating, treading water and kicking and stroking.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain the “Swim to Survive” standard of the Life Saving Society.

indicators.label: e

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Practise canoe strokes (e.g., forward and reverse, draw, pry, j-stroke or stern rudder, sweep and brace) for different purposes.

indicators.label: g

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Apply hiking skills (e.g., pacing, adjusting pack, stretching and resting) when hiking in various terrains, such as urban and wilderness treks.

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Demonstrate safe techniques in climbing activities (e.g., high ropes and wall climbing).

indicators.label: j
indicators.text: Experiment with different snowshoe skills (e.g., step and kick turns, striding, stamping and edging).

indicators.label: k
indicators.text: Practise cross-country ski techniques (e.g., diagonal stride on flat ground, herringbone uphill and snowplough downhill) for different purposes.

indicators.label: l
indicators.text: Engage in outdoor evening activities such as star gazing, identifying moon phases and night hiking.

outcomes.statement: Explore basic and traditional navigational skills.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss Indigenous navigational skills and tools with an Elder or Knowledge Keeper.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research different types of navigation techniques (e.g., natural, celestial, compass and technological).

indicators.label: c
d
indicators.text: Travel on a bearing without a map.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Determine individual pace length and use it to measure distances.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Explain the basic functionality of a Global Positioning System (GPS).

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Use a GPS to navigate a given route and arrive at a destination (e.g., geocaching).

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Orient and interpret a map using the legend and topographical lines of elevation.

indicators.label: b

indicators.label: c

indicators.label: d

indicators.label: e

indicators.label: g

indicators.label: h
indicators.text: Plan a route for others to follow using waypoints.

indicators.label: i

indicators.label: j

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate basic knot-tying skills.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explore the materials (e.g., plant fibres and animal sources) used to make traditional Indigenous cordage.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Review the properties of familiar knots (e.g., tying shoes).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Identify the basic families of knots (e.g., loops, hitches, bends and lashings).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain the properties of an effective knot (e.g., serves the purpose, easy to tie and easy to untie).

indicators.label: e

indicators.text: Discuss the importance of strong cordage and efficient knot skills in Indigenous ways of living off the land.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Apply knot-tying skills to related outdoor skills, such as tying up tarp shelters, tying fishing knots (e.g., fisherman's knot and palomar knot) and tying nets.

indicators.label: c
d
indicators.text: Explain the factors to consider in rope making (e.g., strength and breaking point).

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate the usefulness of paracord in bushcraft survival.

indicators.label: f
indicators.text: Experiment with the application of paracord in paracord crafts (e.g., lanyards and bracelets).

outcomes.statement: Explore traditional and contemporary shelters.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Discuss the cultural and traditional stories and teachings related to Indigenous shelters with an Elder or Knowledge Keeper.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Research traditional Indigenous shelters (e.g., tipi) and their purpose (e.g., housing, sweat and smudge).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore opportunities to participate in a tipi-raising.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Explain the significance of the parts (e.g., bottom, fire, flaps and poles) of a tipi.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Investigate the benefits and drawbacks of different styles of tents.

indicators.label: f
g
indicators.text: Investigate how to erect a tent and secure it using pegs and guy lines.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Demonstrate mindfulness (e.g., take only what is needed) and gratitude (e.g., offering tobacco) when harvesting materials for shelters.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Explore natural environmental features that provide shelter from the elements, such as depressions in the ground, holes from tree roots and lowhanging branches.

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Examine factors that affect shelter choice (e.g., number of people requiring shelter, available materials and their cost, weather and animals).

indicators.label: e
f
g

outcomes.statement: Demonstrate safe knife skills.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate materials (e.g., stone and bone) used by Indigenous people to create traditional knives.

indicators.label: b
c
indicators.text: Compare types of knives for safety features (e.g., locked and fixed blade).

indicators.label: d
indicators.text: Identify parts of knives, including the spine, blade and finger guard.

indicators.label: e
indicators.text: Discuss the use and functionality of different types of knives (e.g., bush, kitchen, hunting and filleting).

g

indicators.text: Explain how to identify a serviceable knife blade (e.g., sharp or dull).

indicators.label: i
indicators.text: Practise safe knife skills with basic knife craft projects (e.g., whimmy diddle, curl sticks and carving wood).

outcomes.statement: Apply safe, advanced knife skills for a variety of purposes.

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Explain the safety benefits of maintaining a sharp knife.

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Practise different knife sharpening techniques (e.g., strop, honing oil and sharpening board).

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Apply safe knife care techniques (e.g., drying and oiling) to maintain knives.

indicators.label: d
e
f
indicators.text: Craft a sharpening board.

indicators.label: g
indicators.text: Explore opportunities and skills required for knife safety certification (e.g., Scouts Canada).

indicators.label: b
indicators.text: Investigate the significance of fire in other cultures.

indicators.label: c
indicators.text: Demonstrate respect for the natural environment by conserving fuel and by practicing an act of mindfulness when harvesting material to burn.

e

indicators.label: g
h

indicators.text: Demonstrate how to determine when a fire is fully extinguished.

c

indicators.label: a
indicators.text: Investigate materials (e.g., stones, wood from local trees, and sinew and bone from animals) used to make traditional Indigenous bows and arrows.
